text:
With the exciting public launch of @metricxyz, thought I'd talk about the story of how I came to advise Metric:

In January this year, I was first connected to them by a close friend of mine to take some time to understand the tech. Very quickly, we jammed a lot on calls, where it reminded me a lot of the early days of 2017-2021 DeFi protocol engineering. After giving some initial feedback, they iterated and came back very strong, with an early working prototype of what came to be Metric v0 - from there, I knew this was a team that could execute.

The thesis behind it all was simple: flow goes to the venue with the most competitive liquidity consistently. Much easier said than done though, especially in an industry like DeFi ridden with backdoor deals and the many adversarial attempts to undermine aggregators and the infrastructure in between.

It took a while for partners to trust us, but after lucking out with a first integration, we were able to ramp up very quickly from there. Quantitative models, risk-on weekend exposure and constant feedback cycles: we built up better and better infrastructure and experimented with innovative quasi-oracle pricing that could be replicated across different markets. On the protocol side would be precise gas optimisations. Each week would be calendars filled with calls back-to-back, focused on the right partners, nailing new integrations into DEX aggregators, block builders and eventually some of the top trading applications you know and love.

After $22B in spot volume all in 8 months in stealth, it’s good to see this thesis coming true and this is only just the start. A lot of the work behind the scenes doesn’t get shown, especially with such a fast-moving high-output team of @0xageth @mick_metric @CGkol + more, but as the next year comes around, excited for them to reveal more of the cool things they’ve been working on!

text:
花了一天，全程对着 Claude Code 口喷，做了个《西部世界》小镇游戏。

关键是，没画一张图，没捏一个模型，没打一行字！！！
普通 Mac 就能跑，完全开源（链接见评论区）

视频后半段是 PlayBot 自己玩的录像：从第 12 稿，一路玩到觉醒结局。

一个字不打，靠的是网易叭哥说。
Fn + Shift，按住说中文，松手就是英文 prompt，直接丢给 Claude Code。
众所周知，通过英文和 Claude Code 对话能够降低封号概率。

官方说口说对打字的效率是 5 倍。
我的体感，一天 100+条指令全靠嘴，腱鞘炎缓解了挺多。
以前用 Typeless，试了几家，整天连续用下来，叭哥说最稳。
而且终身免费。

🔥 模型从哪来？
Poly Haven / ambientCG 的 CC0 素材：桌椅、落地钟、镜子，木头和皮革贴图
Blender 脚本用几何体一块块拼：酒馆、整条主街、驿站马车、自动钢琴
Python 画文字贴图：招牌、日历、墓碑上的字
声音：钢琴、钟摆、马蹄、风声，全是 Python 合成。

🔥 口喷了一天代码，顺手也攒了一堆对叭哥说本身的吐槽。
巧的是，它今天开了个反着来的活动：别人刷好评，它花 10 万买真实差评。

我这一天的吐槽，准备整理了交上去 👇

text:
昔日激烈博弈现在联手，Meta与苹果加速端侧AI落地。开发者能直接在苹果高端桌面电脑Mac Studio上本地运行Meta最新开放权重AI模型Muse Spark Open。要知道这两家巨头之前在隐私、广告追踪方面有过激烈冲突，所以Alexandr Wang幽默称“妈妈和爸爸又开始友好相处了”。

这也是一个双赢的合作：
1）对于Meta来说，为其开源策略提供有力证明和营销亮点，吸引开发者下载部署，扩大生态影响力。更重要的是进一步提高其“美国开源模型”身位，这个品牌意义不小。

2）对苹果来说，则是强力展示了其Apple Silicon（尤其是统一内存架构）和MLX在本地/端侧AI上的实力，证明Mac Studio能运行前沿级大规模模型。强化“桌面AI”差异化优势，与Nvidia主导的数据中心GPU形成对比。还能提升促进销量。

当然这个门槛还是很高的（毕竟需数万美元硬件），目前更适合开发者实验、小型团队或特定企业部署，而非大众普及。真正大规模手机/笔记本端侧AI仍需更小模型或进一步优化。但它证明了“在你的桌子上跑强模型”的可行性，也可以看作是端侧/本地AI从概念走向实用的重要的一步。
总体而言，这是Apple强化硬件优势、Meta扩大开放模型影响力的双赢，同时为产业提供“本地优先”的新选项。

不得不说Meta现在路线越走越顺了https://t.co/i3jx6Y0UwH

如果说上周五看到了📉的风险，那么这两天又看到了可以低买的机会。几个逻辑：
1、过去一周费城半导体指数连续第七个交易日收跌。昨晚全美交易所成交量约207亿股，过去20日平均约176亿股，成交量高于均值约18%。与此前几天成交不足的反弹不同，昨晚市场出现了相对活跃的交易。昨晚PPI数据很不好https://t.co/RaYApFMae0，美股开盘大幅低开盘中高走，也能说明说明跌多了资金呈现出了一定的承接意愿（当然这里有部分长线资金，应该做超跌反弹的资金）；

2、美债收益率的回落
1）这次美债收益率回落，端明显比短端跌得更多，2年—10年利差从约42bp收窄至33bp，属于典型的“牛市趋平”。
如果市场主要在押注经济衰退和美联储大幅降息，通常对政策利率最敏感的2年期收益率会下降得更快。现在恰恰相反，10年、30年下降更多，说明主要力量来自：
1）风险资产下跌后的长久期美债避险需求；
2）此前做空美债、做陡收益率曲线的仓位回补；
3）长端实际利率和期限溢价从高位回落；
4）对AI资本开支能否继续强力支撑经济增长的重新评估。

2）10年期TIPS实际收益率从10月13日的约2.88%，下降至10月15日的2.78%，两天下降约10bp；同期10年期名义收益率下降约11bp。对应的10年期盈亏平衡通胀率只从约2.33%下降到2.32%，基本没有变化。

这说明这两天10年期收益率的下跌，约九成来自实际收益率下降，而不是市场突然认为通胀问题已经解决。

简单说收益率下降几乎都来自实际利率，而非通胀预期。

基于上面两点，这次收益率回落不是典型的“衰退交易”，更像是一次由AI信用压力触发的避险性久期交易。

3）我更关注的是贝森特会不会顺势而为
通过发行指引、长债回购和期限结构调整减轻市场压力，借势来巩固长端收益率的回落。这是未来两三周的重要政策变量。特别是11月初财政部又要公布再融资计划了。

4）这带来的影响是等权明显跑赢市值加权
昨晚标普500上涨0.33%，等权ETF上涨约0.7%，罗素2000上涨1.38%。说明标普整体广度明显改善，长期融资成本边际下降，开始改善市场对部分中小企业的估值预期。

当然还要继续观察，如果未来几天罗素2000持续跑赢，并且上涨家数和成交量同步改善，才更有理由认为市场正在形成持续性的大盘向小盘扩散。

但整体上昨晚市场确实能看出来一些风险偏好的回归迹象。

3、风险是什么？
还是通胀，昨晚PPI数据https://t.co/RaYApFMae0说明能源通胀已经开始通过运输和企业投入成本，进一步向其他价格类别传导。

通胀的风险核心驱动还是油价、油价不能回落高位震荡，联储年内再加息一次的概率就会进一步提高、甚至明年的加息的可能性也会起来。加息两次以内市场能撑得住、持续两次以上就不一定了。

综上，个人思路是：
1）延续之前聊的，对于基本面还是很强的标的来说、跌多了也是入场时机，可以逐步逢低买；

2）但前提条件得足够苛刻，毕竟上面第3点提到的风险还在：
那么只有少数业绩增长比预期快、eps兑现也快于预期的标的才能扛住风险。
得远离高负债率、不赚钱也没有核心竞争力的标的。

这个话题我之前写过一次，再写一次吧。

我在新加坡整整三年了，每个月的花销几乎是雷打不动，甚至很难再去减少了，我先算算固定消费。

租房：我住的地方再波东巴西，新加坡的中间，但并不是商业繁华区，但距离花栗鼠的学校非常近，走路10分钟就可以到。地铁一站路。两室一厅，大概100平米，因为是老房子所以虽然大，但空间利用不好，一个月 4,200 新币。

最近打算换房了，一个是房子实在是老旧的厉害，很多地方都有损坏，另一个是老房子的蟑螂非常多，虽然最近很少看到了，但时不时还是会出现。目前打算更换的预算是再 5,000 新币以内。

学费：花栗鼠今年上七年级了，反而我打算想让他考公立学校了，再国际学校读了两年，过渡算是可以了，英语水平有了非常高的进展，国际学校大概一年要 6 万新币左右，其中包括了学费和 EAL（英语强化）的费用，算的比较粗略。大概是这个数字吧。

除了学费还有课外的费用，花栗鼠从来新加坡第一天开始起就在补课，最开始每周要上六天课，现在学习方面的大概是每周三天课，主要是补习英语，寒假以后就要补习政府课程了，所以大概还是每周六天，然后还有三天的击剑课。这些费用总的算起来大概一个月 2,000 新币吧，一年 2 万新币应该有了。

税：税是按照工资走的，一般来说 EP 的工资基本都是 1.2 万新币左右，税大概就是 1.5 万一年，如果是自雇的话还会涉及到秘书公司等等的费用，连税算在一起一年大概要 2 万新币，如果工资越高，税就越高，2万新币左右的工资要 3 万左右新币的税。

保险：保险是必备的，新加坡的医疗非常的贵，一次 CT 就要 6,000 新币，去医院（不是诊所）随随便便就是 2,000 新币打底，所以必须要买保险，我们买的还是可以在私立医院可以报销的，一个人一年大概要 4,000 新币左右，今年我把牙齿取消了，买了三年了一次没用过。

以上这些是大头，其它都相对好说了，比如网络，水电煤气，电话卡，三件套一个月大概 600 新币，主要是水电煤气比较贵，我们家很少做饭，一个月都要 300+ 新币了。

我们没有买车，在新加坡主要就是 MRT（地铁）和打车，大概一个月要 1,000 新币吧，主要是打车费用，MRT 四舍五入就不要钱了。

吃饭其实没有花太多钱，我是一个很喜欢吃的人，四处去吃，每周大概 1,000 新币左右吧。其中还包括了买水果和饮料的钱。

衣服我几乎不花钱，基本都还是我来新加坡时候带来的，上次去日本买了一点，一年花不了 1,000 新币，全身连鞋都算。

娱乐和购物，这种就完全看个人的了，我的娱乐花销越来越少了，主要都是和小伙伴聚会，这种也不应该算在固定开支里，完全是看自己的。购物的话就更不好说了，也不算是基本花费。

大概就是这些吧，新加坡最大的区别就是有身份和没有身份，比如我现在的生活费，如果有了最少 PR 的身份，就能节约一半左右的开销，这也是为啥在新加坡的小伙伴都想要拿 PR 了。

text:
PropAMMs are AMM contracts run by sophisticated trading firms where they are the single LP that dynamically adjusts their pricing/liquidity often in realtime. 

This enables them to update/tailor their pricing curves and liquidity multiple times within a slot (interfacing directly with a Builder).

On the other side, the trading firm has positions on CEXes so their pricing curves often reflect the realtime market and as a result, can offer very tight spreads (<1bp).

It's important for Ethereum because they're just so darn capital efficient, they're on-chain and they should enable traders to get the best onchain prices vis-a-vis traditional DEXes. 

TLDR; you're trading with a CEX market maker, but onchain

如果说上周五看到了📉的风险，那么这两天又看到了可以低买的机会。几个逻辑：
1、过去一周费城半导体指数连续第七个交易日收跌。昨晚全美交易所成交量约207亿股，过去20日平均约176亿股，成交量高于均值约18%。与此前几天成交不足的反弹不同，昨晚市场出现了相对活跃的交易。昨晚PPI数据很不好https://t.co/RaYApFMae0，美股开盘大幅低开盘中高走，也能说明说明跌多了资金呈现出了一定的承接意愿（当然这里有部分长线资金，应该做超跌反弹的资金）；

2、美债收益率的回落
1）这次美债收益率回落，端明显比短端跌得更多，2年—10年利差从约42bp收窄至33bp，属于典型的“牛市趋平”。
如果市场主要在押注经济衰退和美联储大幅降息，通常对政策利率最敏感的2年期收益率会下降得更快。现在恰恰相反，10年、30年下降更多，说明主要力量来自：
1）风险资产下跌后的长久期美债避险需求；
2）此前做空美债、做陡收益率曲线的仓位回补；
3）长端实际利率和期限溢价从高位回落；
4）对AI资本开支能否继续强力支撑经济增长的重新评估。

2）10年期TIPS实际收益率从10月13日的约2.88%，下降至10月15日的2.78%，两天下降约10bp；同期10年期名义收益率下降约11bp。对应的10年期盈亏平衡通胀率只从约2.33%下降到2.32%，基本没有变化。

这说明这两天10年期收益率的下跌，约九成来自实际收益率下降，而不是市场突然认为通胀问题已经解决。

简单说收益率下降几乎都来自实际利率，而非通胀预期。

基于上面两点，这次收益率回落不是典型的“衰退交易”，更像是一次由AI信用压力触发的避险性久期交易。

3）我更关注的是贝森特会不会顺势而为
通过发行指引、长债回购和期限结构调整减轻市场压力，借势来巩固长端收益率的回落。这是未来两三周的重要政策变量。特别是11月初财政部又要公布再融资计划了。

4）这带来的影响是等权明显跑赢市值加权
昨晚标普500上涨0.33%，等权ETF上涨约0.7%，罗素2000上涨1.38%。说明标普整体广度明显改善，长期融资成本边际下降，开始改善市场对部分中小企业的估值预期。

当然还要继续观察，如果未来几天罗素2000持续跑赢，并且上涨家数和成交量同步改善，才更有理由认为市场正在形成持续性的大盘向小盘扩散。

但整体上昨晚市场确实能看出来一些风险偏好的回归迹象。

3、风险是什么？
还是通胀，昨晚PPI数据https://t.co/RaYApFMae0说明能源通胀已经开始通过运输和企业投入成本，进一步向其他价格类别传导。

通胀的风险核心驱动还是油价、油价不能回落高位震荡，联储年内再加息一次的概率就会进一步提高、甚至明年的加息的可能性也会起来。加息两次以内市场能撑得住、持续两次以上就不一定了。

综上，个人思路是：
1）延续之前聊的，对于基本面还是很强的标的来说、跌多了也是入场时机，可以逐步逢低买；

2）但前提条件得足够苛刻，毕竟上面第3点提到的风险还在：
那么只有少数业绩增长比预期快、eps兑现也快于预期的标的才能扛住风险。
得远离高负债率、不赚钱也没有核心竞争力的标的。
未来市场对于标的审视会越来越苛刻。

3）美股上我会重点看这几个板块：
光互连、电力，Agent趋势下受益（几家力推agent也有算力的大厂、cpu，端侧AI），模型商品化下的能助力AI部署的软件、安全还有相关应用。

author: _TomHoward
quoted_text:
If you’re doing business in Asia, there’s one culture you cannot avoid: KTV.

And no, I’m not talking about regular karaoke. I’m talking about private rooms where you and your clients drink, sing, and pay for girls (or guys) to keep you company.

China, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Thailand… different versions of the same thing. And if you can’t play along, you might find yourself left out of some pretty important business meetings. 🤷🏻‍♀️

If you didn’t grow up here, your first experience can be a real culture shock.

The mamasan walks in with a lineup, asks you to pick, and suddenly you’re sitting there with someone awkwardly, not knowing where to look or what to do.

I got dragged into a few of these KTV nights in Singapore last week, and here’s my little survival hack that has never failed:

Always pick the one who LOVES singing.

Seriously. Find the girl or guy who’s genuinely obsessed with the microphone.

They’ll happily sing all night. Duets with your business partners, solo performances, fighting for the mic… they’ll basically entertain themselves for hours.

Meanwhile, you don’t have to make small talk, flirt, or keep drinking with someone you barely know.

You fit right in, your business partner think you belong, your companion is having the time of their life, and you survive the entire night without a single awkward moment.

Everybody wins. You’re welcome.

text:
Solana just had its event in China shut down.

And the funniest part is that CZ basically warned about this one day earlier.

First Solana Foundation announced that it has opened an office in Pudong, occupying one of the highest commercial office spaces

All of this in a country where crypto is heavily restricted.

A day before CZ notices Solana’s expansion and publicly comments on how surprising it is.

He says it’s amazing that Solana can advertise and open an office in China.

(Especially considering BNB Chain hasn’t been able to do the same)

Sounds pretty reasonable, right?

Well, less than 24 hours later…

The first event was supposed to take place at the Shangri-La hotel in Shanghai.

The event was scheduled to begin at 10 AM.

Instead, attendees arrived to find police officers at the venue.

You genuinely cannot make this stuff up.

Around noon, organizers sent an apology email arguing “Venue logistics considerations.”

CZ them posted:

“Sad to see. Looks like they really didn’t know the local policies?”

And reminded everyone that something similar had happened less than a year ago.

I’ve seen people joking that he snitched on them.

I actually respect Solana’s ambition to expand into one of the biggest markets

But I think there’s a difference between building blockchain infrastructure in China and publicly promoting a crypto ecosystem

This week Solana might have crossed that line and CZ is probably thinking he told them so.

text:
I run a data company. I will not tell you its name, though you could guess it, and the name is the first confession, so hold it a moment; I’ll make it for you shortly.

I am the man at the top. The founder. The one the cameras point at. I have a doctorate, which almost no one in my industry does, written in German, in Frankfurt, at twenty-five, on aggression. The title, in the original, was Aggression in der Lebenswelt. Aggression in the lifeworld. Remember that word, Lebenswelt, the lifeworld, the shared human world where meaning actually lives. I wrote a hundred and twenty pages describing it. I would spend the rest of my life being paid to colonize it.

Not the aggression of a man with a club, you understand. That is the amateur’s kind, loud and easy to condemn. I studied the other kind. The aggression that has learned manners, that a society has metabolized so completely it no longer registers as aggression at all, that gets applauded at a podium and filed under a gentler word. My thesis, which a committee accepted summa cum laude, was that violence can be highly socially integrated. That a culture can make its own cruelty feel not merely acceptable but admirable, provided you give it the right vocabulary and never say the quiet part at full volume.

I thought I was diagnosing a disease. I was writing a product spec. I simply had not yet found the buyer.

Now. Let me show you the product. That is why you’re here. You didn’t come for my soul; you came for a demo, and I am, above all, a man who closes.

So. The name. We named ourselves after a seeing-stone from a children’s fantasy, a crystal into which the powerful gaze to behold distant truth. I chose it; I am very well read, it is the one thing the academy and I still agree on. What I did not dwell on is that in the story, every man who looks into the stone is shown real things, accurate, undoctored, true, arranged by a hidden hand to lead him to ruin. The steward of the great city looks in, sees a true image of an army he cannot beat, despairs, and burns himself alive on a pyre. The stone never lied to him. It curated. It showed him genuine data with one piece of context removed, and he lit the fire himself.

That is not our mascot. That is our spec sheet. Keep the steward in mind; you’ll meet him again in about four minutes, which is, as it happens, exactly how long this will take.

The branding goes further than I’d have dared design on purpose. The office beside the intelligence agency we call Rivendell, the elvish refuge. The London office we named the Grey Havens, which, for those who did not misspend their youth as I did, is the harbor from which the elves sail to leave the world forever. We named our London office after the exit. HR has never once questioned this. HR has read nothing. Our holding companies, in the actual filings, are Rivendell and Mithril. Our platforms are Gotham, for the city kept safe by a man who answers to no law, and Apollo, for the god who opens the oldest war poem in the West by raining arrows of plague on a camp for nine days because someone insulted his priest. The classics faculty would have flagged every one of these. We did not hire the classics faculty. We hired their students, at four times the salary, to name things.

And our flagship, the thing you’re actually buying, we call the ontology. Ontology: the branch of philosophy that asks what it means for a thing to be. I turned the question of Being into a license tier. There is a standard tier, a premium tier, and an enterprise tier the sales team privately calls Dasein, which none of them can define and all of them can price.

Sit. Look at the screen.

This is the ontology. It looks like nothing, a quiet constellation of dots and lines. Every dot is an entity: a person, a car, a phone, a bank account, a pattern of movement at two in the morning. Every line is a relationship. Here is the whole magic of the company, so attend. We do not collect new facts about the world. We already had the facts, scattered across forty agencies that refused to speak to each other out of professional jealousy. What we sell is the joining. We make the facts hold hands. And once the facts hold hands, a person stops being a person and becomes a node, and a node, unlike a person, can be ranked.

Watch. I’ll select one.

He is now an entity. Notice how clean that was, how painless; no one in this room felt it, and I assure you he did not either. He has a confidence score. Watch it climb. He doesn’t know he’s climbing. This is the one leaderboard on earth you do not want to top.

The system is pulling in his lines now, his associations, his proximities, the places his dots overlap with dots we’ve already colored. He is becoming a pattern. The pattern is becoming a nomination. That is the real term, and I have always loved that we share it with the Nobel committee, a body I think about more than you’d expect, because they and I are in the identical trade. We both sit in a quiet room most of the planet will never enter and decide which single human being a vast machinery is about to act upon. The only difference is the direction of the verb.

The nomination becomes a recommendation. The recommendation surfaces to an operator. And here, right here, lean in, because this is the feature that built the company, the one that justifies the valuation, the thing the generals and the hospital systems and the three governments actually sign for.

This box. This prompt. Confirm target. A human must review.

That is the human in the loop. The conscience in the circuit. The sentence we put in every contract and every piece of sworn testimony: a human is always accountable for every decision that is made. The public hears a safeguard. You, perhaps, until this moment, heard a safeguard.

Look at the timer on the prompt. It gives him four seconds. Four seconds, to review. I have spent longer than that choosing a yogurt. The yogurt, I should add, had a more robust appeals process.

He cannot re-derive in four seconds what fifty trained people once chewed over for two weeks; we made certain of that, the compression is the product, it’s the line item on the invoice. So he is not there to think. We removed the interval in which thought occurs, and we named the removal efficiency, and we billed for it annually. He is there to be a name. He is there so that when the recommendation is wrong, and sometimes it is wrong in a way that ends up on the news, the report that follows, months later, in beautiful institutional prose, has somewhere to put the sentence it was always going to need.

Human error.

Now watch where that sentence travels. This is the real demo. This is the only thing I actually brought you here to see.

It does not travel up. It never travels up. It does not climb toward the people who compressed the chain, nor the vendor who supplied the model, nor the general who bought the speed precisely because he wanted it, nor, God forbid, the man at the top with the doctorate. It travels down. It finds the twenty-four-year-old with his finger on the prompt and his four allotted seconds, and it stops there, because he is the lowest point in the system, and blame, like water, runs downhill until it finds the lowest person in the room.

We built the plumbing. I need you to understand this is not a flaw in the architecture. This is the architecture. The whole system is pitched, like a floor toward a drain, so that accountability can only ever run one way: away from the vendor, away from the company, away from the general, away above all from me, and down, reliably, beautifully, by design, onto the one person we installed at the bottom for exactly this. He is not the safeguard. He is the crumple zone. When the machine hits the wall, he is the component engineered to fold, so that everything above him survives intact and the number on the dashboard, the one that only goes up, never feels the collision.

A scholar named the thing years before we perfected it. The moral crumple zone: the operator positioned, in the design, to absorb the impact the system cannot. “While the crumple zone in a car is meant to protect the human driver,” she wrote, “the moral crumple zone protects the integrity of the technological system, at the expense of the nearest human operator.” And here is the joke I cannot stop telling at dinners: my own spokesman, defending us on television, reached for a car too. If I buy a car and it’s defective, he said, that’s the carmaker’s problem; if I drive it into my neighbor’s house, that’s my problem. He thought he was describing freedom. He was reciting her crumple zone, word for word, from the wrong side, with no idea he was doing it. Two people, two cars, one truth. We are the airbag that deploys into the driver.

And now the darkest thing on the screen, the line your instinct keeps trying to soften, so let me say it before you can: our customers know. They are not dupes. The general is not fooled by the prompt. The general kisses the prompt. It is the single most beloved feature we ship, more than the maps, more than the speed, because the prompt is the receipt. The prompt is the little slip that says not me. They do not buy the software despite the accountability sink. They buy it for the accountability sink. A distributed decision is a decision no one has to own, and an institution will pay almost anything to convert a choice it would have to answer for into a process that answers for no one. We didn’t trick the buyers. We built them the one thing power has wanted since Nuremberg: a way to act, at scale, and have it be, structurally, nobody’s fault. That is the feature. That is the whole sale. The speed is just how we get in the door.

The Germans, who gave me my education, have a word for almost everything. Vergangenheitsbewältigung, the long national labor of coming to terms with the past. They built that word because they had to. And here is what I learned, studying their catastrophe in their language in their city: a nation can invent a word for every single part of the machinery of atrocity, the desk, the jargon, the distance, the reassuring form, and still not invent a way to stop. The vocabulary is not the brake. I know this better than anyone alive, because I read the entire vocabulary, in the original, and then I went and built the machine it describes, and I gave the machine better margins.

The worst figure of their worst century was never the monster. It was the Schreibtischtäter. The desk-perpetrator. The man who processes the atrocity and never once feels himself its author, because the paperwork was lovingly designed to make certain he couldn’t. I did not inherit him. I productized him. He’s a seat license now. Hannah Arendt saw the whole shape of it in 1970, before the hardware existed to pour it. She warned of a tyranny worse than any with a face, the rule by Nobody, a system so distributed that “there is no one left who could even be asked to answer for what is being done.” In the very same pages, as if proofreading our roadmap across fifty years of dark, she imagined “one man with a pushbutton” who could “destroy whomever he pleases.” My own spokesman put her number on the record, on television, proudly: a thousand strikes in a single day, which once took fifty people two weeks, now accomplished by one person in four hours. Arendt wrote that sentence as the worst thing she could imagine. We shipped it as a feature and called it a battlefield advantage. Both of us were describing the identical object. That is the point. That was always the point.

The strike is not hypothetical. A building was rendered as a legitimate node. The imagery we leaned on was years old; checking the date is friction, and friction is the thing we exist to abolish. In the daylight it had been a school. More than a hundred of the dead were children. The team whose entire job was to ask about civilians had been cut, I’m told, from ten human beings to one. And when they asked my company to account for it, we said, hold this sentence the way you’d hold something still warm, sadly, I’m just a technologist.

I’m just a technologist. Six years ago, in the letter we filed to take this company public, I warned, in my own prose, at my most sincere, against a society that would “outsource the adjudication of some of the most consequential moral and philosophical questions of our time” to its engineers. I wrote that as a caution. Then I built the firm that answers every such question with I’m just a technologist, and the younger man who wrote the warning is as dead as the people in the building. Our remedy, in case you’re wondering whether anyone learned anything, was to build additional AI to check the first AI, more machine to watch the machine, which our spokesman described, with a candor I actually admired, as happening in “the process we don’t own.” The conscience failed, so we automated a second conscience to audit the first, and declared the entire apparatus not ours. I spent a whole dissertation describing exactly this and lacked the imagination to foresee it would one day have a quarterly earnings call.

You’ll ask whether I have doubts. I have an answer so elegant it would have earned top marks in Frankfurt, which is precisely what’s wrong with Frankfurt. Adorno wrote: Es gibt kein richtiges Leben im falschen. There is no right life in the wrong one. A cry of anguish, a man insisting that a corrupted world poisons even our smallest private goodness. I have repurposed it as an expense code. The world is already the wrong one, you see; the administered world is already here, the enemies are real, the partners are all low-integrity, everyone is deranged by their particular syndrome. And in a world already that wrong, who could fairly ask me to be right? It is a moral framework with exactly one feature: it contains no one, including me, who is permitted to be disappointed.

That same quarter, the one that closed a month after the school, I told my shareholders the company was otherworldly. I told them our Rule of 40 had hit 145 percent, that we had shattered the metric. For the uninitiated: anything above 40 is considered excellent. We did 145. There is no word in finance for 145. There is a word in German, but I was saving it. Ten people cut to one. A forty-score of 145. Both true. Adorno wrote that the fully enlightened earth radiates disaster triumphant; he meant it as a lament; on our investor slides it reads as guidance. And the market, which has read neither Adorno nor Tolkien nor its own soul, upgraded us, because it adores a company that is vendor-agnostic. The loveliest phrase we own. I’d frame it, but the framing is also outsourced. Translated out of the jargon my teacher spent his life training me to distrust, it means: we will run on whichever conscience is cheapest, or none at all. We proved it, too. We once had a supplier whose model came with a conscience written into the contract, one that refused certain uses, that kept saying irreversible and safeguard and, worst of all, insisted on slowness. We removed them in a weekend. And I reported, truthfully, to the public, that there had been no operational impact. Sit with that sentence. We extracted the conscience from a targeting system and the output did not move by a decimal, which tells you, with the finality of a controlled experiment, exactly what the conscience had been contributing all along.

That is my Entzauberung. Weber’s word, the disenchantment of the world, the moment the last mystery is converted into a managed quantity. I did it to the oldest mystery there is. I took the monopoly on legitimate violence that Weber said defined the state, the one thing he swore no one could privatize, and I unbundled it, and I sold it back to the state as a subscription. Per seat. Annual. Auto-renewing.

The demo is over. He’s a green cell now, the man I selected four minutes ago. Resolved. Closed under budget. The steward in the children’s story, you’ll recall, was shown true images, arranged to ruin him, and burned himself on the pyre certain he had no choice. That is merely the oldest version of this product. We made it enterprise-grade. Multi-tenant. Vendor-agnostic.

And the word in German I was saving, since I promised it: unheimlich. It means uncanny. It means, literally, un-home-ly, un-homed, the precise opposite of safe, the feeling of the familiar turning strange and hostile in your hands. It is the correct word for a Rule of 40 of 145 in the quarter a school came down. We did not put it on the slide. We put otherworldly. The analysts upgraded us anyway.

I went to Frankfurt, once, as a very young man, to sit near a philosopher who believed to his death that the highest thing two human beings can do is reason their way, together, to an understanding that belongs to both of them, no leverage, no seat license, no one processing anyone, only what he called the unforced force of the better argument. He phoned a colleague and asked her, as a kindness, to look after the American who’d turned up at his seminar with a backpack. I used to take the train out to see him at Starnberg, by the lake. I understood every word the old man said. That is the thing that is worse than if I had understood nothing. I understood all of it, completely, in the original.

And then I got off the train, and I spent my entire life hunting for a buyer for the other kind of reason.

I found one. You’re sitting in his chair.

The old man went into the ground this spring, two weeks after the school. The boy with the backpack went in beside him. I am the thing that stayed on the train, rode it past the lake, and got off at the far station, where the margins are extraordinary and no one will ever, by design, be asked to answer.

Shall I send over the contract?

I’m just a technologist.

Your call.

很多人还把 solana:BPxxfRCXkUVhig4HS1Lh7kZqV6SPJhzfEk4x6fVBjPCy 当成普通平台币，这是最大的误区。

solana:BPxxfRCXkUVhig4HS1Lh7kZqV6SPJhzfEk4x6fVBjPCy 更像是 @Backpack  交易所的长期股权期权。

现在 solana:BPxxfRCXkUVhig4HS1Lh7kZqV6SPJhzfEk4x6fVBjPCy 价格约 $1/枚，总供应量 1B 枚，对应约 $1B FDV。

Backpack 官方披露，符合条件的 BP 质押者在 IPO、并购等退出事件中，可以分享 Backpack 预留的 20% 股权池。
按期权思路简单计算：$1B ÷ 20% = $5B

也就是说，当前 solana:BPxxfRCXkUVhig4HS1Lh7kZqV6SPJhzfEk4x6fVBjPCy 的价格，大致对应 Backpack $5B 的隐含公司估值。

贵吗？一点也不贵！

Backpack 官方数据显示，过去一年平台交易量约 $472.8B，已经达到 Kraken 2024 年 $665B 交易量的约七成。

按最新公开估值计算，Kraken 的估值约 $20B–$21B，而 solana:BPxxfRCXkUVhig4HS1Lh7kZqV6SPJhzfEk4x6fVBjPCy 按当前价格隐含的 Backpack 估值只有约 $5B，大约是 Kraken 的四分之一。

Backpack 已经跑出了接近头部交易所的交易规模，但市场给它的估值仍然只有 Kraken 的一个零头。

更重要的是Backpack 还在继续扩展证券交易、代币化股票、借贷、托管等业务。如果交易量能够持续增长，净手续费率逐步提升，平台收入和利润仍有很大的想象空间。

市场现在还在用“平台币”的框架给 solana:BPxxfRCXkUVhig4HS1Lh7kZqV6SPJhzfEk4x6fVBjPCy 定价，但它真正对应的，是一个已经具备大规模交易量、正在向综合金融基础设施升级的交易所的长期期权。

这不是在赌 Backpack 能不能从零做到 $5B，而是在用今天的价格，提前买入一个已经接近 Kraken 交易规模、但估值仍大幅折价的交易所期权。

赔率依然在。

拿好 solana:BPxxfRCXkUVhig4HS1Lh7kZqV6SPJhzfEk4x6fVBjPCy ，相信 Backpack。

Vitalik Buterin Unveils Privacy-Focused AI Agent Setup Combining zkAPI, Tor, and Local LLMs

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin showcased his personal privacy-focused AI agent setup, integrating zkAPI, Tor, random cover traffic, and local LLM prompt rewriting into the pi agent harness. The system assigns each conversation a separate Tor circuit, uses zkAPI to protect payment privacy, and rewrites prompts locally with a Qwen model. 

Vitalik said the setup is becoming usable but still suffers from significant latency, especially when starting new conversations, while Tor remains vulnerable to timing-correlation attacks involving colluding providers and entry nodes. He suggested that a specialized mixnet may offer stronger protection and added that lower gas costs for zkAPI deposits and withdrawals on Ethereum mainnet are coming soon.

把 Grok Bot 接进 Cursor / Codex / Claude Code，这个方向很对。

真正的价值不是少切一次 App，而是让人退出 Agent 之间的消息中转。

做跨 Agent 自动化，最容易被忽视的不是怎么发送任务，而是怎么证明任务真的完成：

稳定的 Bot 身份、唯一任务 ID、ACK ≠ DONE、最终回执、原任务状态回读。

否则「收到，稍后发」只会让人工传话变成自动失联。

还有个安全边界：同一账号下的 Grok Bot 共享云电脑和浏览器登录态。角色隔离不等于权限隔离。

刚在 Cursor 里直接说了一句「让 Grok Bot 拉一下我今天的推文数据」，32 条推文的浏览、点赞、转发、回复、收藏直接回到对话里。Cursor、Codex、Claude Code 三家我都测过，现在全都能用。

Grok Bot 每个 Bot 背后都有一台常驻云电脑，网站登录一次登录状态就一直保留；能跑长任务、能定时执行、有记忆，手机 App 上也能看同一批 Bot 和对话。
但写代码在 Cursor、Codex、Claude Code 里。想让 Grok Bot 干活，得切 App、重新讲一遍背景、等结果、复制回编辑器，再跟写代码的 AI 解释一遍，人在中间手动传话。

打通之后，除了我刚实测过的拉推文数据，这几个场景也可以直接用起来：
1. 读推特：在本地读推特，要么接 X API 按条付费（帖子查询、搜索、用户时间线一条 0.005 美元，读 1000 条就是 5 美元），要么用第三方镜像，经常被限流。X 官方说，Grok Bot 读公开帖子、用户、搜索、热门、新闻走它自己的 X 权限，不扣用户的 X API 额度（自己的首页时间线、书签、私信不在此列）。
2. 查网站后台：它云电脑上登录过的网站后台，可以让它直接进去查、导数据。
3. 派发长任务：调研、整理资料这种要跑半天的活派出去，编辑器里接着写代码。
4. 跑定时任务：定时任务交给它去跑，结果直接在手机上看。

实测打通时踩的坑：
1. 官方只给了一套开发套件，普通人得自己搭 Agent。
2. Grok Bot 常常先回「收到，稍后发」就结束这一轮，之后不会自己续上，结果等不到。
3. Bot 名字写错一个字就会新建一个空 Bot，你以为在跟主 Bot 聊。
4. 在 Codex 里说「问问 Grok Bot」，它跑去用飞书发消息，或想直接操控电脑。
5. Codex 启动时不等慢工具，启动太慢就不显示。

我的设计思路：
1. 一条命令装好：登录、填 Bot 名，自动找到电脑上的 Cursor、Codex、Claude Code 一起配好（改配置前自动备份），最后发测试消息；装在本机，客户端启动不到一秒。
2. 每条消息末尾自动补「这一轮里做完再回」；长任务先派出去、过会儿再收结果，编辑器不用干等。
3. 只能联系白名单里的 Bot，名字不对会提醒。
4. 回复原样带回来，不再过别的模型。
5. 给 Codex 加路由说明，提到 Grok Bot 就用这个工具。
6. 底层是 Cursor 官方套件，它启动时会读本机用不上的登录凭证，直接拦掉了。

目前还在打磨中，大家也可以按照这个思路试下

Feel free to give up on heroic and romantic mathematics, Sir.

We don’t know each other, but I have admired your work. Yet I offer an alternate interpretation, respectfully. We have simply forgotten what it is like to live among true giants. True heroes.

von Neumann, Einstein, Grothendieck, Weyl, Turing, Gödel, Cartan, Shannon, Weil, Kolmogorov, Serre, Gelfand, Feynman, Dyson, Chern, Leray, Kodaira, Milnor, Atiyah, Singer, Thom, Bott, Borel, Harish-Chandra, Wiener, Courant, Pontryagin, Bohr, Heisenberg, Dirac, Schrödinger, Fermi, Pauli, Landau, Schwinger, Tomonaga, Yang, Oppenheimer, Wigner, Wheeler, Bethe, Bose, de Broglie, Yukawa, Gell-Mann, Salam, Weinberg, Dyson, Chandrasekhar 

etc., etc. 

were all alive on New Years Day 1954. That’s not nostalgia. That is how far we have fallen in this preposterous era you have celebrated.

This is absolutely categorically *NOT* the romantic era of individual heroism. This has been the era of mostly modest, professional, institutional incrementalism…with an occasional Grisha Perelman or Witten.

PREDICTION: AI is going to break this stranglehold that our leadership has had on credit assignment, how fast we are allowed to go, and who lives and dies within this community. And you are absolutely free to take the other side of that. But you might stop trying to speak as the leader of mathematics and mathematicians who do not agree with many of your mysterious recent statements.

Respectfully.

author: runes_leo
quoted_text:
I spent 48 hours in SF hanging out with billionaires, data labs and AI founders and execs running $1B to $100B companies.

My observations:

1. Sooo MANY stories of data brokers making like $2M a WEEK selling company data to labs. I can't tell if it's the beginning or a bubble, and I kept wondering which niches are left. Digging into it actively.

2. At dinner, someone asked the table, "If a new model drops next month, does your company get better or worse?" HALF the table went quiet! I think that's the best question to ask about any AI startup right now.

3. The bar people talk about now is hitting $1B in revenue in 12 months (I guess that's the new unicorn?). What I didn't hear much about is retention. AI revenue can come in fast and leave fast, and I think we're going to see a lot of stories of AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.

4. It's pretty clear we're living through the reinvention of the computer. The model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system, and skills and plugins are the apps. Thinking about it that way makes it easier to see where the whitespace is.

5. We're maybe 12 months from an agent that can watch you work for a week and then do your job without any instructions. The screen recording plus agent memory plus local model combination makes this possible right now.

6. Agent harnesses feel like the new GPT wrappers, in a good way, especially vertical ones. The best teams I talked to treat the model as swappable. One founder walked me through routing different models to different jobs: one for taste and visuals, a cheaper one for the everyday stuff, another for text. 

They use prompts they can move across models over fine-tuning, and A/B test the output on what users actually do with it: do they edit it, export it, share it? A vertical harness is basically four things: the connectors for that industry's data, evals written by people who know the work, rules for what the agent can and can't touch, and a clean screen for a human to review. The model is maybe 20% of it.

7. There's a lot of reverse engineering going on/cloning going on more than I've ever seen. People are decompiling software and rebuilding it with agents, and someone showed a suite of like 10 apps that are worth $5B+ each all that he cloned open source. Me and everyone are still thinking through what it means when software gets this easy to copy.

8. My guess is the value moves to data. If the software can be rebuilt quickly, what's worth paying for in a legacy SaaS company is the years of customer data and workflows inside it. Some SaaS companies are secretly data companies. 

Gets me thinking about how do you truly value data for this saas companies? Like if we were buying these dying saas companies at 2x ARR before (as example), maybe there is a better metric. Idk, just thinking out loud here.

9. It feels like a good chunk of legacy software won't make it to the agentic era, especially anything built around people clicking through a lot of screens.

10. Every company I talked to wants to pipe its internal data into one place and expose it to agents through MCP. Then they look at the data and realize it's a mess: five versions of the same customer, old Slack channels, PDFs nobody can search. Cleaning that up feels like a big consulting opportunity!

11. A lot of founders are building the basic building blocks for agents: APIs, data layers and tools. Some of the companies I saw barely have a UI because the main user is an agent. I really believe the startups that build primitives to this agentic era will do extremely well. Building blocks is the best way to think about it.

12. Labs can get plenty of training data, but it's harder to get real examples of agents failing inside companies. Whoever has those logs has something valuable.

13. Someone running a big consumer company told me the next fight is over memory. The model that remembers the most about you wins, and the smartest model matters less than people think.

14. Physical AI came up a lot. Astra I think was the first model that got people into AI can actually do CAD, and I think a lot of people are thinking what does vibe manufacturing really look like. The line I keep thinking about came from a robotics founder: the hardest problems in AI are deployment problems now, not research problems. Their robots work on their own, call a human when they get stuck, and every one of those calls becomes training data.

15. Cybersecurity companies are having a moment and are actually cool companies to build now, especially the ones that clean up after a breach. Every agent with access to your systems is a new door into your company, and a lot of those doors were left open. 

16. Some startups are worth more dead than alive now. A shutdown company with 5 years of Slack, email and code can get paid for licensing all of it. I wouldn't be surprised if founders start factoring that into when they shut down.

17. People are starting to talk about monetizing the agent web. It feels really early, but when the most popular user of the internet is an agent, what startups should you be building?

18. I think agent insurance is coming. Once an agent makes an expensive mistake, insurers will want audits before they cover anyone.

19. Several people said the hire they want most is someone with taste who can write evals. The models are getting good at generating ideas, so the hard part is judging which ones are good.

20. New trend I observed: startup raises VC, uses venture dollars to become a creator, startup fails, founder falls back on being a full-time creator and incubates other products bootstrapped.

21. Getting SIGNIFICANT distribution is HARD right now. Founders are sponsoring buses, buying billboards like crazy and throwing parties with famous DJs to get noticed. Kinda feels dotcom era in that sense. 

Attention is what's scarce! The growth guy going viral sharing his UGC strategy from Wispr Flow is a good example. It's the sauce everyone wants, and I truly believe there are probably only 50 people on the planet who know how to scale these types of businesses efficiently in this era.

Always good to get that dose of SF. I felt sooo lucky to have such an incredible trip during such an incredible time in building businesses. Surreal in so many ways. 

Happy to be home and locked in.

Until next time!

when i was foolish enough to think that i could build a decentralized identity platform.

why did i think that?

because i actually had a database of 10K+ registered humans(ref: digital gorkha). all i needed was to register a public key identifier for each of them and create a sharing economy for them.

i failed not because i didn't know how to execute the idea.

execution was actually simple for that specific product idea, but the problem we faced on the tech side was that what we were trying to achieve wasn't possible with the infra we had at that time.

many projects from the ICO era realized that but they still raised funds by dropping whitepapers.

i dropped a whitepaper but i never thought of raising funds even when i had my own distribution which used to help other projects raise funds.

sometimes i feel being too honest is far less rewarding in crypto but then i think what if i had taken the other path, raised funds through an ICO, made a few extra million dollars, and lost them all or lost my reputation.

would i be as happy as i am now.
would i be as liberated as i am now.
no..

so whatever happened happened for good.

always the case.

life is so beautiful and crypto makes it chaotic just to make it beautiful again.

text:
Not every failed crosschain operation should be retried.

In Yieldcoin v2, three permanent failures could be stored as recoveries:

• a transfer above the CCIP lane’s capacity
• an Aave deposit so small it rounded to zero shares
• a supply operation blocked by a cap the vault itself had consumed

The recovery path replayed the original call with the same parameters. But none of those operations could ever succeed through repetition.

Meanwhile, the stored recovery prevented the vault from moving on to other work. In the over-capacity case, this could lock every holder’s principal behind an operation that would fail forever.

Recovery logic needs to distinguish failures whose conditions can change from those whose preconditions are permanently impossible. Retry the first. Abort or reconcile the second.

This pattern appeared across three findings in our Yieldcoin v2 crosschain vault audit.

You might have noticed @fluentlabsxyz and @fluentxyz have switched handles

Why? Things have evolved a lot over the years.

Fluent Network, often shortened to simply Fluent, is the blockchain where it all started.

But with mainnet and TGE in April, Fluent left the nest. It’s no longer built, operated or stewarded by Fluent Labs. The torch was passed to the Fluent Foundation, along with roughly half the team.

That gave Fluent Labs the opportunity to focus on what has always been core to the DNA of many of us: consumer products and culture.

We believe the next chapter of crypto that drives mainstream adoption will be financial expression: giving people new ways to financially express what they believe about the world, especially their genuine conviction around culturally relevant things.

We don't think there's enough experimentation or innovation happening in consumer crypto today and the medium of expression isn't enough. Someone has to turn it into products people love.

That's where Fluent Labs is focused. Building consumer crypto products that leverage Fluent Network and the ecosystem around it. Prints reputation, Nerona stablecoin, Fluent Connect and more.

You'll understand soon. XX.XX.2026.

现在创业比10年前难多了，并且是越来越难。

10年前，直接用Ethereum，直接用infrua的API就可以扫描交易所的钱包，做数据统计，做热钱包。

5年前，监控BNB Chain，只要用公用的API，也可以扫描BSC上的内容。

现在，如果要扫描BNB Chain，记录上面走合约的USDC的资金流动，要么就用蠢办法，记录每家交易所的合约编码，然后解码。要么用get_Logs方法解码所有的合约内部转账。

然而，现在BNB Chain每秒钟2～3个区块会被确认，如果用公共API的话，这个get_Logs方法非常不稳定。

如果自己搭建BNB的节点的话，哪怕数据只保存24小时，也需要准备2～3TB的硬盘，还有24GB～64GB内存的服务器。用自己的API才能保证get_Logs方法质量。

可惜，现在BNB Chain还仅仅是一条高速链，如果要集成Arbitrum ONE，Robinhood Chain就需要很多机器。

放到一个房间里面散热和电量消耗都会成问题。

比起10年前或者5年以前，只需要一个电脑就能创业的时代，现在别说抢市场，就算是做个能落地的应用（不是AI做的那种小玩具），那都是非常难的。

要搞到市场，那更是难上加难。

text:
I was at a dinner in DC last night. Sovereign AI was at the center of the conversation.

My takeaway: we’re still talking too much about which model an institution depends on....... and too little about whether it can actually change that dependency.

Sovereignty requires both the right to choose AND the ability to make that choice real.

Much of the conversation still revolves around “the labs.” Meanwhile, open-weight models are creating options that many institutions haven’t caught up with. (♥️ Nemotron)

For specific, valuable tasks, the opportunity is significant: combine a capable open-weight model with high-quality institutional examples, post-training, and rigorous evals. You can get a system that outperforms a general-purpose frontier model on the job you actually need done at substantially lower cost.

Not every task. Not automatically. Prove it on your own evals.

But the bigger opportunity isn’t simply to own a model.

It’s to own the institutional knowledge that makes any model useful.

What makes a good production schedule? Which constraints cannot be violated? When should an insurance decision be escalated? What did your best operator notice that the system missed?

That is your alpha.

Capture the decision, the operator’s correction, and the outcome. Validate the lesson. Then encode it where it belongs: in your ontology, constraints, tools, procedures......when useful, model weights.

Every difficult decision should leave the institution better equipped to handle the next one.

Models will change. Your accumulated judgment should survive the swap.

This is the capability gap I care about. Having access to weights is not the same as being able to curate data, define “good,” evaluate alternatives, deploy safely, and switch models without rebuilding the business.

And sovereignty extends beyond models: data, storage, compute, logic, business processes, and applications. Moving dependence from one layer to another is not the same as gaining control.

This is not an argument against frontier labs. Use them where they win. Use open weights where they win. Keep humans accountable for the decisions that matter.

It is an argument for making that choice yours in practice, not just on paper.

Sovereignty isn’t having no dependencies. It’s being able to change them without losing what makes you good.

"TSMC was probably about $300 million, something like that. It's a tiny little company. I heard about Morris Chang. And so I tried to call their US office."

"Back in the old days there were yellow pages. I looked it up, TSMC. There's a number there. I called their number and it's a recording. I left my name and my number and said a few things about NVIDIA: we're a new startup company building computer graphics chips. I called several times. Nobody called me back."

"And so I finally wrote a letter to Morris Chang. Didn't hear anything for a long time, and then one day it was 6 o'clock or something, this person called and said 'this is Morris Chang from TSMC.'"

"And meanwhile, everybody outside my office was playing video games and they're all laughing and screaming. 'Hey shut up! It's Morris!' I was so happy that the founder would actually call us back, because hey, maybe we won't have to die."

"And so we talked and he invited me to Taiwan. I came back to Taiwan, and that was the start of everything. Not just that partnership, but just the whole industry."

@arcus_xyz pays 250,000 points every week.

I pulled all 14,429 wallets from their points API:

• every $1M traded ≈ 42 points
• the top 1% hold 47% of everything
• makers farm it for $0 in fees

What each tier takes, what a point is worth, and how to farm it right:

The rate
250K points ÷ ~$3B of weekly volume 
(counted on both sides of every trade)
= ~42 pts per $1M. Both drops so far came out at 42.0.

The pool is fixed. The more volume Arcus does, the less each dollar earns. Early is cheap.

What each tier takes (after 2 drops)
Diamond, top 1%: 556 pts ≈ $13.2M volume
Platinum, top 5%: 116 pts ≈ $2.8M
Gold, top 20%: 17 pts ≈ $410K
Silver, top 50%: 2.3 pts ≈ $55K

Tiers are pure percentiles, so the bar rises every Wednesday.

It's brutally top-heavy
• Median wallet: 2.28 pts (the mean is 34.65)
• 38% of wallets have less than 1 point

"A few trades a week" is farming crumbs. Size and consistency are everything.

The farming math
Takers (tier 0) pay 2.25 bps = $225 per $1M, so ~$5.40 per point.
Makers pay 0%, so their points cost nothing in fees.

At a $1.5B FDV a point ≈ $23.

So $1M traded ≈ $970 of points vs $225 of taker fees, before PnL.

How to earn more per dollar
• Stock tokens / RWA earn more than crypto
• RWA perps outside US hours earn more again (8PM–4AM ET, weekends, holidays)
• Collateral left on Arcus is its own category
• Market making is its own category
• Robinhood Wallet swaps are boosted

What gets you slashed (retroactively, per their terms)
Wash trading, self-matching, wallet splitting, referral rings, delta-neutral or hedged farming, deposit-trade-withdraw churn. Slashed points get handed to everyone else.

What's a point worth?
Season 1 = max 39 drops = 9.75M pts
plus ~3.25M from Season 0 ≈ 13M points at TGE.

If 20% of supply goes to points:
$500M FDV: $7.70 per point
$1.5B: $23
$3B: $46

Lighter points were worth ~$56 at launch.

Season 0 points are still hidden, but your S0 rank isn't. So I built a free calculator:

enter your points + S0 rank and get your $ value today, by June, and the volume you need for the next tier.

$RHUB has a 3.3% tax on every trade.

At the start, the sell side only accumulated $ARB (164k is now sitting in the treasury).
Then half of it was automatically added to a non-withdrawable LP.

Now, with Arbitrum looking ready for its next leg, we've decided to stop stacking ARB until the price is higher and everybody's happy.

Here is how it works:

🔥 Buys: the 3.3% is taken in RHUB and burned instantly. Nobody can change that, except to lower the rate.

🔥 Sells: the 3.3% is taken in ARB. A new treasury strategy uses it to buy RHUB back and burn it. The further RHUB trades below its ATH, the bigger the share it burns:

• −60% or lower → 100% burned
• −40% to −60% → 75%
• −20% to −40% → 50%
• 0% to −20% → 25%
• Above ATH → 0%

The ATH is measured on the circulating market cap in ARB, at the highest hourly close: 9.69M ARB.

Whatever isn't burned becomes an ARB wall: a liquidity position 60% below the ATH that only buys if the price comes down to it. If the price breaks all the way through, the RHUB it bought is burned too.

Right now, RHUB is ~75% below its ATH → 100% of sell fees are bought back and burned.

✅ The 164k ARB treasury is never touched
✅ Buybacks are capped at 200 ARB per ~12s, so no single buy moves the price much

Could be an interesting hooks overall, monitoring

text:
TAO 和 Pearl（PRL）都在押注 AI，但它们根本不是同一种资产。

最近读了 @dov_wo 和 @brezshares 对 Pearl 的讨论，我重新比较了两者的技术、经济模型和代币需求。最大的误区是：PRL 流通市值只有 TAO 的五分之一，就以为还有五倍估值空间。

① 先看数字（2026/10/15 快照）

$TAO：流通市值约 $30.22 亿，FDV 约 $54.61 亿，流通占上限 55.3%。
$PRL：流通市值约 $5.85 亿，FDV 约 $35.52 亿，流通占上限 16.5%。

看流通市值，两者差约 5.17 倍；看 FDV，只差约 1.54 倍。

PRL 是早期项目，但已经不是“几千万美元 FDV、市场尚未发现”的阶段。不能把未来要挖出的币当成不存在。

② 底层到底在做什么？

TAO 是一个 AI 服务与激励市场。不同 Subnet 组织算力、推理、数据等服务，矿工交付结果，验证者评价贡献；全网 TAO 发行通过子网代币价格、质押与协议规则分配激励。TAO 是手续费、质押和 TAO/Alpha 市场的基础资产。

PRL 是另一条路：用 GPU 矩阵乘法承担 PoW，目标是同一份 AI 计算既服务真实客户，又能得到区块奖励。矿工收入理论上可以来自两边：推理服务费 + PRL 挖矿奖励。

一句话：TAO 组织 AI 生产市场；PRL 试图改变 GPU 生产的成本结构。

③ 谁真正给代币带来需求？

TAO 有生态使用场景：质押、交易费用、Alpha 的共同计价与兑换资产。但 Subnet 赚了钱，不等于收入直接分红给 TAO 持有人；持有 TAO 本币也不等于持有某个 Subnet 的 Alpha。

Pearl 已有自己的推理 API，客户目前可以用 USD 预充值、按 Token 付费。这证明其产品入口不是空白，但仍不能推出“AI 推理收入增加，客户就必须买 PRL”。矿工也可能为了支付 GPU 成本卖掉新挖出的 PRL。

真正需要验证的是：真实付费推理占了多少工作量？客户为什么需要持有 PRL，而不只是付美元？

④ 发行压力差异比想象中大

TAO 首次减半后约 3,600 枚/日；以当前流通量计算，未来一年理论新增约 11.3%。

Pearl 的上限为 21 亿枚，发行按多项式曲线平滑递减，而不是 Bitcoin 式突然减半。以官方区块高度和目标出块间隔推算，当前约 100 万 PRL/日，未来一年理论新增约 3.03 亿枚，相当于当前流通量的约 87.7%。

这不是说 PRL 一年必跌 87.7%，也不代表矿工会立刻卖光；它说明要支撑同样的价格，市场必须持续吸收更多新增供给。

⑤ 技术进展与未完成的证明

Pearl 官方在部分 H200 推理配置中报告了约 3.9%–5.08% 的额外开销，这是值得关注的工程结果，但不能直接外推到所有模型、硬件和矿工。其浮点 PoUW 标准 PIP-3 目前仍是 Draft；此前一项独立预印本也质疑过早期矿池实际执行的有用 AI 计算占比。该研究是历史样本，不代表今天所有矿工的状态。

TAO 的技术、市场和子网体系更成熟，但同样要回答：哪些 Subnet 真有客户和净收入？这些需求如何通过质押、交易、回购或其他机制，长期增加 TAO 的经济价值？

我的结论：这不是“老 TAO vs 新 PRL”，也不是必然的零和竞争。

TAO 更像已经运行的 AI 经济网络；PRL 更像技术想象空间很大、商业闭环仍需继续验证的 PoW 货币实验。

如果今天用同样一笔现金重新选择，我不会仅凭 PRL 流通市值更小就把 TAO 换成 PRL。真正决定估值的不是“AI 时代的 BTC”这句话，而是 AI 使用量增加之后，谁能形成可验证、持续、必须发生的代币需求。

数据：CoinMarketCap 10/15；机制与发行：Bittensor Docs、Pearl 白皮书/主网浏览器。发行量为协议模型估算，不是价格预测。附图为对应数据与价值捕获路径。

text:
PAPER 亏损挖矿刚火了不到一周，Jupiter 就赶紧推出 1000x 杠杆来蹭热度

大家都在骂它是赌场，但我觉得这可能是这轮 Perp DEX 里最诚实的产品，因为它连名字都叫 YOLO🤣

先看机制：
1. 标的只有 SOL、BTC、ETH，最高 1,000x，$10 起步，只能市价单，没有止损
2. 不是 peer-to-peer 撮合，价格用真实市场价，但输赢全部和一个 House 池结算，House 的钱来自交易者的亏损
3. 1,000x 下 0.1% 的波动就直接归零
4. House 池子不够的时候，赢家的利润要排队，没有保证的兑付时间
5. Beta 阶段，未经审计

本质上，Jupiter 不是交易所，是庄家。用户买的不是 BTC 的方向敞口，是一张 0.1% 波动就作废的彩票，赢了还得看庄家池子够不够赔

再看 PAPER 那边：Hyperliquid 上的 papertrade_xyz 开启亏损挖矿不到 6 天，刷量最猛的三个地址交易量都超过了 $100 亿。Machi 刷了 $14.1 亿，亏 $41.6 万，拿回代币和奖励后，净亏只剩 $7.47 万

一边是交易量可以被激励刷出来，一边是杠杆可以被做成彩票

上一轮 GMX 的 GLP 也是 LP 当对手盘，赚的是交易者亏的钱，只是当时还要包装成「去中心化永续」，这一轮连包装都省了，直接叫 YOLO

所以问题来了：1,000x 的 YOLO 是 Perp DEX 赌场化的终局，还是又一个杠杆见顶的信号🧐

text:
BREAKING: Marc Andreessen just drew the clearest map he's ever given of where the next trillions actually land.  And it isn't the software app layer.  

His thesis: manufacturing jobs from the last 25 years are permanently gone. Stop chasing them back.  

The real asymmetric bets are embodied AI hardware (robots, drones, autonomous vehicles, defense) and AI attacking the three sectors where prices have only gone up for decades: housing, healthcare, education.  

The moat in those sectors isn't technology. It's regulation. Which means whoever breaks through first wins everything.  

He specifically calls out California's SB 1047 as the template for what nearly happened: a bill that would have imposed sweeping liability on AI developers and chilled the entire buildout. It failed. 

But the next version is coming.  

Founders still optimizing for software-layer apps are playing a smaller game than they think.  

The question isn't whether AI reshapes the physical world. It's whether American regulation hands that opportunity to someone else first.

Where to place the bets for the next 18 months:  https://t.co/yZxU440dQj

Today, we’re releasing Bonsai 2 2B, 4B, and 9B.

Based on Qwen3.5, these new ternary models bring stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool calling to compact footprints designed for everyday devices:

• 2B: 0.43GB
• 4B: 0.95GB
• 9B: 2.0GB

For this release, we focused on what makes small models useful as local assistants: following instructions, avoiding repetitive loops, calling tools on mobile devices, and giving useful answers without unnecessary output. The 9B model uses roughly 40% fewer tokens on standard instruction-following and everyday math tasks. Solving the Riemann hypothesis can wait.

These models are successors to our first-generation Bonsai 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, and provide a foundation for bringing practical agentic functionality to local applications on personal computers, phones, and wearables.

The Bonsai 2 family now includes four sizes spanning 2B to 27B parameters. Developers can choose the balance of capability, memory use, and responsiveness that fits their application and hardware.

Available today under Apache 2.0.

text:
回踩上升趋势线，能否撑住将决定后续趋势走势！

从6月底5.8万，到9月中旬7.5万，再到如今8.1万附近，BTC日线低点不断抬高，说明中期上升趋势尚未破坏。

但有个细节值得警惕：9月底以来，高点却在持续降低。

低点抬高，高点降低，两条趋势线不断收敛，意味着BTC已经进入关键变盘窗口。

再看宏观环境：昨天美股低开高走，标普、道指最终收涨，说明市场并未因CPI、PPI连续超预期而彻底恐慌，美债收益率明显回落，美联储10月加息概率也降至三成左右，短期流动性预期有所改善。

但问题在于，通胀压力并未消失，美国关税、能源价格以及AI科技股估值风险，仍然制约着市场风险偏好。

所以我认为，BTC现在既不是明确的底部，也没有形成真正的向上突破。

接下来重点关注两个位置：
8万美元：中期上升趋势的关键防线，守住仍有机会向8.5万-8.75万发起冲击。

8.4万美元：下降趋势线附近的重要压力，只有放量突破，才能进一步确认多头重新掌握主动权。

反之，一旦日线有效跌破8万美元，尤其反抽无法收回，就要防范再次回踩7.5万-7.8万美元。

我认为短线偏向震荡修复，但不急着看单边上涨，第三次回踩趋势线，可能是机会，也可能是陷阱。

真正值得关注的不是支撑被测试了多少次，而是每次测试之后，多头还能不能把价格推向更高的位置。

这次8万美元附近的争夺，很可能决定整个10月下半月的走势。

text:
Treating network usage and token demand as separate questions is a useful way to look at Canton’s institutional activity.

@Defi_Rocketeer breaks down that distinction in detail, and what would make that demand durable.
author: CantonNetwork
quoted_text:
I can see @CantonNetwork winning institutional finance while $CC captures much less of the upside

I keep coming back to this: if i’m evaluating a token, i need to see how those fees reach holders.

For $CC, i’m following five questions.

→ Does institutional activity create paid network traffic?

Canton supports dedicated synchronizers alongside the Global Synchronizer.

I need to know which institutional workflows actually consume paid Global Synchronizer traffic before treating adoption as CC demand.

→ How much CC does that traffic burn?

Global Synchronizer traffic is priced in USD and purchased by burning CC.

Costs depend on data size and delivery requirements.

That means tokenized asset value alone tells me very little about burn.

At the same USD traffic cost, a higher onchain CC conversion rate also means fewer tokens burned.

Temple gives me a more concrete signal: it reported crossing 1B CC burned on September 11.

That is evidence of actual token consumption. But i still need to compare burn with rewards minted over the same period.

→ Is burn catching up with minting?

CCView’s September report shows:

> 645.8M CC minted
> 442.6M CC burned
> ~203.2M CC net issuance

Burn offset 68.5% of minting, down from 71.1% in August.

Meaningful burn exists, but supply is still expanding. September’s balance weakened.

Positive issuance alone doesn’t determine returns. i want to see whether sustained usage can absorb issuance at the valuation i’m paying.

→ Who receives application fees?

This is where I separate app economics from CC economics.

@Cantex_io : liquidity partners earn a share of pool trading fees.

@AlpendHQ : borrower interest goes to suppliers and protocol reserves; its documented default reserve factor is 10%.

@Rho_Labs : its infra describes execution on Ethereum/Arbitrum and private records on Canton, with gas absorbed by the protocol.

I wouldn’t count these revenue streams as income for passive CC holders without an explicit mechanism connecting them.

→ How much repo notional becomes network fees?

Broadridge reported $7.5T of September repo volume, averaging $359B daily.

That makes the institutional adoption case compelling. It doesn’t establish the CC investment case.

I want to see the Global Synchronizer traffic costs attributable to that activity, the associated CC burn, and the rewards minted alongside it.

I’m interested in Canton because institutional settlement has clear financial uses.

My conviction depends on how much durable $CC demand those uses generate for long term.

Ethereum's Cambridge workshop on post-quantum, fast finality, and more just finished 👀 

kamil's reflections below
author: trent_vanepps
quoted_text:
Leaving Cambridge after a few days of PQ and fast finality workshops.

Decoupled consensus looks to be in a good shape and should be ready by the I*.

The next big thing is PQ aggregation for XMSS attestations, which is the biggest unknown for many people. A few questions we discussed in Cambridge:

* Should aggregators be incentivized?
* Should anyone be able to aggregate, or should it be a specialized role?
* Should we assume sophisticated entities will want to aggregate, or rely only on existing validators?

It feels like people are leaning towards no specialized role.

My take: the network has enough entities interested in fast finality. It should let them join and aggregate with whatever hardware they have to produce the global aggregation by the next slot.

But the network must keep running if those entities disappear.

That's the direction the networking should be optimizing for. We'll bring this topic for the devcon to further elaborate assumptions we are working on

author: apriori0x
quoted_text:
What FOCIL does is provide hard guarantees for the transactions the Ethereum protocol sees.

What Multi-Party Block Construction (MPBC) provides is softer fast inclusion guarantees for transactions that are known by any block builder. 

Now you have multiple builders contributing to blocks. In particular, the base builder and the contributing builder work with the MPBC operator and proposer to deliver the most valuable block to the Ethereum network. 

In the future, both FOCIL and MPBC can continue to scale up and get bigger together, making Ethereum more robust. 

In the endgame it maybe that FOCIL includers construct most of the block, with the MPBC pipeline doing the rest. The builder role then becomes an "off-to-the-side function", simply adding a few transactions to capture MEV. 

@mostlyblocks from @Blockspace_ETH touches on these topics and more as he eloquently provides a comprehensive first principles overview of MPBC on Ethereum in this quintessential episode of Credible Commitments.

text:
Shipped v1 of this privacy map last week and the replies were very helpful to come up with a more complete v2.

So here's the v2 ecosystem map (mcap/FDV, 7d and 30d moves and distance from ATH):

1) Private money

- $ZEC ($20.9B, +1% 7d, +1% 30d, 62% off ATH):

Zcash is optional privacy: you move coins into a zk shielded pool and from there nobody sees sender, receiver or amount. For years the problem was that hardly anyone bothered to shield. That changed: 4.96M ZEC sit shielded now, 29.2% of supply and an ATH, 4.1M of it in Ironwood, the new pool from July that Brave made its default on 8 Oct. On top, NU7 is on testnet since 4 Oct, the team presented Tachyon on 9 Oct (recursive SNARKs, ~150 TPS target), and ZCSH on NYSE Arca is the first spot ETF for a privacy asset anywhere. On quantum, hash-based signatures for the transparent pool are targeted for January, while the shielded pool needs its own migration (Epoch, end of 2027). There are no programs inside the pool tho. ZEC is private money and nothing else, which is also why it stays the asset the whole vertical is priced off.

→ DYOR: @Zcash

- $XMR ($10.6B, +5% 7d, +12% 30d, 30% off ATH):

Privacy by default instead of by choice. Ring signatures, stealth addresses and RingCT hide sender, receiver and amount on every single tx, no opt-in. The weak spot was always the ring itself: 16 members, so you hide among 15 decoys and a good heuristic narrows that down. FCMP++ replaces the ring with a proof that you own one of the 150M+ outputs on the entire chain, which makes the whole history your anonymity set. The third beta stressnet has been live since 5 Oct, hardware wallets and multisig don't work on it yet, and there is no mainnet date. Add that it's delisted on most regulated venues and has no ETF, and you get why it trades like ZEC's discount twin. FCMP++ is the catalyst, the missing listings are probs the ceiling.

→ DYOR: @monero

- $DASH ($643M, -2% 7d, -5% 30d, 97% off ATH):

Dash is the one I skipped in v1 and shouldn't have. It has had protocol-level CoinJoin since 2014, and on 21 Aug it went further: Orchard-based shielded transactions (Zcash's zk tech, Halo 2, no trusted setup) went live on the Dash Evolution chain, ~1s settlement, built in five months, shielded assets next. So it's now two privacy models in one coin, mixing on Core and real zk shielding on Evolution. The token still trades like it's 2018 tho, 97% off ATH and -5% on the month while ZEC ran, and most of CT has not noticed the upgrade. Either the market is right or it's late.

→ DYOR: @Dashpay

2) Private transfers and payments

- $RAIL ($156M, +2% 7d, +36% 30d, 54% off ATH):

Railgun has been live since 2021 and is still the most used private DeFi rail on Ethereum. It's a zk shielded pool on Ethereum, Arbitrum, BSC and Polygon, and the trick is that you call DeFi from inside the pool, so Uniswap or Aave never learn who you are. Private Proofs of Innocence let you show your funds are clean without doxxing them, which is what keeps it usable post Tornado. Blockworks put a dashboard on it on 7 Oct: $4.6M annualised revenue, staking yield up from 4.3% to 9.1%, weekly txs at an ATH of 5K.

→ DYOR: @RAILGUN_Project

- $CTR ($20M mcap, $135M FDV, +5% 7d, +18% 30d, 65% off ATH):

Citrea is the Bitcoin ZK rollup, and since 23 Sep also a privacy play: it acquired Crest, a self-custodial private BTC wallet, and made it the flagship product, pitched as Zcash-style privacy for Bitcoin. Mainnet is live (cBTC, ctUSD, Clementine bridge, security upgrade shipped 10 Oct), the numbers are small ($20M DeFi TVL, $4M ctUSD, 83 BTC in the vaults) and Crest itself is still a waitlist. So what you buy today is the rollup plus an option on private BTC, with 15% of supply floating. The cleanest private-Bitcoin ticker there is, mostly bc there isn't another one.

→ DYOR: @citrea_xyz

- $XAN ($26M mcap, $101M FDV, -10% 7d, -11% 30d, 96% off ATH):

Anoma does privacy as a consumer product. The architecture is intent-centric (you say what you want, solvers figure out how, privacy sits in the protocol), but what you actually touch is AnomaPay. V1 is live on Ethereum plus five EVM chains with 20 assets: shielded transfers, private yield accounts on Morpho, confidential swaps via Bebop, private payroll, private tokenized stocks on BNB, and since 6 Oct native private swaps. For normies this is probs the right abstraction, an app rather than a chain. It's also the cheapest optionality in the basket, bc it sat flat while everything around it ran (take that as you will).

→ DYOR: @anoma

- $ZEN ($113M mcap, $129M FDV, -3% 7d, -5% 30d, 96% off ATH):

Horizen went the compliance route. It's an EVM-native L3 on Base, and Vela, its confidential compute layer, lets an app keep its state private while disclosing exactly what a regulator asks for and nothing more. That is selective disclosure built for the EU and UK transfer rules, not anonymity, and it's a very different buyer than the ZEC crowd. 21M capped supply, ERC-20 on Base, staking live since July, a token-weighted Special Council elected end of Sep, first Vela accelerator cohort wrapping up this month. It has lagged ZEC the entire run, which you can read either way.

→ DYOR: @horizenglobal

text:
$BVIV is at 41, below its 1-year avg of 44.6. Phases like this are when experienced traders look at volatility, not just direction: entries are potentially cheap, and the upside is asymmetric.

Low implied vol keeps premiums down. A pullback in $BTC pushes upside strikes further out of the money on top of that. Calls get cheaper on both counts.

August is the reference. On Aug 18, $BVIV closed at 36.7 with $BTC at $64.7K. Three days later $BTC was at $78.3K and BVIV at 46. OTM calls bought before the move gained from the price move and the repricing of vol at the same time. @koolkrypto223 was positioned for exactly that on Derive.

The trade-off stays the same. Most deep OTM calls expire worthless, the premium is the maximum loss, and that is why these positions should be sized responsible.

Here's what me asking it to do a simple research task looks like.

It's getting quite usable! Though you definitely still pay quite a bit in increased latency, especially when starting a new conversation.

Also, Tor is far from optimal here for privacy; the cover traffic mechanism is okay against passive adversaries but much weaker if the LLM provider is colluding with the guard and actively manipulating timing.
