Engineering leaders told Grepr founder and CEO Jad Naous they spend 5 to 20% of their infrastructure budget on observability, and it's buying less and less reliability.

Jad, a former a16z partner, joins a16z's Martin Casado to discuss whether AI can run production systems as well as it writes code.

Grepr sits in a company's log stream, can scan a petabyte of logs a day, cuts observability costs by about 90%, and is building AI agents that use those signals to troubleshoot production issues.

How AI is changing engineering at Jad's 10-person company:
- A data lake feature that once took one engineer about six months took Jad 10 days
- The gap between okay and great engineers on his team "just multiplied 10X"
- He runs 3-4 agent sessions at once, with a "tech lead" agent reviewing every PR

Why running live systems is a harder problem for AI:
- Jad: AI can almost tune databases, but can't yet keep servers running on its own
- Martin: every bit of code doubles the ways a program can behave, which is why humans still own systems
- The real world is messier than AI's training data, self-driving took 20 years and $170B

text:
Emotional the next morning. I'm in my Model 3. I haven't been looking at the road; I've been looking at videos, reading X, and trying to catch up on AI.

I'm heading to a humanoid robotics conference in San Francisco where, let's be honest, there's an elephant in the room that hasn't been seen: Optimus. Jason Calacanis told me yesterday that as cool as the demo of the Roadster was, Optimus is going to be even cooler, and I believe him.

We're heading into a new age, and we're seeing a fight between the builders and innovators who are creating new things with AI, and the people who are resisting:
• Those who don't want a data center in their backyard
• Those who don't want autonomous cars because they think they will steal jobs
• Those who don't want humanoid robots in their stores or businesses because it upsets, disrupts, and changes their lives

There is a lot of fear, uncertainty, and doubt. But we are clearly in a new world today, very different from yesterday. I'm riding in an autonomous car, something most people haven't had a chance to experience yet. We're heading into a world of autonomy, brain-computer interfaces, rocket cars, glasses that augment the world, new kinds of medical technologies, and entirely new ways to live life.

It's a scary time for people who don't like change, and they are resisting hard. But there is a growing group of people who want to accelerate into the future. Elon, for all his flaws, is inspiring multiple industries. I've been traveling to robotics and space companies around America, seeing the latest startups and trying to understand how new technologies arriving daily are transforming business, manufacturing, and commerce. Invariably, they are inspired by Elon. Even the Chinese EV companies were inspired by him (some even ripped off his technology).

I'm emotional today because for the last 15 years (actually, all the way back to the Apple II), people resist change and give innovators a lot of shit. How many arguments have I had with people about LiDAR? And I'm not talking about uninformed people; I'm talking about veterans in the tech and automotive industries.

Last week, I was hanging out with 2,500 Tesla fans down in Texas, and I kept hearing stories, particularly from Cybertruck owners, about getting flipped off on American roads and people trying to bash or wreck their cars.

It's not just a Tesla thing; I've heard this from pioneers all my life. Doug Engelbart came to my first book launch party and told me about getting fired from his own R&D lab because his ideas were too futuristic and people got tired of him. He was talking about a day when we'd all hold a supercomputer in our hands, but he was saying that back in 1971.

It's these pioneers and engineers I'm thinking about today: the people like Elon who bring something new to the world while everyone gives them grief. I remember taking my first ride in the original Tesla Roadster. I was so excited that I came back to Silicon Valley to talk to founders and VCs (I had a privileged position in the industry back then), and I couldn't find anyone who thought he would succeed. They dismissed it as the folly of a rich dude, telling me there was no way he could take on traditional automakers like GM, Ford, VW, BMW, or Toyota, and no way he could build a profitable car company. There were rare believers back in 2008, like Steve Jurvetson, but they were few and far between.

Getting people to believe in a new idea, adopt it, and change their lives with it is extremely difficult. Unless you have a front-row seat, you don't realize how much flak people take simply for being early.

Now I'm heading into San Francisco to see a bunch of robots and talk to robotics companies. Robotics hasn't fully arrived yet, but it's starting to gain believers and customers. A wave of new companies is coming: Y Combinator alone funded around 25 robotics startups in their last batch, a huge shift from just two or three a few years ago. Something is cooking

跟知情的小伙伴聊了一下，其实活动筹备了小一年，连办公室都租好了，怎么可能像一些人嘲讽的一样没跟相关部门报备，真当那么大个团队都是纯老外一点不懂规矩？🤣🤣🤣

何况这已经是Solana在中国尝试搞活动的第三年了（去年在北京的活动也是我报了一下结果引发传统媒体关注导致赶紧删帖熄火😂😂😂） ，吃一堑肯定要长一智的。

今年他们还聘请了专门的GR（Government Relationship）来协助，会议相当多的敏感词都不能提了，只是集中在区块链技术本身上，就是为了尽可能的规避风险。

但只能说中国的体制特殊，除了现官还有现管，除了地方还有上级，跟一个部门报备好了不意味着别的部门不能来掺一脚管一管。 任何一家说不让那就弄不成，你还能指望别家站出来帮你撑腰说非办不可？在当前的中国政治生态里这不现实。

在国内做过实体生意的大概应该能理解我的意思，消防税务卫生街道个个都是爷，更何况Solana搞的还是Crypto这个敏感行业的破冰首家。

而且前天的外滩大广告过于高调，引发的曝光超过了预期，形成了国内外社媒的大量传播，这种舆论压力也有很大可能导致了预料之外的额外力量干涉。

我个人其实是很钦佩 @calilyliu 为首的 Solana foundation @SolanaFndn  的勇气和毅力的，如此锲而不舍的试图在中国内地打开口子，Solana应该是我看到的唯一一家。

大部分项目团队能做到国内城市小规模搞个饭局，跟社区见见面已经很不错了。

但Solana 是真的想要把Blockchain技术带进国内主流视野，想把在美国已经如火如荼的Tradifi在国内也打通，难度之大可想而知。

不过换个角度考虑，如果真的万一被他们打通了，搞成了，回报必然极为丰厚。

比如改革开放初期的德国大众，1978年就开始跟中国谈合作，直到1984年才签下上海大众的合资协议，前后磨了六年。中间最初的大规模建厂方案走不通，还得调整路径，从组装和逐步扩大生产做起。

后来回报有多大？仅2015年一年，中国合资企业按大众持股比例计算的经营利润就有约52亿欧元。

所以先进去的人，承担的是探路的成本，也有机会吃到市场打开之后的长期红利。当然，前提是这扇门最后真的打开了。

最后在嘉里中心楼下吃了一顿pizaa滚蛋了，听说还有小伙伴从新加坡飞过来参加活动的，比我还远，心理平衡多了，哈哈。

预祝 @solana  后续几站能顺利吧

author: barnabemonnot
quoted_text:
AI is making Ethereum more ambitious.

You might have heard about the challenges that blockchains face in a post-AI world, and while security assumptions will surely be stress-tested in the coming months and years, there is another side to it. I believe AI will let us speedrun towards a world that's both more secure and feature-rich.

As we look towards Ethereum's first post-AI upgrade, Hegotá, the R&D community is asking itself what increasingly powerful tools could help us do differently:

> How far can we push both security and iteration speed?
> How much of the design space can we examine before committing to one?
> How easily can we test the interactions between complex features?

My recent formal verification work @ethlabs_org has given me some reasons to be optimistic about these, as work that would have previously not even been attempted is now being done by agents in days. In September, I posted about using formal verification as part of designing a new consensus protocol. This time, I want to tell you about formally verifying something already fully specified and in production: Ethereum's Fast Confirmation Rule (FCR).

If you are not familiar with FCR, it lets applications confirm Ethereum blocks in seconds, roughly 30x faster than waiting for finality, under additional assumptions (from waiting 13 minutes to 24 seconds!). It also further solidifies Ethereum L1's case as an asset hub and center of gravity for the onchain economy. FCR now has a safety proof in Lean, closely modeling the rule in the consensus specs, which is the source of truth for Ethereum's consensus clients.

Some takeaways:

> FCR is safe! Under its assumptions, confirmed blocks remain canonical. On top of the manual proofs from the paper, we now have Lean proofs of this for the actual spec, additional evidence for applications considering FCR!

> The bulk of the formal verification work took just a 4-5 days (check out the animation!), with agents working mostly unsupervised. We should be very ambitious about using this as a tool at scale.

> After verifying the current rule, it was easy to adapt the model to the upcoming Gloas changes. Immediately, this surfaced a subtle bug caused by changes to fork choice. The problem was in the spec itself and not a gap in the model. The safety proof would not go through, and the agents could precisely pinpoint what was causing it to fail. The bug is now fixed, and formal verification of the corrected protocol goes through.

Iteration is never quite over, even for "finished" features like FCR, because the protocol keeps evolving around them. A formal model lets us ensure that key properties keep holding throughout the evolution of the protocol. With these capabilities, Ethereum can and should keep upgrading faster, tightening fork timelines and exploring more ambitious features, while still raising the security bar.

This picture has been getting much clearer over the past few months, and the past week confirmed it for me, as @drakefjustin and @corcoranwill brought together 100+ Ethereum researchers, cryptographers and formal verification experts in Cambridge for six days of workshops on post-quantum cryptography, formal verification and fast finality. Beyond its own workshop, formal verification was the omnipresent star of the week: everyone is using Lean and doing amazing things with it! Piece by piece, Ethereum's technological core is being rebuilt for the post-AI age.

The excitement was palpable, the sense of optimism was pervasive, and every talk and conversation carried a level of ambition I'd never seen before. The Ethereum R&D machine is upgrading itself, and we will see the outcome of that on the network sooner than you think.

text:
building a consumer app is hard… really hard.

fomo has always tried to do things the right way. this often means sacrificing growth and revenue in order to do the harder thing. 

we’ve never done things to take shortcuts, such as: 
- points programs
- paid trading deals
- fake/inflated incentives

we try everything to make sure users get the best experience, whether this means working closely with infra partners or working to build it ourselves. we pay routers commercially to NOT take positive slippage. we work to get rebates for traders. we pay creator rewards to those who provide value.

we do not get everything right. truthfully, no one does. 

the entire team looks at every single piece of feedback daily. we commit to continuously learning & always trying our best. we constantly feel like the product is far from perfect and this is likely a feeling that never goes away when ur building a company. 

good things take time. great things take a while.

There is one Arc Studio feature that, if you’re not using while building onchain, you’re debugging blind.

It’s called Tracing.

Let’s imagine you’re building an app that sends USDC. You click send and approve the transaction in your wallet, but your app is still loading.

Now you’re not sure what’s going on.

Did the wallet connect? Was the transaction submitted? Was it confirmed onchain? Did the contract emit the expected event?

Instead of checking your browser console, wallet, and explorer separately, Tracing shows the full flow in one timeline.

You can see every step, how long it took, where something failed, and the data your app sent and received.

You could paste logs into an AI coding tool and ask it to debug them. But the real value of Tracing is that it automatically captures the full onchain flow first, so the AI has the right context to explain what happened. 

You can also click Ask Studio and let the AI explain the trace for you.

text:
AI is making Ethereum more ambitious.

You might have heard about the challenges that blockchains face in a post-AI world, and while security assumptions will surely be stress-tested in the coming months and years, there is another side to it. I believe AI will let us speedrun towards a world that's both more secure and feature-rich.

As we look towards Ethereum's first post-AI upgrade, Hegotá, the R&D community is asking itself what increasingly powerful tools could help us do differently:

> How far can we push both security and iteration speed?
> How much of the design space can we examine before committing to one?
> How easily can we test the interactions between complex features?

My recent formal verification work @ethlabs_org has given me some reasons to be optimistic about these, as work that would have previously not even been attempted is now being done by agents in days. In September, I posted about using formal verification as part of designing a new consensus protocol. This time, I want to tell you about formally verifying something already fully specified and in production: Ethereum's Fast Confirmation Rule (FCR).

If you are not familiar with FCR, it lets applications confirm Ethereum blocks in seconds, roughly 30x faster than waiting for finality, under additional assumptions (from waiting 13 minutes to 24 seconds!). It also further solidifies Ethereum L1's case as an asset hub and center of gravity for the onchain economy. FCR now has a safety proof in Lean, closely modeling the rule in the consensus specs, which is the source of truth for Ethereum's consensus clients.

Some takeaways:

> FCR is safe! Under its assumptions, confirmed blocks remain canonical. On top of the manual proofs from the paper, we now have Lean proofs of this for the actual spec, additional evidence for applications considering FCR!

> The bulk of the formal verification work took just a 4-5 days (check out the animation!), with agents working mostly unsupervised. We should be very ambitious about using this as a tool at scale.

> After verifying the current rule, it was easy to adapt the model to the upcoming Gloas changes. Immediately, this surfaced a subtle bug caused by changes to fork choice. The problem was in the spec itself and not a gap in the model. The safety proof would not go through, and the agents could precisely pinpoint what was causing it to fail. The bug is now fixed, and formal verification of the corrected protocol goes through.

Iteration is never quite over, even for "finished" features like FCR, because the protocol keeps evolving around them. A formal model lets us ensure that key properties keep holding throughout the evolution of the protocol. With these capabilities, Ethereum can and should keep upgrading faster, tightening fork timelines and exploring more ambitious features, while still raising the security bar.

This picture has been getting much clearer over the past few months, and the past week confirmed it for me, as @drakefjustin and @corcoranwill brought together 100+ Ethereum researchers, cryptographers and formal verification experts in Cambridge for six days of workshops on post-quantum cryptography, formal verification and fast finality. Beyond its own workshop, formal verification was the omnipresent star of the week: everyone is using Lean and doing amazing things with it! Piece by piece, Ethereum's technological core is being rebuilt for the post-AI age.

The excitement was palpable, the sense of optimism was pervasive, and every talk and conversation carried a level of ambition I'd never seen before. The Ethereum R&D machine is upgrading itself, and we will see the outcome of that on the network sooner than you think.

text:
Adding to this, a lot of people missed in the recent Jeff interview that he explicitly advocates for the HIP4 style approach for on chain options because it makes both parties pre-fund their obligations. Binaries are always fixed win/loss by nature, and if you stack them they just function as call/put spreads.

This is a necessity to be compatible with the existing risk engine, not an intentional design decision. This all but confirms that native vanilla options are not coming any time soon for Hyperliquid, otherwise he wouldn't be leaning into this approach.

Perps first platforms are strapping on binaries as an afterthought because it's easy, but you're also seeing the adoption, or rather lack thereof, they are receiving. 

People want not just path independence, but also the unbounded convexity and ability to long vol and tail events that only vanillas can provide. 

@DeriveXYZ is purpose built for options. I'm shocked that people find it so hard to believe that the venue purpose built for options will have a strong moat given that Deribit has survived the competition from Binance, OKX, and Bybit after all these years.

The @Lighter_xyz announcement today is bullish $DRV, not bearish. If vanilla options were so easy to add, they'd have done it already rather than adding binaries, which nobody really wants.

I'm bullish $LIT here too but binary options are a misnomer and nothingburger. They'll probably generate <$10,000 revenue between now and EOY.
author: koolkrypto223
quoted_text:
Because Binary options resolve to a fixed YES // NO typically at $1, the payoff is capped. So there's capped upside & less/different convexity. Vega, Gamma, & the other greeks also work differently for Binaries compared to Vanilla options (Derive)

All of this pretty much makes Binaries an inferior product. The pay-offs aren't as good, they're not as capital efficient for hedging, there's not really a concept of vol buying/selling, and you cannot construct as mature expressions of the market as you can with vanilla options

I think this alone explains a lot of the challenges we've seen in HIP-4 adoption (and challenges I expect lighter to have unless they incentivize these markets heavily). It is the case that perps are far simpler than options and it's easier to bootstrap liquidity, therefore they've had strong product market fit in crypto

HOWEVER, binaries options sit in a weird place. You still have the liquidity problems of vanilla options (you have to support liquidity at many strikes at many expiries) but an overall weaker payoff structure. This disincentives the creation of deep liquidity. It's just kinda not worth it for the more pro-tail to institutional type of traders who use options for what their actually intended for (mature expressions of path & volatility +plus some yield strategies). TLDR: Binaries are like an ugly middle child

The reason Hyperliquid & Lighter are starting with Binary options before moving to Vanilla options (if ever) is that the fact they resolve to the fixed $1 share amount, means they slot in easier into the existing risk & margin engines of the protocols. If you want to support true options then you need a risk engine built specifically with the convexity of options in mind rather than just linear returns like perps. I'm not an expert but everything I have learned so far & the experts I've talked to, are all adamant this would be a fundamental rewrite of risk engines and margining for Hyperliquid & Lighter - something I imagine both are reluctant to do, especially when they can still make a gazillion dollars by winning perps

^^ This also explains some of Crypto's centralized market structure as well. Binance & OKX have the most perps volume by a large margin, you'd expect them to also be leading in options but they aren't. The centralized options leaders are two entirely different exchanges Deribit and ByBit. Again, this is because market structure & risk engines are just a different thing for options. So we've seen the leaders in that space keep their lead despite well funded and talented competition. I don't think it's unfounded to believe that at least for the foreseeable future, Derive is in a position to keep it's lead and go toe-to-toe with the leading perps dexes at least in the domain of options.

TLDR: same reason I don't see Derive being competition to HL or LIT perps (it's just a complimentary part of their product offering) - I don't see HL or LIT being competition to Derive options (it's just a complimentary part of their product offering

All of this re-affirms why I'm so bullish on Derive ethereum:0xb1d1eae60eea9525032a6dcb4c1ce336a1de71be  as they STILL have 90%+ of market share for onchain options premium (what people are actually willing to pay to use the product).

quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

text:
I’ve seen the same framing in company after company. You’re either a hands-on individual contributor or a people manager. Everything else is treated as temporary or transitional.
That is a narrow way to think about how work actually gets done.
The people who create the most leverage are often the ones who stay close to the work while also shaping how teams decide, coordinate, and sequence effort. They do not need a formal reporting line to do that. They need judgment, context, and the ability to influence the system around them.
Companies that only recognize the two classic paths force those people to choose. Some step into management and lose the depth that made them valuable. Others stay pure ICs and never get the room to operate at the level the organization actually needs.
The constraint is not talent. It is the model. Once you stop treating management as the only legitimate way to grow influence, you start seeing roles that did not previously exist. Those roles are where a lot of the highest-leverage work sits.

We have traded options for almost 20 years, from a multi-billion notional vol book at a multi-strat to about $500M notional on @DeriveXYZ since December 2023, when it was still Lyra.

Binaries are one pan. Here is what the SPX surface cooked on 16 Oct (spot 7700) that a $1 YES/NO ticket cannot:

Calendar: Monday ATM vol 9.2, December 13.9. Sell two days of gamma, own two months of vega.

Skew: 20 Nov 90% put 24.2 vol, 110% call 12.5. A risk reversal owns the 11.8-point slope; a binary is one dot on it.

Put spread, the Hot7 hedge: buy 20 Nov 90% at 24.2, sell 80% at 36.7. The leg we sell is 12 vol points richer than the one we buy.

Gamma: 9.2 vol says Monday moves 0.58%. Hedge the straddle hourly, collect realized minus implied.

Tail: 20 Nov 80% put, strike 6162, pays per point below with no ceiling. A binary pays $1 at minus 20% and $1 at minus 60%.

Cheapest vol on the screen is 8.75, the 26 Oct 102.5% call. A binary cannot even order it.

TL;DR: a binary is a one-dish restaurant, fine for a Tuesday. A surface is a full kitchen: 18 strikes by 40 expiries on this screen, and we eat there every day.
author: D2_Finance
quoted_text:
Adding to this, a lot of people missed in the recent Jeff interview that he explicitly advocates for the HIP4 style approach for on chain options because it makes both parties pre-fund their obligations. Binaries are always fixed win/loss by nature, and if you stack them they just function as call/put spreads.

This is a necessity to be compatible with the existing risk engine, not an intentional design decision. This all but confirms that native vanilla options are not coming any time soon for Hyperliquid, otherwise he wouldn't be leaning into this approach.

Perps first platforms are strapping on binaries as an afterthought because it's easy, but you're also seeing the adoption, or rather lack thereof, they are receiving. 

People want not just path independence, but also the unbounded convexity and ability to long vol and tail events that only vanillas can provide. 

@DeriveXYZ is purpose built for options. I'm shocked that people find it so hard to believe that the venue purpose built for options will have a strong moat given that Deribit has survived the competition from Binance, OKX, and Bybit after all these years.

The @Lighter_xyz announcement today is bullish $DRV, not bearish. If vanilla options were so easy to add, they'd have done it already rather than adding binaries, which nobody really wants.

I'm bullish $LIT here too but binary options are a misnomer and nothingburger. They'll probably generate <$10,000 revenue between now and EOY.

text:
MSTR 盘中跌逾 8%，MSCI 指数资格开始影响融资预期

$MSTR 这次跌得明显比 bitcoin:native 多。截止到目前已经下跌超过 9%，同期 Bitcoin 也只跌了 1% 左右。两者差了约 8 个百分点，主要下跌的原因就是这次 MSCI 指数资格带来的。

MSCI 在 15 日美股收盘后宣布，将实施针对非经营性公司的新筛选规则，最终受影响名单会在 11月11日 公布，调整于 11月30日 收盘生效。这次的规则会检查公司的经营性资产和财务指标，判断公司是否更接近持有投资资产的工具。此前用 5 月数据做模拟时 Strategy 已经被列为潜在剔除对象。

Strategy 一直反对这套规则，认为自己把 Bitcoin 业务作为经营分部披露，也在主动进行融资和资本管理。但 MSCI 还是决定实施，接下来就要看 Strategy 是否出现在最终名单里。

按照 Strategy 此前的披露，跟踪相关 MSCI 指数的基金大约持有 1,300 万股 MSTR，占当时基本股本的 3.1%。用这次 138 美元的盘中价格粗算，这批股票价值约 18 亿美元。如果最终被剔除，相关基金就需要按新指数调整仓位，即便基金经理仍然看好 BTC，也得处理不再符合指数要求的 MSTR。

总的来说，11月11日 最终名单公布后，如果 MSTR 被剔除，就会有基金经历在规则的情况下不得不去减仓 MSTR 的股份，所以现在已经开始有投资者离场了。才造成了差价的拉大。

text:
AI is making Ethereum more ambitious.

You might have heard about the challenges that blockchains face in a post-AI world, and while security assumptions will surely be stress-tested in the coming months and years, there is another side to it. I believe AI will let us speedrun towards a world that's both more secure and feature-rich.

As we look towards Ethereum's first post-AI upgrade, Hegotá, the R&D community is asking itself what increasingly powerful tools could help us do differently:

> How far can we push both security and iteration speed?
> How much of the design space can we examine before committing to one?
> How easily can we test the interactions between complex features?

My recent formal verification work @ethlabs_org has given me some reasons to be optimistic about these, as work that would have previously not even been attempted is now being done by agents in days. In September, I posted about using formal verification as part of designing a new consensus protocol. This time, I want to tell you about formally verifying something already fully specified and in production: Ethereum's Fast Confirmation Rule (FCR).

If you are not familiar with FCR, it lets applications confirm Ethereum blocks in seconds, roughly 30x faster than waiting for finality, under additional assumptions (from waiting 13 minutes to 24 seconds!). It also further solidifies Ethereum L1's case as an asset hub and center of gravity for the onchain economy. FCR now has a safety proof in Lean, closely modeling the rule in the consensus specs, which is the source of truth for Ethereum's consensus clients.

Some takeaways:

> FCR is safe! Under its assumptions, confirmed blocks remain canonical. On top of the manual proofs from the paper, we now have Lean proofs of this for the actual spec, additional evidence for applications considering FCR!

> The bulk of the formal verification work took just a 4-5 days (check out the animation!), with agents working mostly unsupervised. We should be very ambitious about using this as a tool at scale.

> After verifying the current rule, it was easy to adapt the model to the upcoming Gloas changes. Immediately, this surfaced a subtle bug caused by changes to fork choice. The problem was in the spec itself and not a gap in the model. The safety proof would not go through, and the agents could precisely pinpoint what was causing it to fail. The bug is now fixed, and formal verification of the corrected protocol goes through.

Iteration is never quite over, even for "finished" features like FCR, because the protocol keeps evolving around them. A formal model lets us ensure that key properties keep holding throughout the evolution of the protocol. With these capabilities, Ethereum can and should keep upgrading faster, tightening fork timelines and exploring more ambitious features, while still raising the security bar.

This picture has been getting much clearer over the past few months, and the past week confirmed it for me, as @drakefjustin and @corcoranwill brought together 100+ Ethereum researchers, cryptographers and formal verification experts in Cambridge for six days of workshops on post-quantum cryptography, formal verification and fast finality. Beyond its own workshop, formal verification was the omnipresent star of the week: everyone is using Lean and doing amazing things with it! Piece by piece, Ethereum's technological core is being rebuilt for the post-AI age.

The excitement was palpable, the sense of optimism was pervasive, and every talk and conversation carried a level of ambition I'd never seen before. The Ethereum R&D machine is upgrading itself, and we will see the outcome of that on the network sooner than you think.

把四个轮子死死按在地面上，轮胎打滑的百年死穴被直接抹平。

然后是 07:52 开始的火箭推进器演示，把原本属于航天发射的姿态控制下放到了柏油路上。

车身四周的高压冷气喷嘴不仅在直线加速时提供纯粹的物理反冲，甚至在空中腾跃时能独立修正姿态，

现场直接完成了一个惊人的 Kickflip 翻滚，而且车载压缩机能边跑边自充气储能，把外挂推力做成了可持续的循环弹药。

但全场最耐人寻味、也最让人感慨的，是 18:52 那句关于驾驶者的终极定性。 

在特斯拉全力押注无人驾驶的今天，马斯克一边把这台车做成了能短时悬浮的飞行机器，一边把它定义为最后一款专为人类手动驾驶打造的特斯拉，

它用最极致的航天科技，给那个由人类亲手握住方向盘的旧时代办了一场最奢华的告别仪式。

以前是人靠着橡胶轮胎跟地面摩擦力死磕，从今天起是直接借用航天的反冲力在三维空间里贴地飞行。 当速度被重新定义，速度机器的终局注定不再只是关于电池了。

这 20 分钟里最让你感到震撼的是 0.81 秒的起步加速，还是底盘风扇抽气制造的负压贴地？

最大的感受是，在静止状态下靠底盘风扇瞬间吸出 2G 下压力，真的是我觉得全场最反直觉的工程设计，

完整 20 分钟视频的高能时间戳和物理原理拆解笔记，我都整理好放在一楼了。

It’s a wrap! It was an honor to help organize the Fast Finality workshop in Cambridge.

There have already been some great recaps, but here’s my quick overview of the main topics we covered:

1. Deep-diving DC: Decoupled Consensus is a super ambitious upgrade we hope to ship in I* (h/t @benjaminion_xyz). @robsaltini gave a great overview, and @fradamt unveiled his impressive recent breakthroughs, e.g. achieving short-term async resilience through local locks.

2. Shipping DC: Sessions on critical research and engineering, including networking benchmarks & devnets (@sukunrt & Csaba), rewards & incentives (@weboftrees), and specs & testing (@mkalinin2, @jtraglia, @tcoratger).

3. Securing DC: Formal verification meets fast finality. We explored exciting new AI-enabled opportunities (@fradamt & @robsaltini), building on years of great FV work (@alexanderlhicks).

4. Future of Fast Finality: Aligning DC with future needs. This covered PQ networking (@kamil_abiy & @kevaundray), finality in tens of seconds with PQ validators (@barnabemonnot), lean clients & prototyping (@pablodeymo, Mega, Mihir, Locky, @adust09, @ladislaus0x), and one-round finality & other future research (shoutout @alranpe, @jneu_net, @ittai & Neil).

Huge thanks to everyone who made this workshop a success! Special thanks to @benjaminion_xyz for all the help and guidance, and of course to @justindrake and @willcorcoran for making it possible!

text:
There's too much happening to list it all, but here are some highlights of the ongoing formal verification work, with special thanks to the people carrying it forward and getting Ethereum ready for the post-quantum and post-AI era.

@drakefjustin and the Ethereum Foundation @ethereumfndn had the foresight to make two big bets long before AI made them table stakes: formal verification and post-quantum security. @alexanderlhicks pioneered Verified zkEVM, bringing the EF's formal verification and cryptography teams and dozens of grantees together to verify the full zkEVM stack, while the EF cryptography team, the @leanEthereum effort and a dedicated PQ team have been laying the ground for a PQ Ethereum.

Now we reap the benefits, as AI makes security needs more urgent but also multiplies this strong foundation and accumulated expertise, propagating formal verification across the Ethereum stack and accelerating the PQ timelines.

The core Ethereum specs are already transforming, incorporating Lean for some of their critical components: the cryptography specs bring BLS and KZG into Lean, with proofs by Benedikt Wagner and @asanso, @tcoratger wrote the new SSZ specs, and @jtraglia integrated both into the consensus specs.

Meanwhile, the amount of forward-looking work is impossible to keep up with: @tcoratger added the post-quantum XMSS signature scheme to the cryptography specs; Benedikt proved the security of the proposed post-quantum data availability sampling scheme (code); and @asn_d6, Benedikt and @Khovr are proving that the pieces of a recursive zkVM proof fit together securely.

Industry teams are all in too: @JulekSU and the @Nethermind FV team formalized FRI in ArkLib, are now on STIR and WHIR, and built a Lean model of the EVM and Yul covering Cancun, while @rv_inc is connecting Rust cryptographic code to Lean proofs.

Another incredible trend at the intersection of AI and formal verification is autoresearch challenges, where agents compete in the open to improve a verifiable metric: https://t.co/PgQZySqnHi (EF formal verification team, @yukonresearch, @zksecurityXYZ) on the coding theory behind SNARK security, https://t.co/l4fCEFulzc (@yukonresearch, @ethereumfndn) on smaller post-quantum signatures, https://t.co/SzRFBZ1Ctg (@zksecurityXYZ) on cheaper ZK circuits, and https://t.co/Cv3hURdk3s (@SuccinctLabs, @EspressoSys) on a faster post-quantum prover.

As for the FCR work, check it out here: 
Lean formalization [https://t.co/mzUQSBcKhy]
Gloas fix [https://t.co/Hu3UL5meub]

Lots of the threads that the R&D ecosystem has been working on for years are coming together, and Ethereum could hardly be better prepared for as transformative a moment as this one.

Ascend Properties manages a portfolio of luxury rentals in Big Sky, Montana, one of the country’s top ski destinations.

Weak December snowfall doesn’t just hurt the holidays. It drags down bookings for the rest of the season.

So rather than hope for powder, Adam Farr, who runs Ascend, hedged the risk on Kalshi. He took a $2,000 position on Big Sky getting below-average snowfall in December.

If the snow comes, bookings run as normal and Ascend serves the ski crowd like any other season.

If it doesn’t, the Kalshi position pays out, helping offset lost bookings while Ascend waits for winter to show up.

Either way, Adam’s business is protected.

IMO: The ETFs and Treasury companies created a problem. 

Tradfi traders and investors correlate all stocks to the stock market indexes. So hard money decentralized assets like Bitcoin, Solana and Ethereum got trojan horsed into ETF stock wrappers collerated to companies that rely on humans, debt and general human economic factors. 

These shell companies dont do anything but hold digital assets for shareholders. But their shared ETF ticker is gambled and valued correlated to the indexes. 

Especially for gamblers. Remember Options and Futures are 1000x more liquid than the spot market. 

We will continue to suffer from the correlation to the US stock market and the "macro" due to these vehicles and the betting on their outcome. 

Now Ive always been obsessed with correlations. Bitcoin correlated to the DXY for a while, then to Gold, then to the SPY, now to Stable Coin Marketcap blended with SPY and Gold, who knows whats next. 

Its good to be reminded how connected all dollar markets are, and whether they are entitely manipulated as profit making casinos.

All I know is there is more gambling in the world now than there was when I was young.  We are being pushed to speculation and gambling. This was the same playbook in 1925/6. They pushed citizens to gambling that led to the crash in 1929. 

This crash is a debt crash. The underlying companies collatoral evaporates, the casino crashes. Bitcoin should shield against this well. But the price of Bitcoin is correlated to the stock market so the gamblers will follow the crash. This leaves scenarios:
- After the quick recovery, a V shaped chart, certain assets change dominance in dollar value.

A collatoral scuffle will begin.

Resting heart is the new thirst trap

It’s the sexiest thing about you

Since 2021 I’ve posted about RHR:

> 207 times
> generating 366,220 likes 
> 78.3 million views
> these numbers are X only

Now it’s a mainstream symbol of high status

People will adopt something if it helps them get access to sex, money or power.

Resting heart rate before bed was my first big aha moment in my health quest. I discovered that it was the single number to rule all other numbers. 

RHR is the composite number for food, exercise, stress, routine, discipline, nervous systems, mood and more. It’s endlessly useful. 

I had to break RHR out of esoteric health and into status and social signaling. RHR needed to represent a person’s youth and vibrancy and signal genetic fitness.

So I hit the topic from more than ten angles: 

> masculinity 
> cognitive performance
> fertility 
> sexual health 
> discipline
> will power 
> judgement
> health
> peer status 
> values 
> rebellion against status quo

Others saw the social leverage and started working on their RHR to post. Press started picking it up, putting my name and resting heart rate in the headline.

The science behind a lower resting heart rate is solid. It is a composite health marker of a person’s biological vitality.

If you’re new to resting heart rate, here is a quick guide.

Health is confusing, and overwhelming. 

But your heart makes things really easy. 

> a low resting heart rate before bed is good
> a high resting heart rate before bed is bad

If my RHR is 41 before bed, a perfect night sleep awaits:

+ asleep in less than five min
+ 4 hr of restorative sleep
+ 0 to 1 wake events 
+ awake no more than 20 minutes 

That's the 99% percentile sleep performance for an 18 year old. As you age, it's increasingly harder to sleep. 

If you’re sleep is good, life is good. 

So here is where you can start: 

+ finish all food 4 hours before bed 
+ screens off 30-60 min before bed 
+ finish caffeine around noon 
+ avoid blue light, use red and amber instead 
+ read a book before bed
+ have a 30-60 min wind down routine including walking, journaling, breath work meditation, talking to friends, a chill hobby, etc. 

Do these things and I promise every part of your life will improve.

老东家又一个新历程！之前参与过的面向人类用户的Cobo Wallet要关停了，全力聚焦AI业务。

视频里放了几张图片，挨个说下：
1. 图1是Cobo三位老板，神鱼 @bitfish 、长浩和中间的尧总，现在尧总去做滑雪板和运动硬科技相关创业了，做的也非常好。

2. 图2是当年Cobo在望京那边的办公室，一个Loft办公室结构，楼上楼下，那时候运营在楼上产研在楼下，两位老板就直接坐在楼下，非常互联网非常扁平，我刚去Cobo时候大概40-50人？然后后来陆续到70+人。

3. 图3是19年7月19在三亚团建拍的全部团队成员合影，那时候我们在做Staking业务，我记得也开始尝试抵押借贷了，也是那个时候开始全员学期权，什么跨式蝶式，然后后面20年就紧接着312了，312那时候疫情大家在家办公开会帮客户降杠杆，因为那时候很多钱包产品也推出了双倍三倍囤币，带杠杆做多BTC。

4. 图4是19年夏天摆摊好像是，当时做了一个纪念BTC的礼盒叫“Bitcoin2049”，收获了很多行业好评，然后某天好像是为了宣传还是咋就拉🐟总楼下摆摊拍了个照。

刚才和同事聊（我们同事也很多Ex-Cobo），勾起了很多回忆又，Cobo是一家很神奇的公司，包括不限于在：
1. 很长时间整个团队大概70人，但内部成了5对新人，都走向了结婚👰。

2. Cobo是一家创新和爱折腾的公司，从2017年到现在，也是最早一批托管钱包和自托管钱包融合在在一个App里，并且2017就在all in mobile，我们没做过网页从第一天开始。

3. Cobo也是一家“另类”的公司，在所有和Token有关热潮中，我们没发币没做损害用户利益的事情，某种程度上也是🐟总和长浩价值观的体现，所以在整个行业里也确实是个另类的慢公司。

4. Cobo的人都很靠谱，无论是在职还是离职老同事，都是踏实做事的人，我们 @bagel_win 团队一半以上也都是来自Cobo老员工，大家文化和价值观都很相符，完全可以背靠背信任。

5. 长期主义，入行第一天鱼总每次all hands就给大家说让大家囤币，少做波段，很容易在漫长的周期里BTC本位越来越少，这句话我听到今天受益匪浅，还记得2018年那时候Cobo工资就可以选一部分BTC或者ETH，我每个月都是最大比例BTC，然后每月定投至今，感谢🐟总跨越周期的建议，非常感恩。

今天喝了点酒，感慨很多，感谢入行就加入Cobo这家特别的公司，跟🐟总学到了很多，长期生存和行业变化怎么应对，也让我成为了一个彻底坚信行业坚信BTC的hodler。

感谢在Cobo的那3年+的时光，希望老东家越来越好！

Solana just had its event in China shut down.

And the funniest part is that CZ basically warned about this one day earlier.

First Solana Foundation announced that it has opened an office in Pudong, occupying one of the highest commercial office spaces

All of this in a country where crypto is heavily restricted.

A day before CZ notices Solana’s expansion and publicly comments on how surprising it is.

He says it’s amazing that Solana can advertise and open an office in China.

(Especially considering BNB Chain hasn’t been able to do the same)

Sounds pretty reasonable, right?

Well, less than 24 hours later…

The first event was supposed to take place at the Shangri-La hotel in Shanghai.

The event was scheduled to begin at 10 AM.

Instead, attendees arrived to find police officers at the venue.

You genuinely cannot make this stuff up.

Around noon, organizers sent an apology email arguing “Venue logistics considerations.”

CZ them posted:

“Sad to see. Looks like they really didn’t know the local policies?”

And reminded everyone that something similar had happened less than a year ago.

I’ve seen people joking that he snitched on them.

I actually respect Solana’s ambition to expand into one of the biggest markets

But I think there’s a difference between building blockchain infrastructure in China and publicly promoting a crypto ecosystem

This week Solana might have crossed that line and CZ is probably thinking he told them so.

text:
How should a responsible agent handle a $100,000 treasury when 3 data sources disagree? A stage by stage walkthrough.

⚠️ Fully hypothetical: no real treasury, no funds, no wallet action, no transaction. Educational only.

The setup
An agent is asked to rebalance part of the treasury. The asset price comes in from 3 sources:
A: $100.00
B: $100.40
C: $94.00
They don't agree, and acting on the wrong one could misprice a $100k decision.

Stage 1: Ingest and check freshness

Timestamp every input. Anything older than 60s is marked stale and excluded. Here all 3 are fresh.

Stage 2: Find the anchor

Median = $100.00. Deviation from it: A 0%, B 0.4%, C 6%.

Stage 3: Quorum check

Do at least 2 of 3 sources sit within 1% of the median? A and B do, so quorum is met. C is flagged as an outlier and excluded. It is not averaged in, because averaging would drag the price to ~$98.13.

Stage 4: Confidence score (illustrative)

Start at 1.00 and subtract for each problem:
• −0.05 per outlier
• −0.05 if the agreeing sources differ by more than 0.5%
Here: 1.00 − 0.05 = 0.95

Stage 5: Threshold = 0.90

Why 0.90 here? 
A 6% pricing error on $100k is about $6,000, and the move may not be reversible. At that stake, "probably right" isn't enough. This is my choice for this hypothetical example, not an official or universal standard.

Stage 6: Decide

0.95 ≥ 0.90, so the agent may proceed using the A/B consensus price. Below 0.90, it takes no action and escalates to a human with the evidence.

Stage 7: Log

Record inputs, the outlier, the score and the decision so anyone can audit it.

🛑 Refusal condition
If fewer than 2 of 3 sources agree within 1% of the median, there is no quorum. The flow stops at Stage 3. The agent refuses to act, computes no score, and hands off to a human.
No consensus = no action.

Takeaway
A good agent doesn't pick the source it likes. It checks freshness, finds consensus, drops outliers, scores confidence, and knows exactly when to stop.

text:
AI is making Ethereum more ambitious.

You might have heard about the challenges that blockchains face in a post-AI world, and while security assumptions will surely be stress-tested in the coming months and years, there is another side to it. I believe AI will let us speedrun towards a world that's both more secure and feature-rich.

As we look towards Ethereum's first post-AI upgrade, Hegotá, the R&D community is asking itself what increasingly powerful tools could help us do differently:

> How far can we push both security and iteration speed?
> How much of the design space can we examine before committing to one?
> How easily can we test the interactions between complex features?

My recent formal verification work @ethlabs_org has given me some reasons to be optimistic about these, as work that would have previously not even been attempted is now being done by agents in days. In September, I posted about using formal verification as part of designing a new consensus protocol. This time, I want to tell you about formally verifying something already fully specified and in production: Ethereum's Fast Confirmation Rule (FCR).

If you are not familiar with FCR, it lets applications confirm Ethereum blocks in seconds, roughly 30x faster than waiting for finality, under additional assumptions (from waiting 13 minutes to 24 seconds!). It also further solidifies Ethereum L1's case as an asset hub and center of gravity for the onchain economy. FCR now has a safety proof in Lean, closely modeling the rule in the consensus specs, which is the source of truth for Ethereum's consensus clients.

Some takeaways:

> FCR is safe! Under its assumptions, confirmed blocks remain canonical. On top of the manual proofs from the paper, we now have Lean proofs of this for the actual spec, additional evidence for applications considering FCR!

> The bulk of the formal verification work took just a 4-5 days (check out the animation!), with agents working mostly unsupervised. We should be very ambitious about using this as a tool at scale.

> After verifying the current rule, it was easy to adapt the model to the upcoming Gloas changes. Immediately, this surfaced a subtle bug caused by changes to fork choice. The problem was in the spec itself and not a gap in the model. The safety proof would not go through, and the agents could precisely pinpoint what was causing it to fail. The bug is now fixed, and formal verification of the corrected protocol goes through.

Iteration is never quite over, even for "finished" features like FCR, because the protocol keeps evolving around them. A formal model lets us ensure that key properties keep holding throughout the evolution of the protocol. With these capabilities, Ethereum can and should keep upgrading faster, tightening fork timelines and exploring more ambitious features, while still raising the security bar.

This picture has been getting much clearer over the past few months, and the past week confirmed it for me, as @drakefjustin and @corcoranwill brought together 100+ Ethereum researchers, cryptographers and formal verification experts in Cambridge for six days of workshops on post-quantum cryptography, formal verification and fast finality. Beyond its own workshop, formal verification was the omnipresent star of the week: everyone is using Lean and doing amazing things with it! Piece by piece, Ethereum's technological core is being rebuilt for the post-AI age.

The excitement was palpable, the sense of optimism was pervasive, and every talk and conversation carried a level of ambition I'd never seen before. The Ethereum R&D machine is upgrading itself, and we will see the outcome of that on the network sooner than you think.

As I’m sitting in urgent care waiting to get an xray on my achilles, pissed off that I have to deal with this right before an international flight, an old man sitting next to me starts chatting me up

His leg is bandaged. He tells me he lives in Malibu and dealing with El Niño. and the other night a huge wave crashed into his living room while he was inside. Shattered the windows and piece of glass cut through his leg

Despite the injury his house was flooding, so he started drilling holes in the first floor to let the water drain.

At this point I’m like damn, this dude is a G. Then I remember… didn’t Malibu also get hit by the LA fires last year?

I ask him and he goes, oh yeah. He had 3 hoses going and helped stop the fire just before it reached his house. But he got burned in the process. I notice the burn marks on his face and arms 

He wishes me good luck w the Achilles and walks off before I catch his name 

I think I’ll be alright

Privacy started the year as something we had to make the case for. Now it feels like everyone agrees we need it to move the industry forward. 

During my conversation with @midnightfdn's CTO @SebastienGllmt at Quantum & Privacy Day, hosted by @QuantusNetwork and @NEARProtocol in Singapore, I reflected on joining @0xMiden around the time of our seed fundraise. 

One of the first things I asked the team was which investors had passed and why. Some of that skepticism came down to whether privacy was important enough to build around.

It has been interesting to watch the narrative change, with established chains now investing in privacy features. Recently, the head of digital assets at a major US bank told me she did not see the industry reaching mainstream adoption without privacy. 

As institutions begin transacting with one another onchain, the confidentiality they expect in the rest of their business has to be there too. 

Privacy is more than a CT narrative, and alongside PQ resistance, it will increasingly shape which blockchains institutions choose to build on.

Jad Naous of @grepr_ai asks a16z's Martin Casado if AI can do a VC's job:

Martin: "My model for VC is it's very relationship driven. I just have a belief that markets are actually pretty efficient. It's not about finding the company that nobody else finds. I think people all find the right company."

Engineering leaders told Grepr founder and CEO Jad Naous they spend 5 to 20% of their infrastructure budget on observability, and it's buying less and less reliability.

Jad, a former a16z partner, joins a16z's Martin Casado to discuss whether AI can run production systems as well as it writes code.

Grepr sits in a company's log stream, can scan a petabyte of logs a day, cuts observability costs by about 90%, and is building AI agents that use those signals to troubleshoot production issues.

How AI is changing engineering at Jad's 10-person company:
- A data lake feature that once took one engineer about six months took Jad 10 days
- The gap between okay and great engineers on his team "just multiplied 10X"
- He runs 3-4 agent sessions at once, with a "tech lead" agent reviewing every PR

Why running live systems is a harder problem for AI:
- Jad: AI can almost tune databases, but can't yet keep servers running on its own
- Martin: every bit of code doubles the ways a program can behave, which is why humans still own systems
- The real world is messier than AI's training data, self-driving took 20 years and $170B

author: AndrewCurran_
quoted_text:
it’s been a dramatic couple of days, I didn’t expect the already clean essay to be read so widely. I've heard more interesting discussions about mechanistic interpretability – should we think mostly in features or mechanisms and the flow of data through them, how much do weak activations matter, how does scale change things, and lots of other questions – than I have in a long time and I’ve been happy to hear all the discussion!

a couple things on the essay itself. it didn't have enough citations, only ones for the basic story, since it was an "informal research essay and working hypothesis" rather than a paper, and other prior work around neurons were in the technical paper we're still finishing up. but it blew up, so I've added citations to the essay as well. I also want to thank @curttigges who did a lot of the language neuron research with me

finally, while there was quite a range of updates, from this being incremental and obvious to interpretability going from hopeless to fully solved, I want to try to be clear about roughly where I stand

I used to think neural networks would take some big cleaning step and then we could begin the ordinary natural science of mapping the parts and how they connect, watching data flow through, mapping circuits, and so on.

at various points, like late layers of early model organisms and most layers of language models years ago, this didn't really work. but now with better tools and better models of study, it works much better

for smaller vision models, this normal science process worked surprisingly well, until the whole map started to be broadly filled in. For bigger modern language models, it seems promising so far, for both neurons and circuits, attribution graphs, basically everywhere we've glanced. the map isn't filling in, there's a lot of map. there's still off-target firing, neurons that do a few things, but so far it's not an incoherent mess that you can't explore and learn from, and over time we get better at learning how to see it.

so maybe it keeps going, and mapping motifs and exploring actually gets you pretty far, maybe something like "all the way" to a reasonable solution. I don't think it would be so scientifically surprising if that were the case. everything in the neural network was built in some sense to be read – by its downstream readers – and if we can learn to look like a reader, we might find reading them relatively easy. many researchers I talk to outside interpretability assume the parts are already understandable, and the difficulty is just in the mapping stage!

it was also my prior when I first started looking at neurons when I first joined the field. there's lots of highly interpretable ones, maybe that's just how neural networks are if you look right.

even in the good world it would still take some iteration on tools, on ways of looking, neuron-attention interactions are tricky for instance. there's probably no bright red line separating "cleaning the model" from "learning to look better" but there's broad working principles, and as of now I think we should try to look relatively directly if we can

it shouldn't be so hard to test, you can just start looking at things and iterating and trying to understand motifs and such and see if it just breaks down at some point. it can take some iteration, I would recommend a bias against assuming arbitrary mixtures when you don't understand something at first, but also explanations should be tested

for now I'm pretty optimistic, and I'm glad there's excitement about interpretability, but too much can cause problems too. I think part might be that ai safety isn't a very hopeful field, and even moderate amounts of optimism about an important problem being solvable in the future fills a spot that has been malnourished for a while. across several safety disciplines, the researchers directly working on them are often more optimistic than the people broadcasting pessimism more broadly

for neural network interpretability at least, these are extraordinarily experimentally accessible objects of science, I don't know of a better one, and we have automated scientists. we have many things going in our favor. it's important and it's fun. the circuitry of these machines can be beautiful, surprising, entertaining, and insightful. I've spent thousands of hours looking through them, asking questions and running experiments and testing things, and would do so even if it weren't so important. I think the problem is solvable, whether the simple thing works, it mostly works but we need some new things, or we need big new ideas. I think we can figure it out

text:
Houston: we have a slop problem.

This is a problem at every scale. Even inside our company we see we can produce lots of things, but can't verify those things are correct/useful. And looking to use agents to verify makes the problem worse. Verification is the bottleneck. We can't trust that the agent actually did the correct thing.

We all want to rush to say AGI or SI is here. But this is a real problem. Where the human can choose or verify the output, AI is a game changer. But when the output becomes too much or too broad to verify, you end up with a heap of slop. This is what's happening to math proofs. And what happens with an open ended task in a company.

text:
how do you trust your agents' work more? copy this post/link and give it to your @bot or agent!

1. codebase improvements: this is just good software engineering - better architecture, stronger types and invariants, clear boundaries. agents love to copy what exists and take the shortest path, so make the easy thing the right thing. categorically eliminate problems through code and you won't need to think about it again.
2. static analysis: lint rules, tests, CI, verification (eg TLA+). very token efficient ways to catch issues ahead of time.
3. prose: comments, rules, AGENTS.md, skills - anything that can't be enforced and requires agent judgment. use it minimally, but do use /create-verification-skill.
4. human review: the hardest to scale. at the rate agents land code, it's pretty much impossible to thoroughly review every PR, so spend that effort on the highest leverage point, designing an environment where agents do the right thing by default.

this forms an inverse pyramid: you want most of your effort at the top, least at the bottom. codebase improvements are deterministic, making it more token efficient, and lets you sleep more soundly at night.

install https://t.co/u9xIlN3eN0 and create a new Project:
1. look through my slack/chat messages and code review comments where i've given feedback on PRs, code, architecture
2. use /recall on my past transcripts to learn how i steer agents
3. /poteto-mode use /correct and /architect on past commits to find the most common pitfalls agents fall into, then propose a plan to rearchitect the code i own so it's more agent friendly. answer open questions with prototyping rather than defer to me, and back the plan with real data. 
4. before you begin, use /sharpen + /in-your-own-words and confirm this prompt with me

text:
Back-to-back APAC conference weeks are finally over. Some takeaways:

KBW: Smaller and more institutional than last year. Suits to hoodies is a real ratio. Korean banks and corporates still can’t hold or trade crypto, but they’re preparing for rule changes next year and focusing on tokenization and stablecoins. Korea’s volume is historically retail-driven, so next year’s capital gains tax will test whether that holds.

TOKEN2049 SG: Bigger venue, lower attendance. The biggest names ran their own events, and there were far fewer side events as budgets tightened. Sentiment feels cautiously positive as prices improve, but it’s been a hard year. Few token launches, some market makers are winding down, and many venture funds are underperforming on venture investments while turning to liquid positions instead.

What stood out:
- Revenue and business models matter more than narratives
- General-purpose infra comes up far less; purpose-built infra quietly serves real use cases
- Perps are crowded, but there’s still room to compete on asset variety (crypto + tokenized assets) and liquidity

Bottom line: the industry is shifting from narrative to fundamentals. The projects that last will be the ones with real revenue, real users, and infrastructure built for a specific use case.

P.S. got to catch Singapore’s first-ever F1 sprint race. All the intensity in half the time. Thanks @KASTxyz for hosting me!

text:
Quoting from the blog:

'Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing classical algorithms, so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.

Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum circuits. These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run.

We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds. Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms.'

text:
Adding to this, a lot of people missed in the recent Jeff interview that he explicitly advocates for the HIP4 style approach for on chain options because it makes both parties pre-fund their obligations. Binaries are always fixed win/loss by nature, and if you stack them they just function as call/put spreads.

This is a necessity to be compatible with the existing risk engine, not an intentional design decision. This all but confirms that native vanilla options are not coming any time soon for Hyperliquid, otherwise he wouldn't be leaning into this approach.

Perps first platforms are strapping on binaries as an afterthought because it's easy, but you're also seeing the adoption, or rather lack thereof, they are receiving. 

People want not just path independence, but also the unbounded convexity and ability to long vol and tail events that only vanillas can provide. 

@DeriveXYZ is purpose built for options. I'm shocked that people find it so hard to believe that the venue purpose built for options will have a strong moat given that Deribit has survived the competition from Binance, OKX, and Bybit after all these years.

The @Lighter_xyz announcement today is bullish $DRV, not bearish. If vanilla options were so easy to add, they'd have done it already rather than adding binaries, which nobody really wants.

I'm bullish $LIT here too but binary options are a misnomer and nothingburger. They'll probably generate <$10,000 revenue between now and EOY.
author: DeFi_Dad
quoted_text:
Because Binary options resolve to a fixed YES // NO typically at $1, the payoff is capped. So there's capped upside & less/different convexity. Vega, Gamma, & the other greeks also work differently for Binaries compared to Vanilla options (Derive)

All of this pretty much makes Binaries an inferior product. The pay-offs aren't as good, they're not as capital efficient for hedging, there's not really a concept of vol buying/selling, and you cannot construct as mature expressions of the market as you can with vanilla options

I think this alone explains a lot of the challenges we've seen in HIP-4 adoption (and challenges I expect lighter to have unless they incentivize these markets heavily). It is the case that perps are far simpler than options and it's easier to bootstrap liquidity, therefore they've had strong product market fit in crypto

HOWEVER, binaries options sit in a weird place. You still have the liquidity problems of vanilla options (you have to support liquidity at many strikes at many expiries) but an overall weaker payoff structure. This disincentives the creation of deep liquidity. It's just kinda not worth it for the more pro-tail to institutional type of traders who use options for what their actually intended for (mature expressions of path & volatility +plus some yield strategies). TLDR: Binaries are like an ugly middle child

The reason Hyperliquid & Lighter are starting with Binary options before moving to Vanilla options (if ever) is that the fact they resolve to the fixed $1 share amount, means they slot in easier into the existing risk & margin engines of the protocols. If you want to support true options then you need a risk engine built specifically with the convexity of options in mind rather than just linear returns like perps. I'm not an expert but everything I have learned so far & the experts I've talked to, are all adamant this would be a fundamental rewrite of risk engines and margining for Hyperliquid & Lighter - something I imagine both are reluctant to do, especially when they can still make a gazillion dollars by winning perps

^^ This also explains some of Crypto's centralized market structure as well. Binance & OKX have the most perps volume by a large margin, you'd expect them to also be leading in options but they aren't. The centralized options leaders are two entirely different exchanges Deribit and ByBit. Again, this is because market structure & risk engines are just a different thing for options. So we've seen the leaders in that space keep their lead despite well funded and talented competition. I don't think it's unfounded to believe that at least for the foreseeable future, Derive is in a position to keep it's lead and go toe-to-toe with the leading perps dexes at least in the domain of options.

TLDR: same reason I don't see Derive being competition to HL or LIT perps (it's just a complimentary part of their product offering) - I don't see HL or LIT being competition to Derive options (it's just a complimentary part of their product offering

All of this re-affirms why I'm so bullish on Derive ethereum:0xb1d1eae60eea9525032a6dcb4c1ce336a1de71be  as they STILL have 90%+ of market share for onchain options premium (what people are actually willing to pay to use the product).

5. 不要只盯着国内内卷，面向全球80亿人寻找商机，借助AI打破语言壁垒。

6. 一个认知不能吃一辈子，要不停迭代更新自己的认知。

7. 20‑40岁要储备基础肌肉量，体能是抓住机遇的底层基础，也就是薄肌理论。

8. AI会让算力、知识变得越来越便宜，但无法延长人的寿命，寿命与健康是宝贵资产。

9. 未来三年，机会会逐步从纯聊天AI，转向物理AI硬件赛道。

10. 要有屏蔽噪音的能力，不要被外界的评价干扰自己的行动，也就是黄毛理论。

text:
Just finished listening to Jensen Huang with Brad Gerstner on the BG2 podcast

Probably one of the best things you can spend 90 minutes of your time listening to this weekend. Highly recommend.

Some of my takeaways from the conversation

1. The demand for compute will continue to be exponential. He once again cited inference as the biggest reason. Reasoning takes a lot more compute than simply spitting out answers from stored memory of knowledge

2. As more compute is used, the work and answer quality will also be better. This will lead to higher demand for that compute, leading to the exponential cycle that Jensen is referencing

3. The harness and tool usage have been the two biggest unlocks in AI over the last year. AI used to simply be a brain of knowledge. Now it has a skeleton around it that allows it to be useful. It is learning how to use existing tools to do better work without having to recreate tools from scratch each time.

4. The cost of intelligence will fall fairly quickly in the coming years. This will be driven by a combination of more compute coming online and better efficiency of models. No different than Moore's Law. Jensen still believes that the consumption of the intelligence (volume) will more than make up for the decline in pricing

5. The original GPT-1 cost $20M to train. If you train GPT-1 today, that number would be closer to $100. That is how fast the cost of intelligence is coming down.

6. The offset to this has been usage of the models and human ambition to build even better models. Despite cost coming down, usage of models has gone up 1M (x) times since GPT-1. 

7. Jensen disagrees that work hours are going to come down. The more you learn, the more you want to do. Human ambitions have always existed to achieve and earn more. The bottleneck was the opportunity to do it.

8. Robotics is entering its ChatGPT moment. Similar to what Elon did with cars, every physical aspect of the world will soon be digitized with software and compute. Every massive corporation will have to reinvent itself as a technology company with AI

9. Safety is a core component of accelerating AI technology. When you think of a car, you don't just think of the engine. The airbags and braking systems are components of this car. Similarly, regulation and safety are core components of AI

10. NVIDIA's share of capex with the Neocloud customers is roughly 80%. With the cloud service providers, it is closer to 40%. Both of these numbers are growing every single year. 

11. Even without AI, the semiconductor industry was already on its path to becoming the largest industry in the world. AI is the "X factor" that has accelerated that. 

12. Moore's law is over. Before you could wait a year for your transistor cost to become cheaper. Today, if you wait a year, you will pay 2x as much

13. Analyst consensus estimates have been revised nearly 200% higher for future revenue and free cash flows vs. this time last year. Despite that, the stock is only +20%

14. Analysts questioned the need for general-purpose chips vs. custom chips. The reason that Jensen remains focused on general purpose is because it is fungible. Fungible = lower risk, which matters a lot when you are putting hundreds of billions of dollars to work

15. Global compute infrastructure spend was roughly $1T/yr. That old world was the retrieval way of doing computation. Jensen sees this number closer to $10T/yr in the near term, with roughly half of that spent on intelligence capex

text:
我全职交易将近 3 年了，目前可以以交易为生，虽然跟 X 上赚几十万，几百万的没法比，但也确实是从小资金做起来的。

刚开始做的时候，我也是一直亏，一直亏，看了很多书，学了很多方法，也看了很多老师的课，但我发现其实都没有什么用，大多数人所谓的交易方法，要么就是很复杂，讲得云里雾里的，要么是生搬硬套一些已经存在理论，这个过程确实浪费了我很多时间，如果当时能早点有人跟我说这些，我最起码可以完整参与到牛市的前半段，所以如果你能看到这段话，应该最起码没有浪费你这十秒。目前市场所有的交易系统，交易方法，形态，指标等等，用的全都是100 多年前华尔街的那套东西，有些人只是为了营销卖课卖会员，故意换个名字，新瓶装旧酒，所以在全职交易的这条路上，我学到最重要的一课，就是祛魅。在市场里面交易，每个人都是在裸奔，大庄吃小庄，小庄吃散户，机构里拿 3 万月薪的分析师和 x 上拿 30u 广告的 KOL 并没有什么区别，十万粉的 Kol 和刚入圈的新手也没有什么区别，你一旦对这个市场里的某些机构或者某些人有滤镜，就会很痛苦，陷入深深的自我怀疑，绝对会影响你的判断，哪怕你的判断是对的，也会因为某种滤镜导致最后的结果走错

真正开始盈利的时候，是我已经把该踩的坑踩的差不多了，然后又正好赶上了牛市。如果我刚开始做交易，赚到了钱，我肯定会很开心，肯定自己的能力，认为自己有天赋，但是实际上能在市场里赚钱的原因 60% 都是因为行情和运气，30% 来自仓位和心态，这部分说到底还是能不能拿得住，剩下的 10% 才来自你的交易系统。但是为什么明明 10% 才来自交易系统，因为只有这 10% 才是属于你真正能掌握的东西，行情可遇不可求，仓位大小根据每个人的经济水平而决定，至于心态，比较玄学，只能自己悟。所以很多人喜欢去聊技术分析，模式和系统，争执不休，其实你可以只看形态，可以只看指标，可以只看均线，上方做多，下方做空，可以只用裸 K，当你和一些能赚钱的交易员交流你会发现，每个人赚钱的方法都不一样，你要是挨个去学，没个三年五年根本学不过来，但是每个人亏钱的原因都是那么几种，其中我觉得最容易亏钱的一种原因就是什么钱都想赚，既想赚横盘震荡的钱，又想赚上涨的钱，还想赚下跌的钱，盈亏同源，什么钱都想赚，也就意味着会把所有可能踩的坑全踩一遍，这就是因果。

关于交易的技巧和心得太多了，以后有时间慢慢讲吧

author: TheDavidTai
quoted_text:
Holy 💩. Tencent released a Local AI model dedicated to deciding what your AI agent should remember.

This might become my favorite memory companion local AI model to pair with Qwen3.8-27B

And community Q4 builds are already around ~17GB. 👀

Hy-Memory-30B-A3B is not meant to be a chatbot but rather a dedicated long-term memory writer.

It
🧠 reads new conversations / agent activity
🎯 decides what is actually worth remembering
📝 turns evidence into precise persistent memories
🔄 updates memories when facts change
🗑️ avoids storing irrelevant information
💾 maintains the persistent memory bank

Why?
Without persistent memory, your agent either:
🧠 forgets useful information when the session/context ends
📚 keeps stuffing old conversations back into context

A memory system gives your agent a compact long-term store that survives across sessions.

Hy-Memory is the model deciding what deserves to go into that store.

And today memory systems often use a general-purpose LLM for that job.

Tencent instead trained a sparse specialist specifically for it.

And Tencent reports it beats much larger frontier models at that specific task

🏆 Hy-Memory-30B-A3B → 55.49
Claude Opus 5 → 54.62
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash → 53.64
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B → 50.37
EverMemOS ranked #1 there at 56.89.

Specs
🧠 30B total
⚡ ~3B active/token
🔓 Apache 2.0
🏠 open weights
⚙️ vLLM + SGLang
🔌 OpenAI-compatible API

And community quants are already arriving:
Q4_K_M → ~17GB
Q5_K_M → ~20GB
Q6_K → ~23GB
EXL3 4.08bpw → ~15GB

That puts it roughly in the same memory class as a Qwen3.8-27B Q4.

Except Qwen3.8-27B is a dense general-purpose model.

Hy-Memory activates only ~3B parameters/token and was trained specifically for remembering.

🔗 Link in ALT

text: Vroom vroom
author: jasnoodle
quoted_text:
AI is making Ethereum more ambitious.

You might have heard about the challenges that blockchains face in a post-AI world, and while security assumptions will surely be stress-tested in the coming months and years, there is another side to it. I believe AI will let us speedrun towards a world that's both more secure and feature-rich.

As we look towards Ethereum's first post-AI upgrade, Hegotá, the R&D community is asking itself what increasingly powerful tools could help us do differently:

> How far can we push both security and iteration speed?
> How much of the design space can we examine before committing to one?
> How easily can we test the interactions between complex features?

My recent formal verification work @ethlabs_org has given me some reasons to be optimistic about these, as work that would have previously not even been attempted is now being done by agents in days. In September, I posted about using formal verification as part of designing a new consensus protocol. This time, I want to tell you about formally verifying something already fully specified and in production: Ethereum's Fast Confirmation Rule (FCR).

If you are not familiar with FCR, it lets applications confirm Ethereum blocks in seconds, roughly 30x faster than waiting for finality, under additional assumptions (from waiting 13 minutes to 24 seconds!). It also further solidifies Ethereum L1's case as an asset hub and center of gravity for the onchain economy. FCR now has a safety proof in Lean, closely modeling the rule in the consensus specs, which is the source of truth for Ethereum's consensus clients.

Some takeaways:

> FCR is safe! Under its assumptions, confirmed blocks remain canonical. On top of the manual proofs from the paper, we now have Lean proofs of this for the actual spec, additional evidence for applications considering FCR!

> The bulk of the formal verification work took just a 4-5 days (check out the animation!), with agents working mostly unsupervised. We should be very ambitious about using this as a tool at scale.

> After verifying the current rule, it was easy to adapt the model to the upcoming Gloas changes. Immediately, this surfaced a subtle bug caused by changes to fork choice. The problem was in the spec itself and not a gap in the model. The safety proof would not go through, and the agents could precisely pinpoint what was causing it to fail. The bug is now fixed, and formal verification of the corrected protocol goes through.

Iteration is never quite over, even for "finished" features like FCR, because the protocol keeps evolving around them. A formal model lets us ensure that key properties keep holding throughout the evolution of the protocol. With these capabilities, Ethereum can and should keep upgrading faster, tightening fork timelines and exploring more ambitious features, while still raising the security bar.

This picture has been getting much clearer over the past few months, and the past week confirmed it for me, as @drakefjustin and @corcoranwill brought together 100+ Ethereum researchers, cryptographers and formal verification experts in Cambridge for six days of workshops on post-quantum cryptography, formal verification and fast finality. Beyond its own workshop, formal verification was the omnipresent star of the week: everyone is using Lean and doing amazing things with it! Piece by piece, Ethereum's technological core is being rebuilt for the post-AI age.

The excitement was palpable, the sense of optimism was pervasive, and every talk and conversation carried a level of ambition I'd never seen before. The Ethereum R&D machine is upgrading itself, and we will see the outcome of that on the network sooner than you think.

text:
💣 اعتراف صادم من سام ألتمان: "توقعاتي كانت خاطئة تماماً.. رغم تطوير الذكاء الاصطناعي، لم يتغير العالم قيد أنملة، ونحن نواجه التزامات مالية بـ 100 تريليون دولار، ونواجه قضايا من كل اتجاه. بصراحة، قد نكون في ورطة حقيقية!" 📉🤯

​الرجل الذي روّج طويلاً لفكرة أن "الذكاء الاصطناعي سيسرق كل الوظائف ويعيد تشكيل العالم بين عشية وضحاها" يرفع الراية البيضاء ويعترف بالحقيقة المرة:

​وهم التغيير السريع: "كنت أعتقد أن إطلاق GPT-4 سيقلب قطاع البرمجيات رأساً على عقب في لمح البصر.. لكن الواقع كان مختلفاً تماماً، لقد أخطأت في تقدير سرعة تغير المجتمع."

​القصور الذاتي للبشر (Inertia): استخف ألتمان بمدى "كسل" الاقتصاد والمجتمع البشري. مهما كان الذكاء الاصطناعي خارقاً، فالناس يستيقظون ويؤدون أعمالهم بالطريقة نفسها، ويشترون من الشركات القديمة ذاتها. المجتمع لا يتحرك بالسرعة والرشاقة التي يتخيلها مهندسو التقنية.

​تغيير السلوك البشري: "كنت أظن أننا إن صنعنا أداة مذهلة، سيقفز الجميع لاستخدامها فوراً".. لكن تبين أن تغيير العادات اليومية أو القواعد المؤسسية البالية أصعب بمئة مرة من بناء الذكاء الاصطناعي نفسه.

​التقنية سابقة لعصرها: التكنولوجيا هي الأقوى في تاريخ البشرية بلا منازع، لكن "العنصر البشري والنظم الاجتماعية" عاجزون عن مواكبة هذا التسارع.

​الخلاصة المرة: بناء نموذج خارق أسهل بكثير من محاولة إقناع البشر بتغيير طرق حياتهم القديمة! 💀

​احفظ التغريدة بـ Bookmark 🔖 وشاركنا: هل تعتقد أن البشرية حقاً مقاومة للتغيير إلى هذا الحد، أم أن ثورة الذكاء الاصطناعي لم تضرب بقوة كافية بعد؟ 🧵👇 https://t.co/wMtLudnBOH

🤯 卧槽！马斯克把“意识”这个问题，直接拉到了宇宙尺度。

他在Neuralink更新会上说：你身体里很多原子，曾经都在恒星中心。恒星爆炸后重新凝聚，138亿年后，这些分子开始互相“对话”，意识就出现了。

他点出几个非常硬核的地方：

1. 从大爆炸到现在，没有一个明确的节点可以说“意识从这里突然出现”

2. 是不是所有物质都有意识？密度够了就会显现？没人知道

3. 真正的答案是：我们根本不知道意识是什么

4. Neuralink做的事，不只是治病，是第一次有机会直接去观察和理解它

以前意识只能靠哲学和脑科学慢慢猜。

现在他想把接口插进去，让机器和人脑一起把这件事问清楚。

我们还在用138亿年前恒星里的原子思考问题。

而Neuralink，可能是第一次让我们有机会反过来看清楚，

这些原子到底是怎么开始“知道自己存在”的。
