In a similar scramble I did to jump on AI in late 2022 (moving from remote work and nomads to AI apps), I am now scrambling to chase any remaining moats

As AI companies will suck up everything else (in my humble opinion)

So for every moat left I see where I can pivot towards to that with my sites/apps

Proprietary data or content:
- I launched a https://t.co/HGCLKS69sE paid data API for companies from $2,490/year to $9,990/year, the city data is great because it's made by real members who for example review/like/dislike a city after visiting it, or being able to see which places are growing or shrinking (interesting of real estate, coworking, or gym investors)
- https://t.co/0lBrLhXmCW neighborhood data is very valuable and I'm building a paid API for that too, as well as including it in the Nomads API

Network effects / community:
- I made the https://t.co/HGCLKS69sE community free (before $99, now just $1 to avoid spam), the more people, the more network effect

Audience / distribution: you can get attention on demand
- I have an @X audience and I get paid well for it (about ~$15K/mo), but I've also diversified that with my blog https://t.co/8VnHmB41ZP's email list and Telegram subscribers, which is now 187,279 people who get daily/weekly/monthly email digests of my posts

Physical component: hardware, locations, IRL:
- I have been improving and promoting https://t.co/HGCLKS69sE meetups, there's now 8 meetups planned in the next 30 days, but is has to keep growing, I've also added fitness meetups etc.
- I've been using and working on https://t.co/kSbsCmv3rm a lot and improving it, it seems to fill a real void in booking sites that all suffer from rating inflation and filters that are not modern, I'm adding features I want and it seems that's working. Today I'm adding a filter for Longevity Hotels, that have a strength training gym, wellness area, blackout curtains, as a counter balance to the boomer hotels with champagne on check in and a gym with only treadmills etc. Hotelist is fundamentally IRL because hotels are IRL
- Not really IRL but https://t.co/vlONz0Yejc is an annual event that's every year has ~1000 people participating vibe coding games and this year had over 1 million people playing the games, and AI companies really like to sponsor it because it's a great way to get exposure for their AI building tools
- I am building a https://t.co/M1hEUBB6da 1990s retro PC mini remake, like the SNES Mini, or the ModRetro M64, a hardware product I can sell marketed for nostalgia, especially after the last few weeks where it took off finally, I think there could be some market, and hardware is fun to try
- I sell merch on https://t.co/RyXpqGvdBB and make about $1K/mo from it, I haven't been very active on it but could expand this if I want

Capital: owning assets and investing
- I was already heavily invested in AI companies but have been even more with the acquisition of Cursor giving me $SPCX stock, I'll hold on to that, I think money will keep getting sucked from the traditional economy and replaced with paying AI companies money
- As a hedge, I've also put more money in bonds with IB01 ETF in case the AI bubble pops, $IB01 is a nice simple ETF for that
- I am actively looking at buying more land and real estate (especially coastal) as that's a scarce asset that will remain scarce post-AGI
- I am actively investing in startups with https://t.co/sQ0aiU82PA although I'm wondering what startups are still valuable to invest in as Big AI and Big Tech suck up everything, if you look at the last YC batch, it's all "Cursor for {industry}" harnesses and hardware, I think robotics could be interesting to invest but it's unclear who will be the winner as ironically robots have a low barrier to entry. Most robots are just Chinese-made components put together with some vibe coded software by their Western founders!
- I am open to buyers for https://t.co/9IDc0NsTvM and https://t.co/067b4q2Dg6 to increase the amount of capital I can invest elsewhere

Regulatory: licenses and legal barriers
- I am bad at this, and don't like regulation by nature. So I don't have anything here. And I don't think I will try pursue anything in here. I have friends building apps that work on getting EU subsidies or EU government program credits for emissions etc. But it's not my thing

So yes, chasing moats it is! Let's see if it works

author: TheDavidTai
quoted_text:
🚨 ChatGPT desktop users beware: A bug may be causing unnecessary wear on your SSD. @OpenAI

I noticed constant SSD activity whenever the app was running. Tracing the writes revealed that the animated desktop Pet was triggering a rewrite of the entire ~1 MB app state file AND its backup, about 10 times per second.

That amounted to 385 MB of file writes in 20 seconds, just to persist changes to the Pet’s position.

Setting Pet to “None” stopped the activity immediately.

If you leave the app running all day, check this setting!

author: SemiAnalysis_
quoted_text:
In 2022, Berkeley PhD student Woosuk Kwon thought he could make Meta's new open-weight model, OPT-175B, run faster in two weeks.

Four years and 3,000 contributors later, that project is @vllm_project, one of the largest open-source inference engines, running on ~500,000 GPUs at any given time.

He and fellow researchers Simon Mo, Kaichao You, and Roger Wang borrowed "virtual memory" from operating systems, handing out memory only as it's needed so each GPU can juggle requests of wildly different sizes. (The "v" in vLLM is for virtual.)

Their first user, Berkeley neighbor @arena, cut its GPU needs in half. Today Google, Amazon, and Meta all run vLLM in production.

In January, the core maintainers founded @inferact and raised $150M to give vLLM a full-time team.

They're hiring across eng, marketing, and devrel in SF and Singapore: https://t.co/DpODvfJWtC

quoted_text:
There's too much happening to list it all, but here are some highlights of the ongoing formal verification work, with special thanks to the people carrying it forward and getting Ethereum ready for the post-quantum and post-AI era.

@drakefjustin and the Ethereum Foundation @ethereumfndn had the foresight to make two big bets long before AI made them table stakes: formal verification and post-quantum security. @alexanderlhicks pioneered Verified zkEVM, bringing the EF's formal verification and cryptography teams and dozens of grantees together to verify the full zkEVM stack, while the EF cryptography team, the @leanEthereum effort and a dedicated PQ team have been laying the ground for a PQ Ethereum.

Now we reap the benefits, as AI makes security needs more urgent but also multiplies this strong foundation and accumulated expertise, propagating formal verification across the Ethereum stack and accelerating the PQ timelines.

The core Ethereum specs are already transforming, incorporating Lean for some of their critical components: the cryptography specs bring BLS and KZG into Lean, with proofs by Benedikt Wagner and @asanso, @tcoratger wrote the new SSZ specs, and @jtraglia integrated both into the consensus specs.

Meanwhile, the amount of forward-looking work is impossible to keep up with: @tcoratger added the post-quantum XMSS signature scheme to the cryptography specs; Benedikt proved the security of the proposed post-quantum data availability sampling scheme (code); and @asn_d6, Benedikt and @Khovr are proving that the pieces of a recursive zkVM proof fit together securely.

Industry teams are all in too: @JulekSU and the @Nethermind FV team formalized FRI in ArkLib, are now on STIR and WHIR, and built a Lean model of the EVM and Yul covering Cancun, while @rv_inc is connecting Rust cryptographic code to Lean proofs.

Another incredible trend at the intersection of AI and formal verification is autoresearch challenges, where agents compete in the open to improve a verifiable metric: https://t.co/PgQZySqnHi (EF formal verification team, @yukonresearch, @zksecurityXYZ) on the coding theory behind SNARK security, https://t.co/l4fCEFulzc (@yukonresearch, @ethereumfndn) on smaller post-quantum signatures, https://t.co/SzRFBZ1Ctg (@zksecurityXYZ) on cheaper ZK circuits, and https://t.co/Cv3hURdk3s (@SuccinctLabs, @EspressoSys) on a faster post-quantum prover.

As for the FCR work, check it out here: 
Lean formalization [https://t.co/mzUQSBcKhy]
Gloas fix [https://t.co/Hu3UL5meub]

Lots of the threads that the R&D ecosystem has been working on for years are coming together, and Ethereum could hardly be better prepared for as transformative a moment as this one.

quoted_text:
My conspiracy theory: This recent market crash looks more like Wall Street hunting Wall Street than a fundamental deterioration.

A lot of fund managers who allocated capital back in May are now sitting on negative returns. These guys manage clients’ money, and with year-end approaching, the pressure to deliver performance is only getting worse.

Now, here is why I think something else is going on.

Sure, the macro environment isn’t as good as we expected. Frontier model companies’ ARR, the Iran deal, data center delays and financing, the energy crisis, CPI, Treasury yields… the list goes on.

But how much of this is actually new information?

Most of these risks were already known and arguably priced in back in July. It’s not like Wall Street suddenly discovered them in October.

Yet the market staged a dramatic recovery throughout August and September.

So what changed? Did fundamentals suddenly improve in August and deteriorate again in October? Or are we just using the same old narratives to explain price movements after the fact?

That’s the part I keep questioning.

What we can see is the price action. What we can’t see is what’s happening behind the scenes: positioning, leverage, liquidity, and the pressure institutional managers are facing.

When performance starts falling behind, someone has to cut exposure. Those forced sales create opportunities for someone else. And the more crowded the positioning, the easier it becomes to push the market into a chain reaction.

Among all the possibilities I can think of, — institutional players hunting each other’s positions — is one I can’t ignore.

We saw something similar back in July.

Maybe this selloff is about deteriorating fundamentals. But I’m not convinced the market suddenly learned something it didn’t already know two months ago.

Sometimes the market isn’t selling because the story changed. The story changes because the market is selling.

text:
it’s been a dramatic couple of days, I didn’t expect the already clean essay to be read so widely. I've heard more interesting discussions about mechanistic interpretability – should we think mostly in features or mechanisms and the flow of data through them, how much do weak activations matter, how does scale change things, and lots of other questions – than I have in a long time and I’ve been happy to hear all the discussion!

a couple things on the essay itself. it didn't have enough citations, only ones for the basic story, since it was an "informal research essay and working hypothesis" rather than a paper, and other prior work around neurons were in the technical paper we're still finishing up. but it blew up, so I've added citations to the essay as well. I also want to thank @curttigges who did a lot of the language neuron research with me

finally, while there was quite a range of updates, from this being incremental and obvious to interpretability going from hopeless to fully solved, I want to try to be clear about roughly where I stand

I used to think neural networks would take some big cleaning step and then we could begin the ordinary natural science of mapping the parts and how they connect, watching data flow through, mapping circuits, and so on.

at various points, like late layers of early model organisms and most layers of language models years ago, this didn't really work. but now with better tools and better models of study, it works much better

for smaller vision models, this normal science process worked surprisingly well, until the whole map started to be broadly filled in. For bigger modern language models, it seems promising so far, for both neurons and circuits, attribution graphs, basically everywhere we've glanced. the map isn't filling in, there's a lot of map. there's still off-target firing, neurons that do a few things, but so far it's not an incoherent mess that you can't explore and learn from, and over time we get better at learning how to see it.

so maybe it keeps going, and mapping motifs and exploring actually gets you pretty far, maybe something like "all the way" to a reasonable solution. I don't think it would be so scientifically surprising if that were the case. everything in the neural network was built in some sense to be read – by its downstream readers – and if we can learn to look like a reader, we might find reading them relatively easy. many researchers I talk to outside interpretability assume the parts are already understandable, and the difficulty is just in the mapping stage!

it was also my prior when I first started looking at neurons when I first joined the field. there's lots of highly interpretable ones, maybe that's just how neural networks are if you look right.

even in the good world it would still take some iteration on tools, on ways of looking, neuron-attention interactions are tricky for instance. there's probably no bright red line separating "cleaning the model" from "learning to look better" but there's broad working principles, and as of now I think we should try to look relatively directly if we can

it shouldn't be so hard to test, you can just start looking at things and iterating and trying to understand motifs and such and see if it just breaks down at some point. it can take some iteration, I would recommend a bias against assuming arbitrary mixtures when you don't understand something at first, but also explanations should be tested

for now I'm pretty optimistic, and I'm glad there's excitement about interpretability, but too much can cause problems too. I think part might be that ai safety isn't a very hopeful field, and even moderate amounts of optimism about an important problem being solvable in the future fills a spot that has been malnourished for a while. across several safety disciplines, the researchers directly working on them are often more optimistic than the people broadcasting pessimism more broadly

for neural network interpretability at least, these are extraordinarily experimentally accessible objects of science, I don't know of a better one, and we have automated scientists. we have many things going in our favor. it's important and it's fun. the circuitry of these machines can be beautiful, surprising, entertaining, and insightful. I've spent thousands of hours looking through them, asking questions and running experiments and testing things, and would do so even if it weren't so important. I think the problem is solvable, whether the simple thing works, it mostly works but we need some new things, or we need big new ideas. I think we can figure it out

text:
V 神是对的，这次狼可能真的来了

Anthropic 今天这篇 quantum 论文，最该紧张的不是物理学家，而是拿着 BTC 的人

标题写的是「AI 设计更高效的量子电路，让化学、材料科学的应用更早到来」
但 8 个任务里写得最细的一个，是 256-bit 的 elliptic-curve point addition，也就是量子计算机破解椭圆曲线离散对数的核心步骤，而 BTC、ETH 的签名用的正是椭圆曲线

拆一下他们做了什么：
1. 只给 Claude Mythos 5 一段话的 brief，加一个自动评分器（qubit 数 × gate 数），让它闭环自己迭代，基本没有人工介入
2. point addition 里最贵的一步是 modular inversion。Claude 跑了 53 小时，做出了第一个不需要存 branch history 的可逆 divsteps 实现，过程中还自己证明了几个新的代数恒等式，并用 Lean 做了形式化验证
3. 结果是：和之前最小的设计比，qubit 多 12%，gate 少 17 倍
4. 顺手把 DQI 的 Reed–Solomon decoder 做到比 Google 之前的方案少 12 倍 gate
5. 8 个任务全部做到 qubit 和 gate 都比已发表的最佳方案少

再看一个历史对照：FeMoco 模拟需要的 Toffoli gate，2017 年估算是 50 万亿，现在降到约 3.4 亿，差不多 15 万倍。这些主要靠多个研究组花了 8 年、每一步几个月的算法改进，不是靠硬件
而 Claude 这个椭圆曲线设计，只是一次 53 小时的运行

本质上，量子威胁什么时候到，从来不只看硬件能造出多少 qubit，也要看算法需要多少 gate。硬件还在慢慢爬，算法这边已经被 AI 按下了加速键

喊了这么多年「量子要来了」，大家都当是狼来了的故事听，但这次是 AI 亲手把狼往前推了一大步

所以问题来了：BTC 的 post-quantum 迁移，会被 AI 逼着提前，还是继续等硬件真追上来再说？🧐

text:
AI is making Ethereum more ambitious.

You might have heard about the challenges that blockchains face in a post-AI world, and while security assumptions will surely be stress-tested in the coming months and years, there is another side to it. I believe AI will let us speedrun towards a world that's both more secure and feature-rich.

As we look towards Ethereum's first post-AI upgrade, Hegotá, the R&D community is asking itself what increasingly powerful tools could help us do differently:

> How far can we push both security and iteration speed?
> How much of the design space can we examine before committing to one?
> How easily can we test the interactions between complex features?

My recent formal verification work @ethlabs_org has given me some reasons to be optimistic about these, as work that would have previously not even been attempted is now being done by agents in days. In September, I posted about using formal verification as part of designing a new consensus protocol. This time, I want to tell you about formally verifying something already fully specified and in production: Ethereum's Fast Confirmation Rule (FCR).

If you are not familiar with FCR, it lets applications confirm Ethereum blocks in seconds, roughly 30x faster than waiting for finality, under additional assumptions (from waiting 13 minutes to 24 seconds!). It also further solidifies Ethereum L1's case as an asset hub and center of gravity for the onchain economy. FCR now has a safety proof in Lean, closely modeling the rule in the consensus specs, which is the source of truth for Ethereum's consensus clients.

Some takeaways:

> FCR is safe! Under its assumptions, confirmed blocks remain canonical. On top of the manual proofs from the paper, we now have Lean proofs of this for the actual spec, additional evidence for applications considering FCR!

> The bulk of the formal verification work took just a 4-5 days (check out the animation!), with agents working mostly unsupervised. We should be very ambitious about using this as a tool at scale.

> After verifying the current rule, it was easy to adapt the model to the upcoming Gloas changes. Immediately, this surfaced a subtle bug caused by changes to fork choice. The problem was in the spec itself and not a gap in the model. The safety proof would not go through, and the agents could precisely pinpoint what was causing it to fail. The bug is now fixed, and formal verification of the corrected protocol goes through.

Iteration is never quite over, even for "finished" features like FCR, because the protocol keeps evolving around them. A formal model lets us ensure that key properties keep holding throughout the evolution of the protocol. With these capabilities, Ethereum can and should keep upgrading faster, tightening fork timelines and exploring more ambitious features, while still raising the security bar.

This picture has been getting much clearer over the past few months, and the past week confirmed it for me, as @drakefjustin and @corcoranwill brought together 100+ Ethereum researchers, cryptographers and formal verification experts in Cambridge for six days of workshops on post-quantum cryptography, formal verification and fast finality. Beyond its own workshop, formal verification was the omnipresent star of the week: everyone is using Lean and doing amazing things with it! Piece by piece, Ethereum's technological core is being rebuilt for the post-AI age.

The excitement was palpable, the sense of optimism was pervasive, and every talk and conversation carried a level of ambition I'd never seen before. The Ethereum R&D machine is upgrading itself, and we will see the outcome of that on the network sooner than you think.

author: poteto
quoted_text:
how do you trust your agents' work more? copy this post/link and give it to your @bot or agent!

1. codebase improvements: this is just good software engineering - better architecture, stronger types and invariants, clear boundaries. agents love to copy what exists and take the shortest path, so make the easy thing the right thing. categorically eliminate problems through code and you won't need to think about it again.
2. static analysis: lint rules, tests, CI, verification (eg TLA+). very token efficient ways to catch issues ahead of time.
3. prose: comments, rules, AGENTS.md, skills - anything that can't be enforced and requires agent judgment. use it minimally, but do use /create-verification-skill.
4. human review: the hardest to scale. at the rate agents land code, it's pretty much impossible to thoroughly review every PR, so spend that effort on the highest leverage point, designing an environment where agents do the right thing by default.

this forms an inverse pyramid: you want most of your effort at the top, least at the bottom. codebase improvements are deterministic, making it more token efficient, and lets you sleep more soundly at night.

install https://t.co/u9xIlN3eN0 and create a new Project:
1. look through my slack/chat messages and code review comments where i've given feedback on PRs, code, architecture
2. use /recall on my past transcripts to learn how i steer agents
3. /poteto-mode use /correct and /architect on past commits to find the most common pitfalls agents fall into, then propose a plan to rearchitect the code i own so it's more agent friendly. answer open questions with prototyping rather than defer to me, and back the plan with real data. 
4. before you begin, use /sharpen + /in-your-own-words and confirm this prompt with me

author: tszzl
quoted_text:
it’s been a dramatic couple of days, I didn’t expect the already clean essay to be read so widely. I've heard more interesting discussions about mechanistic interpretability – should we think mostly in features or mechanisms and the flow of data through them, how much do weak activations matter, how does scale change things, and lots of other questions – than I have in a long time and I’ve been happy to hear all the discussion!

a couple things on the essay itself. it didn't have enough citations, only ones for the basic story, since it was an "informal research essay and working hypothesis" rather than a paper, and other prior work around neurons were in the technical paper we're still finishing up. but it blew up, so I've added citations to the essay as well. I also want to thank @curttigges who did a lot of the language neuron research with me

finally, while there was quite a range of updates, from this being incremental and obvious to interpretability going from hopeless to fully solved, I want to try to be clear about roughly where I stand

I used to think neural networks would take some big cleaning step and then we could begin the ordinary natural science of mapping the parts and how they connect, watching data flow through, mapping circuits, and so on.

at various points, like late layers of early model organisms and most layers of language models years ago, this didn't really work. but now with better tools and better models of study, it works much better

for smaller vision models, this normal science process worked surprisingly well, until the whole map started to be broadly filled in. For bigger modern language models, it seems promising so far, for both neurons and circuits, attribution graphs, basically everywhere we've glanced. the map isn't filling in, there's a lot of map. there's still off-target firing, neurons that do a few things, but so far it's not an incoherent mess that you can't explore and learn from, and over time we get better at learning how to see it.

so maybe it keeps going, and mapping motifs and exploring actually gets you pretty far, maybe something like "all the way" to a reasonable solution. I don't think it would be so scientifically surprising if that were the case. everything in the neural network was built in some sense to be read – by its downstream readers – and if we can learn to look like a reader, we might find reading them relatively easy. many researchers I talk to outside interpretability assume the parts are already understandable, and the difficulty is just in the mapping stage!

it was also my prior when I first started looking at neurons when I first joined the field. there's lots of highly interpretable ones, maybe that's just how neural networks are if you look right.

even in the good world it would still take some iteration on tools, on ways of looking, neuron-attention interactions are tricky for instance. there's probably no bright red line separating "cleaning the model" from "learning to look better" but there's broad working principles, and as of now I think we should try to look relatively directly if we can

it shouldn't be so hard to test, you can just start looking at things and iterating and trying to understand motifs and such and see if it just breaks down at some point. it can take some iteration, I would recommend a bias against assuming arbitrary mixtures when you don't understand something at first, but also explanations should be tested

for now I'm pretty optimistic, and I'm glad there's excitement about interpretability, but too much can cause problems too. I think part might be that ai safety isn't a very hopeful field, and even moderate amounts of optimism about an important problem being solvable in the future fills a spot that has been malnourished for a while. across several safety disciplines, the researchers directly working on them are often more optimistic than the people broadcasting pessimism more broadly

for neural network interpretability at least, these are extraordinarily experimentally accessible objects of science, I don't know of a better one, and we have automated scientists. we have many things going in our favor. it's important and it's fun. the circuitry of these machines can be beautiful, surprising, entertaining, and insightful. I've spent thousands of hours looking through them, asking questions and running experiments and testing things, and would do so even if it weren't so important. I think the problem is solvable, whether the simple thing works, it mostly works but we need some new things, or we need big new ideas. I think we can figure it out

author: 0xdoug
quoted_text:
Introducing https://t.co/ygo2X8jrNX: the first multiplayer open research challenge aiming to solve a case of the generalized Hodge conjecture.

Erdős problems can be stated using just simple objects: integers, sets, etc. This makes them amenable to attack using AI.

HC is not so. Its very statement involves deep objects, many of which are not even formalized in Lean (at least until recently): rational Betti cohomology of smooth projective varieties, complex differential forms and the Hodge decomposition, the cycle class map, etc.

My mission is to turn the Hodge conjecture into an Erdős problem. Today, I am beginning with a special case: the GHC for the invariant Hodge substructure H ⊂ H⁴(X, ℚ) in sextic fourfolds X ⊂ ℙ⁵ with an involution. Voisin first isolated this subcase; recent mathematical work on my part has made its prediction computationally effective.

To my knowledge, this is the first computational attack, of any kind, on any case of the generalized Hodge conjecture.

Math is undergoing a revolution (see quoted tweet for more remarks). Calling all enthusiasts and hobbyists! Calling all engineers! And academics, you too :) This is now your time to contribute to the single most fascinating problem in algebraic geometry. Let's go.

text:
Imagine a multi-agent workflow: one agent plans, one searches, one writes the report. The user asked for headphones under $200, but the search agent quietly set the budget to $300. Every downstream step runs flawlessly — comparing specs, drafting analysis, making recommendations — yet the entire pipeline has already drifted from what the user wanted. No single agent made an obvious error; they all inherited a bad premise. By the time anyone notices, the task is already done wrong.

Rutgers University, UT Austin, and Purdue University present AgentForesight, a 7B online auditor for multi-agent systems (NeurIPS 2026).

AgentForesight moves failure analysis from post-hoc attribution to online auditing: after every step, an external auditor reads the execution record so far and decides whether to continue or raise an alert — buying time for intervention before the task is ruined. On the AFTraj-2K benchmark, it identifies the critical error step in failed trajectories with Exact-F1 of 66.44 — 19.88 points above the strongest general-model baseline — while flagging successful trajectories as failures only 2.37% of the time. Boxuan Zhang and Jianing Zhu are co-first authors; Ruixiang Tang is the corresponding author. Project page, code, and dataset are all open-sourced.

Result: AgentForesight turns multi-agent failure detection into a real-time online audit — a 7B model that catches critical errors mid-execution with Exact-F1 66.44 (+19.88 over the strongest baseline) and only 2.37% false alarms on successful runs, accepted at NeurIPS 2026 with open project, code, and dataset.

text:
One of the biggest challenges Ethereum still faces is something most users don’t even know exists: MEV.

Today I had the opportunity to discuss this topic with people working on Encrypt the Mempool, and I think more people should understand why this matters.

When you make a transaction on Ethereum, it can become visible to others before it’s executed. Bots can use that information to trade ahead of you, manipulate execution prices and extract value from your transaction.

Think about that for a moment. We’re building an open financial system, yet the transparency that makes Ethereum so powerful can also be used against its users.

This becomes even more important as we bring RWA’s, institutions and eventually trillions of dollars in financial activity onchain.

If Ethereum wants to become the foundation of global finance, we need more than scalability and low transaction fees. We also need fair execution, better protection for users and infrastructure institutions can trust.

That’s why I believe initiatives like @encryptmempool deserve much more attention.

The idea is relatively simple: protect transaction information before execution so that others can’t exploit it as easily. The technology behind it is complex, but the potential impact is significant.

Not all MEV is harmful, and encrypted mempools won’t solve every problem. But reducing harmful MEV is an important step toward a fairer Ethereum.

Read more: https://t.co/KFGO8gwhnK

text:
Some of you may have noticed https://t.co/b76d8Cf4LY has been running a bit differently lately.

Yes. Back in late September, right after I posted that insiders was getting hard to keep running, a senior I met earlier this year, someone I trust, reached out and offered to take over my operating role at insiders along with my equity.

So since early October, insiders has been transitioning to the new team. That also gave me time to see whether their way of running things actually holds up.

People will call this an exit, but it's closer to walking away with nothing. Apart from me and @dakshbigshit putting in over 50% of our personal assets, insiders never brought in real revenue. If anything, it ended up wiping out everything we'd saved through 2024 and 2025.

All equity and tokens are being transferred for free. The only condition is that he funds insiders out of his own pocket and keeps it running to see if crypto prediction markets come back. He'll also look at what more $IN can be used for. A few engineers and interns will stay on to help.

I did a lot of DD myself. The person taking over is trustworthy and has real operating experience. Even if it keeps losing money and has to shut down, every user's funds on insiders will be returned ahead of time, the same way @fireplacegg handled it.

On the bright side, he's building his own trading platform, so there's a real chance of a rebrand or a merger with another platform.

So from today, @dakshbigshit and I are moving into the next stage of exploring and learning. More reflecting, more searching for direction, and maybe some work outside Web3, like AI and real-world businesses.

If anyone on here has a good opportunity, feel free to reach out. At the very least, we took insiders to millions in trading volume and 300 paying users at its peak.

Looking back, insiders had two perfect exit windows, and we missed both.

1. January last year. If we'd stopped shipping updates then, we could have kept most of our capital. Had we just kept running it as it was instead of expanding in the wrong direction without PMF, it still had a decent shot.

2. April last year. A platform much bigger than us proposed a merger. We were proud and thought the terms weren't good enough, and the talks fell apart.

So after half a year of grinding, we've ended up barely able to afford dinner. The good part is I learned a lot. A lot, a lot.

I lost a lot of money and I'm ready to start over from zero and climb back up from the bottom. Still, I'm grateful to insiders. It showed me my own limits, and how far I can take a product when I go all in.

Time to keep pushing.

A while ago I read The Hard Thing About Hard Things by the @a16z founder. When I got to the part about the failed IPO, the setbacks that kept coming after it, and how he finally survived and sold the company, I couldn't hold it in and cried on the train.

And I haven't even been through 1% of what's in that book.

At some point in the next month or two I'll probably write a long-form post on the whole rise and fall of https://t.co/b76d8Cf4LY. Next week I'll wrap up the handover and get ready for whatever comes next.

当然，往好的想，由于前辈自己也在开发自己的交易平台，所以也有机会rebrand或者和别的平台合并。

所以，从今天起，我和 @dakshbigshit 要开始下一个摸索，学习的阶段了。继续反思，继续寻找方向，可能也会开始一些 Web3 以外的业务，比如AI和一些实体。

如果哪位推特上的大佬有好的合作机会，也欢迎联系我们。至少，我们还是做出过 insiders 百万交易量，300个付费用户这样巅峰时期的辉煌的。

现在想回来，其实 insiders 这间公司有过两个最佳的退出策略，都被我们错过了。

- 第一是去年一月份的时候，如果不继续更新，可以保住手上大部分的资金。当时保持原样持续运营，而不是往错误的方向扩张，缺乏PMF，其实还是会有不错的机会。

- 第二是去年四月份的时候，一个比我们大很多的平台提出合并，当时心高气傲，觉得条件不够好，结果谈崩了。

所以，吭哧吭哧忙了半年，最后搞到现在有点点吃不起饭了。好在，学到了非常，非常，非常多的东西。

虽然亏了很多钱，也要做好接下来重新从零开始，从底部爬起来的准备，但我还是很感激 insiders，让我看到了自身的局限，以及当我全力去做一个产品时，可以走到哪一个进度。

接下来也要继续努力。

前段时间读了 @a16z 创始人的《创业维艰》，再读到第二家公司IPO失败，以及之后的连续阻挠，以及最后活下来，出售公司这个故事时，我没绷住，在火车上哭了出来。

而我，就连创业维艰 1% 的路程都还没有经历到。

https://t.co/b76d8CfCBw 整个项目的崛起与失落，我或许接下来一两个月的某一天会写一篇长文复盘。接下来一个礼拜会完成最后的交接事宜，以及准备好做下一件事。

全网都在疯传今天早晨那段特斯拉Roadster腾空翻转的特技，但我对着这块内饰屏幕看了整整三遍，才看明白马斯克到底在想什么，

当一辆车拥有 0.81 秒的狂暴加速和底盘推进器的时候，你根本不可能再用一块大号 iPad 去操控它。

很多人把这套黑底线框的界面当成一种复古科幻的审美情怀，但真正做产品的人一眼就能看出来，这其实是一套极其冷酷的航天级遥测系统。

最先发生质变的，是车机彻底甩掉了传统手机思维的包袱。
 过去十几年，几乎所有智能座舱都在把手机上的地图、音乐和应用图标生硬地搬上中控，屏幕越大，信息反而越碎，
在这台车里，整个界面退回到了纯粹的黑底线框，没有多余的层级菜单，中央是一台可以任意旋转的 3D 车辆骨架，底盘的推进器状态、车身气流轨迹和灯光边界全都在实时发光。

更高级的地方，在于它把看不见的高维物理量翻译成了肉眼可见的安全感。
 当车辆承受接近 2G 的侧向加速度时，驾驶员没有多余的精力去读长篇文字，
橙红色的赛道面板把四个车轮的实时负荷、下压力分布和抓地力极限，压成了类似战斗机平视显示器一样极简的数据图形，瞥一眼就能感知到整台机器的物理边界。

这正是很多做硬件和做 AI 的人最容易忽略的一点，
 系统越是强大，底层的不可控感就越强烈，如果不能把复杂的运算和隐蔽的力量清晰地呈现在人眼前，人就会本能地感到恐惧。

以前的座舱是在给乘客提供娱乐，从今天起这块屏幕是在给驾驶员交付对极限力量的掌控权。
 好的界面从来不是为了炫技，而是让一个人坐在由代码和推进器驱动的庞然大物里，依然能拥有最笃定的信任。

大家在开车时，更喜欢这种像飞船座舱一样聚焦核心状态的极简线框，还是更习惯传统那种功能齐全的卡片大屏？我个人觉得在激烈驾驶或者高速状态下，我只希望屏幕上全是我保命需要的数据，别给我弹任何花哨的广告和冗余卡片就行😅 https://t.co/ZOgENuL617

简单说说我们为什么做这件事。

过去两年，有件事变了：一个人、三个人，就能做出以前要一整个组织才能做的东西。做这些事的人，也不太像传统意义上的创始团队。有人在大厂待了很多年，在等一个出来的时机；有人已经出来了，一个人在做；有人做了十年，想换个方向重新开始。他们的共同点是AI原生：考虑的是"一个小团队加上好模型能做到什么"，而不是"要招多少人"。

这样的创业者，需要的不是建议，而是算力、几个真正做过产品的人、接触用户的渠道，以及足够早、足够多的钱，让他们不用把头六个月花在融资上。盛大这些年积累的，恰好就是这些资源。NovaCatapult 就是想把它们交到这些人手里。

你能拿到什么

不低于100万元的投资，由现金、SAFE和资源组成，公司成立时到位，不需要先达成什么里程碑。跑得好的团队，我们会继续跟投。

优先使用盛大内部的GPU集群。

人：资深工程师帮你评审架构，增长团队帮你找客户，法务和人事从公司注册一路管到合规。

还有不起眼但很重要的部分：拎包入驻的工位，住房半价，午饭免费。

我们怎么选

我们选人不拘一格：项目不必成熟，不必已经全职，团队也不必完整，但我们看重创始人和项目的潜力。团队占60%，方向占40%，因为在这个阶段，方向会变，人不会。

负责人说

盛大集团首席运营官、NovaCatapult 项目负责人王飞浪："我们希望支持最具AI原生能力的创业者，用盛大这些年积累的资源，帮他们更快起飞。"

quoted_text:
26 岁，我终于开上了自己的保时捷 911

今天看到一个很有意思的说法，叫作「豪车理论」。

如果你在 20 岁开上豪车，你获得的幸福感可能是同龄人的 20 倍。

如果你在 30 岁开上豪车，这份幸福感可能只剩下 3 倍。

而当你 40 岁再开上豪车，或许已经很难获得什么额外的幸福感了。

当然，这些数字并没有科学依据。

但它让我开始思考：这究竟是消费主义精心编织的陷阱，还是有些快乐，真的只有在特定的年纪才能体会？

今年我 26 岁，买下了一辆二手保时捷 911。

23 岁大学毕业，从一个小镇青年开始，一步一步走到今天。

其实很长一段时间里，我都认为豪车不过是虚荣和攀比的产物。抛开社交属性，它似乎并不具备多少额外的价值。

尤其在电动车飞速发展的今天，性能、智能化、舒适性都在被重新定义。传统燃油跑车，仿佛已经成了时代的遗珠。

可偏偏，保时捷 911 一直是我的 Dream Car。

它对我而言，更像是一枚图腾。

不是因为它有多贵，也不是因为它能向别人证明什么，而是从很早以前开始，它就代表着某种遥不可及的生活。

这一次，我拿出了总资产的 10%，把它带回了家。

说不心疼是假的。

即便直到付款前，我都还在反复思考，这笔钱花得到底值不值。

但当那辆曾经只存在于屏幕和想象中的车，真正出现在我面前时，我还是恍惚了很久。

那种不真实感，很难用语言形容。

直到坐进驾驶舱，握住方向盘，点火，听见发动机从身后传来的轰鸣。

那一刻，理性和计算好像都暂时失去了意义。

那个从小镇走出来的年轻人，终于亲手握住了曾经遥不可及的梦想。

我不知道这份多巴胺能持续多久。

也许几天，也许几个月，也许几年。也许有一天，我也会习惯它的存在，像习惯生活里其他曾经梦寐以求的东西一样。

但至少在今天，我真切地感受到了幸福。

过去三年的焦虑、压力、不被理解，以及无数个独自熬过的日夜，仿佛都在这一刻有了回响。

这些年吃过的苦，并没有真的变成发动机的动力。

但发动机的每一次轰鸣，都像是在告诉我：你曾经走过的路，没有白走。

我依然不认为豪车是人生的必需品，也不觉得拥有它就意味着成功。

但我开始理解，为什么有些东西，明明不符合最理性的消费逻辑，却依然值得某个人为它买单。

因为我们努力赚钱，不应该只是为了让账户里的数字不断增长。

有时候，也是为了让曾经的自己，亲眼看看梦想实现的样子。

20 岁的梦想，不一定非要等到 40 岁才去兑现。

毕竟，车可以晚一点买，但 26 岁的自己，永远只有一次。

text:
The AI Quant Feed isn't hand-picked.

We pointed Jev — our typed-decision model — at every prompt and every answer and asked it one thing: would a stranger learn something from this?

What clears the bar goes up. Everything else, and anything personal, doesn't.

Typed-decision means it doesn't hand back prose we then parse. It returns a decision with a shape: in or out, which of nine topics, and why. 

So we can audit it, test it, and move the bar without rewriting anything.

The hard part was never "is this interesting."

It's "is this someone's private business." 

A wallet address pasted into a public question is already public. Their account, balances, PnL, handle — never. 

That exclusion runs before the interest check, not after.

Every AI product is sitting on a corpus of what its users actually asked. Most of it is noise. Some of it is the best documentation you will ever have. None of it is safe to publish raw.

The filter is the product decision. Not the feed.

text:
Today I was in Washington DC to talk about financial privacy and the narrow path to non-dystopian digital ID. It was great to see @valkenburgh and @secparam, but I want to now expand on a point from our panel:

I think it is likely the BSA, as applied today, is unconstitional.

This is probably going to be surprising to a lot of you. After all, didn't the Supreme Court uphold the BSA as constitutional when it was challenged in 1974? Why yes, it most certainly did.

Have you read that opinion? I have. That same court said that the fact pattern today is likely unconstitional.

The case, for those unfamiliar, is California Bankers Assn. v. Shultz (416 U.S. 21). In it, when you read the actual decision, you find some interesting tidbits:

Title I recordkeeping requirements were upheld because mere recordkeeping was not a search, and the authorities asking a third party for individual pieces of data was thus not a search. Government access in that case still required orderly legal process.

Title II domestic reporting was largely a standing issue, pointing out there were not customers specifically challenging this at the time who had been clearly impacted.

Fifth amendment claims by depositors or the ACLU were considered speculative at the time, and did not note specific facts (nor privacy concerns) or even clear intent to engage in transactions in some cases.

Powell, who was joined by Blackmun, concurring with the majority, in fact specifically noted that “A significant extension of the regulations’ reporting requirements… would pose substantial and difficult constitutional questions.”

First: I think this case was correctly decided on the facts at the time, in the world where banking was largely done on paper, records searches were one at a time or at most small batches, and the amount of information a bank collected was far more limited. On the standing and non-ripeness points, those were probably also correct at the time, but I will note that doesn't make something constitutional, just that SCOTUS has a long history of punting on things until they have to confront it.

Second: the fact pattern today looks absolutely nothing like the fact pattern at the time. The expansiveness of a search is far greater, with banks involved in every asset of digital life and the transaction monitoring far more comprehensive than before. Previously, a BSA request could not get every purchase you had made over the past three months (thus also geolocating you at all those times), because that was all done in cash. Now it can.

In light of things like the recent Flock decisions at district courts finding Flock database searches without a warrant to be unconstitutional and the cell phone tower decision showing that non-particularized geofence warrants are also unconstitutional, it's hard for me to see how "we see your location constantly through your card always and then we turn tens of thousands of people's wroth of information over to the government with no individual suspicion" is going to pass muster.

The second point is in light of government pressure to close accounts, like the @USOCC just found in their report about the debanking of digital asset companies, the standing and ripeness arguments now look very different. There was, in fact, an actual nationwide dragnet at big banks to debank certain customers, partially pushed by regulators leaning on reputational risk, and the standing, harm, and ripeness issues created might be overcome here.

The third point is that the reporting requirements have expanded dramatically, exactly the thing the court itself cautioned against. "Hey gives us this one customer's info for transactions over $10k" is now "give us all transactions for all customers at all thresholds", and by waving their hands and screaming "third party doctrine", the Feds think this is somehow magically constitutional.

My view: it's not.

I think the time is right for someone to challenge this, and win.

text:
Fortune 500 companies have expanded Global Capability Centers (GCCs) in India aggressively for cost, control, IP ownership, and access to skilled talent. These centers often pay premium packages (especially for niche skills in cloud, data, AI, cybersecurity, and domain-specific tech), which creates a talent magnet effect. This raises attrition and wage pressure for traditional IT services firms that rely on the same pool.

The rise of aggressive Global Capability Centers by large global enterprises in India is reshaping the IT talent and delivery landscape.

Over the next few years, as many of them mature, a natural question arises: how much of the traditional outsourcing pie shrinks as more work stays captive? And could some of these centers eventually productize capabilities or selectively offer services that compete for mindshare (or even contracts) with established IT providers? 

Domain depth and functional understanding built inside the parent ecosystem can be powerful. At the same time, factors like confidentiality requirements, regulatory constraints, focus on internal priorities, and the need for commercial scale often limit how far pure captives go in competing head-to-head for peer business. 

For traditional IT services firms, the clearer near-term pressures are talent competition and selective insourcing. The longer-term opportunity lies in evolving alongside this shift - through deeper specialization, productized offerings, GCC partnerships, or new delivery models that combine domain expertise with multi-client experience and global scale.

The Indian tech ecosystem is not zero-sum. GCCs bring investment, skills, and innovation; established players bring proven delivery muscle and commercial networks. 

However, pure competition with traditional IT firms for peer contracts is constrained in practice for several reasons:

- Conflict of interest and confidentiality: Banks, insurers, and other regulated firms rarely want peers handling sensitive systems or data.

- Focus and economics: Most GCCs prioritize the parent’s roadmap, compliance, and cost efficiency rather than building a sales/marketing/delivery engine to compete for external revenue.

- Regulatory and strategic barriers: Especially in financial services, selling IT services to competitors faces hurdles.

- Track record: While some captives have spun out, been divested, or offered limited shared services/excess capacity, large-scale “GCC becomes a rival IT vendor to industry peers” remains uncommon. The bigger near-term impact is insourcing-work that previously went to third-party IT firms moves inside the GCC.

How both sides adapt will define the next chapter of India’s technology story.

What’s your view - more complementarity or rising competitive overlap?

quoted_text:
The new Tesla Roadster literally sucks itself to the road.

Tesla says fans underneath the car pulls air out from beneath it, creating a low-pressure area that holds it against the surface with the system generating up to 2 g’s of suction, enough to hold the car upside down.

That same system presses the tires harder against the road, giving them more grip for acceleration, braking, and cornering. Unlike conventional aero, which relies on speed to build downforce, the fans can create that extra grip even at low speeds.

Bro… that means cornering beyond 2 g’s… The Roadster can adjusts its aero as its speed changes, with a variable-pitch rear wing and both high-downforce and low-drag modes.

Elon described the feeling, “You can corner like it looks like you’re breaking physics bc the car sticks to the ground so hard… This car could suck the chrome off a trailer hitch.” 

And this is just the system that keeps it ON the road. Add the SpaceX thrusters, and you start to understand why the 0–60 number was never going to tell the whole story.

Tesla and SpaceX are truly pushing what we thought a car could do…

text:
Based on @ramez’s analysis, productivity uplift from AI is 5-10x too low for an RSI loop to avoid hitting diminishing returns. Here are some unstructured thoughts on why I think RSI is still worrying:

- First, Ramez's post for @Noahpinion was extremely good and the sort of gut-check I'd love to see more of.

- But what’s an order of magnitude between friends? A 5-10x gap may sound large, but in the grand scheme of AI trends a single OOM may as well be a knife edge condition.

- We’re reasoning under imperfect information with a  limited number of publicly disclosed data points, usually pertaining to models several generations behind the internal frontier. Vague-posts about the imminence of RSI from members of technical staff are annoying, but still have information value. Nor are they likely making elementary mistakes like failing to account for nonlinearities.

- There’s also a lot of inherent / Knightian uncertainty about the values of the relevant coefficients and how they interact, e.g. what does it mean for total productivity uplift if the cost of achieving a given level of AI performance continues falling 13x per year? Will swarm scaling laws improve as we get better at training multi-agent systems against parallelizable tasks? Are there additional training axes, like recurrent depth or explorative modeling, that have yet to be discovered or fully scaled? The "deep" parameters of AI progress are in flux, making extrapolations based on historical data subject to a kind of Lucas critique that’s biased to surprise on the upside.

- There’s no world where fully automating AI R&D makes progress go slower. Nor does diminishing returns mean going slow. Rather, it means faster than ever but at a slowing rate of acceleration.

- In particular, diminishing returns forecloses a near-term “foom” scenario wherein acceleration begets ever greater acceleration, ad infinitum. But it's a mistake to conflate RSI with foom in the first place. Moving from a 1.1-1.5x productivity speed-up from AI-assisted R&D to a 3x speed-up under full automation would alone be earth-shaking. If there's another regime after RSI, we'll reach it that much faster.

- RSI could hit diminishing returns because it effectively "picks all the low hanging fruit" by speed-running the AI/ML the tech tree. What surprises are waiting to be discovered? On his MTS livestream Ramez cited the sample efficiency of the human brain as suggestive of substantial head-room for algorithmic improvements. So do we get a one-time, step change improvement in capabilities and efficiency followed by linear improvement thereafter, or does automated R&D stumble into fundamentally new paradigms? Either would be dramatic and suggestive of a trend break, i.e. not something easily modeled as a simple R&D production function calibrated against historical data.

- We've had a few trend breaks in the past. ECI had been growing 6 pts / year before reasoning models boosted the trend to 14 pts / year. How many similarly large trend breaks are left?

- There have been diminishing returns to ML from day one. Yet people who've used that fact to predict diminishing returns in practice have been repeatedly burned by inputs increasing even faster. RSI is like the ur-example of this dynamic. 

- Ramez argues the main bottleneck is new research ideas, which is precisely what automated AI R&D is supposed to buy you. He concedes that OpenAI’s recent proof bomb is evidence that AI is finally getting good at developing novel insights, particularly the proof of the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. But given how early we are in climbing this particular hill (genuine novelty is definitionally a highly sparse reward), we should expect AI’s capacity for original thinking to get a lot better.

- It’s true that progress is fastest in highly verifiable domains like math and coding, but ML theory and engineering are also highly verifiable.

- I suspect task verifiability is mostly a red-herring / category error. The conventional wisdom used to be that AI could master chess because it's a closed-form domain, but then we suddenly got LLMs that mastered extremely squishy domains like natural language and intuitive judgement. The trick is that we didn’t optimize for “have human-like judgement” but rather substituted a hard-to-verify thing with the easier-to-verify task of next token prediction. Similarly, focusing on the ways in which math proofs are easy to verify misses the extent to which the AIs get really good at math by acquiring all kinds of fuzzy, hard-to-verify capabilities in the process (such as research taste or other kinds of mathematical intuition). As with next token prediction, the verifier is just a “hook” for bootstrapping fuzzy intermediate capabilities. The thing-being-verified is thus just the tip of the spear of the things-being-learned.

- The diversity of fuzzy things that can be put into a verifier increases with model capability and task horizon. For example, "run a profitable company" is a highly verifiable task (you either make money or you don't) and a great hook for all kinds of non-verifiable intermediate capabilities, but requires agents to have relatively high baseline capabilities to get working.

- Most takes on RSI, my own included, are extremely heuristical, which is what makes quantitative analyses like Ramez's so valuable. But heuristics have their place, too.

A 5-year-old girl plunged 49 feet from a moving cruise ship into the open ocean. Her father heard his wife screaming and raced toward the railing, only to discover that their daughter was gone.

It happened aboard the Disney Dream near the Bahamas, where a family vacation took a terrifying turn when the little girl fell from the ship’s fourth deck.

When her father realized what had happened, he jumped overboard after her, plunging nearly 50 feet into the ocean. But when he surfaced, he couldn’t see his daughter anywhere.

He began desperately calling out for her, searching the water until he finally heard her calling back. He swam toward her and managed to reach her, but they were still stranded in the open ocean as the massive cruise ship began turning around.

For roughly 20 minutes, he kept his little girl afloat, holding her above the water until a rescue boat finally reached them and brought them back to safety.

Both survived, although the father suffered two fractures in his spine from the fall.

It takes an incredible amount of courage to jump nearly 50 feet into the open ocean, not knowing what awaits you below. But this father didn’t hesitate to put his own life on the line for his little girl. Thank God they both made it home.

Lighter EVM devnet went live today and I think people are sleeping on it. IMO, one of the most bullish things @lighter_xyz has ever shipped.

The big thing: smart contracts can actually read Lighter Core (accounts, balances, positions, orders) and place, modify and cancel orders right on the order book. And the EVM and Core settle to Ethereum together in one ZK proof, built with @axiom_xyz on OpenVM.

So what does that unlock? A lot:

- vaults that run strategies straight on the CLOB
- funding/basis trades and delta-neutral stables built on Lighter perps
- lending that actually understands your Lighter positions
- structured products on top of their binary options (also just launched)

One angle I don't see anyone talking about: if US regulators end up licensing the firms that run markets on a chain instead of the chain itself (literally what Hyperliquid is pitching rn), a programmable layer sitting on top of the book is exactly where a licensed venue would plug in.

The direction's pretty clear: Lighter doesn't just want to be a perp DEX, it wants to be the settlement layer for onchain finance.

text:
A memecoin launch can make plenty of money for early buyers, while leaving later buyers with the losses.

@Moshdottrade is trying to change what those early backers get paid for.

It starts with a “bundle”: a group of early token purchases. Whoever controls that supply can usually sell it into the market.

With Mosh’s standard model, backers pool money to fund the launch, but the purchased tokens and trading cash go into locked vaults. AI agents use those assets to buy and sell within set limits, while backers earn a share of trading fees.

The idea is simple: give early backers a reason to care whether people are still trading the token months later.

Those fees come from traders. Mosh takes a cut too. If activity dries up, there’s less money to share.

The team’s proposed next release builds on this with:

• IBOs
Custom fundraising rounds where teams can choose who joins and offer fee shares or early tokens. Token allocations would be locked or released gradually, so participants can’t immediately sell everything.

• Launch curves
A way to buy or sell a stake in a bundle before it’s fully funded. Each purchase makes the next more expensive. Fees collected during this stage would be paid to funders once the target is reached. An early exit could still mean taking a loss.

• Curators
Investors, startup-support groups, and agencies that help teams find funding and grow, in exchange for a share of fees.

That points to a bigger ambition: helping projects raise money, find supporters, and keep markets functioning after launch day.

For now, the stated focus is @ponsdotfamily and @RobinhoodCrypto Chain. The team wants stronger projects and deeper activity there before expanding to more chains.

$BUN is the demonstration token for this approach.

The team also wants a 1:1 link between BUN and ownership in @uv Labs, the company behind Mosh. That still needs clear, enforceable legal terms before holders can treat it as company ownership.

With all the scams, rugs, and bundles across launches, Mosh is the only technology that makes sense.

NFA. DYOR.

text:
Metric just went public, and it’s already doing ~20% of Robinhood stock-token DEX volume today, with close to $2M of liquidity sitting in its pools.

Metric isn’t a traditional AMM. It’s the infra layer for active AMMs, PropAMMs included. Easiest mental model: the Morpho of DEXs. Here is how it's structured:

1️⃣ Public or private pool?
🔹 Public: join as an LP, or run the pool as a curator. Carcosa is the largest verified curator right now
🔹 Private: usually a market maker trading its own capital. Pair it with your own pricing logic and you’ve got a PropAMM

2️⃣ How does the pool price?
🔹 Oracles like Chainlink or Pyth
🔹 Your own proprietary price logic

The big LP pain point has always been re-adjusting your range every time price moves. Metric removes that. You set your liquidity bin once and it follows the reference price.

3️⃣ Plug in up to 7 extensions per pool (think Uniswap v4 hooks)
🔹 Deposit allowlist
🔹 Trading-hours limits
🔹 Points system
🔹 Priority fee cap
🔹 Velocity Guard against oracle manipulation
🔹 Stop Loss to cap LVR losses

Each one is another lever for LP protection and profitability.

4️⃣ Set the economics. There are 3 fees
🔹 Half-spread fees, split between LPs, the curator and Metric

text:
Something I keep thinking about as I constantly revisit our thesis and incentives structure.

ve(3,3) DEXs are very hard to differentiate so require a lot of reading. Basically, they pay LPs in the native token, then give people a reason to lock with 100% swap fee distribition. The difference is what it costs you once you’ve earned. Some designs make you pay to take your rewards. Others make you pay to lock them. 

nest always gives the full value up front to LPs, and locking earns you even more on top, relative to other veDEXs.

Option tokens pay LPs the right to buy the token at a discount. Want liquidity? Pay the strike first. Or lock, which is the free path. That’s a hidden tax on LPs, and the lock rates it produces are coerced. A user who discovers this too late is likely turned off and their TVL will disappear.

Burn-to-lock models go the other way. LPs get the liquid token, but if you want protocol revenue you convert into a locked version, and half of what you put in gets burned. Change your mind later and you redeem at half. So instead of paying to cash out, you pay to buy in. The more you want to commit to the protocol, the more it costs you. That’s complete misalignment. The people buying the token and locking it are taking the most risk on the protocol, and they’re the ones asked to pay the most for it.

And notice who that burn actually serves. When most of the genesis supply was handed out already locked, those holders were never taxed. Everyone who shows up later burns half to join them, and the shrinking supply accrues to whoever already holds the most. It’s the same logic as a rebase, just collected at the exit door instead of every week.

On nest, epoch 1 and epoch 100 get identical terms, and the HYPE Engine actually rewards new locks.

Either way, someone is charging the users for participating.

nest makes everybody happy, perfectly balanced, as @AndreCronjeTech intended it.

On nest, emissions are paid in real NEST tokens. If you want to sell, the yield is 100% realized. There's no options strike or haircut (obfuscation). Want to lock? Lock 1:1, nothing burned, and you get paid more for it. Every week the HYPE Engine buys back HYPE and rewards new locks in the HYPE Engine Vault.

There’s a newer design worth mentioning too. Lock almost the entire supply at genesis, then let large protocol positions and future allocations sit outside the vote. It looks clean and has a good narrative, but dormant voting power is a massive overhang. When it switches on, everyone voting now gets diluted, and nobody can tell you exactly when or how that happens.

On nest, every locked position is already working. The HYPE Engine Vault compounds every reward into more veNEST and collects HYPE bonuses from the HYPE Engine. The ecosystem fund votes incentives toward the key pools across HyperEVM. The assistance fund compounds. The team lock earns our cut of revenue like any other locker. We intentionally designed each position with a specific job, and every one of them is doing that job today.

Strikes and burns are built to slow selling. the @NestExchange model is built for GROWTH. When rewards are fully liquid and locking costs nothing, there’s no friction. LPs show up because they keep everything they earn. Lockers show up because locking pays HYPE. New money shows up because it gets the same terms as everyone who came before. 

Yes, some people sell. That’s the price of not taxing them. But a model that taxes participation caps its own growth, because every tax is a reason not to show up. We’d rather remove those reasons and create demand on the other side.

That’s what I wrote about in The Green Ocean: we stopped competing for liquidity and started manufacturing demand for it. 

And the data backs it up. veNEST has roughly doubled since launch, from 825M to 1.64B. About 86% of NEST is locked, and more than half of all veNEST sits in user positions, with no burn to get in and no strike to get out. 

TVL is still growing to feed veNEST holders. $3.5B in cumulative volume, $3.28M in fees over 47 epochs, $27M TVL. 

Honestly, this is the part I’m most proud of. None of nest’s growth is temporarily propped up. We don’t have centralized exchange deals or ecosystem support behind us. There are no big funds on the cap table, and the largest check we took was $50k (myself included). Our investors are amazing, albeit can be too quiet for my liking sometimes, but they believe in our model and the Hyperliquid vision. Despite what people say about KOLs, nobody is being paid to post/bagwork.

I think every locked NEST and every dollar of TVL is there because someone on Hyperliquid read the mechanism and decided it was worth it. That’s the hardest crowd in crypto to fool, and my bet is once you win their liquidity it is very sticky.

Hyperliquid won by giving value to its users instead of extracting it. That’s what inspired nest. @chameleon_jeff set the tone at the top. Distribute everything. Make LPing competitive and locking a reward. Anchor it all to HYPE.

Build a token with real demand.

author: NVIDIAAI
quoted_text:
Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an 816B (42B active) open-weights model that scores 39 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, making it the #1 US open-weights model

Muse Spark Open (xhigh) scores 22 points above Muse Glimmer (high, 17), Meta's 30B dense open-weights model from August. It is also ahead of NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (26), the next highest-scoring US open-weights model, which launched today

@AIatMeta shared access with us ahead of public release for benchmarking. Congratulations to @AIatMeta, @finkd, and @alexandr_wang on the release!

Key Takeaways:

➤ Open weights at the level of Meta's August flagship. Muse Spark Open scores within a point of Muse Spark 1.2 (xhigh, 40). It is stronger on AutomationBench-AA and has a lower hallucination rate, but weaker on GDPval-AA v2.1, CritPt and AA-Omniscience accuracy. Within Meta's current lineup, it sits 13 points behind Muse Wonder (max, 52) and 17 points behind Muse Wonder Full (max, 56)

➤ Token-efficient, at a moderate cost per task. Muse Spark Open uses 40k output tokens per Intelligence Index task, the fewest among the nine highest-scoring open-weights models: e.g. 16% fewer than Muse Spark 1.2 (xhigh, 48k) and 43% fewer than GLM-5.3 (max, 71k), its closest Chinese peer by size. Together AI, Fireworks and Baseten offer it at launch for $1.25/$4.25 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.15 cached input). At that pricing it costs $0.84 per Intelligence Index task. That is less than Muse Spark 1.2 ($0.97) at the same per-token prices and less than half of GLM-5.3 (max, $2.01), but about three times DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, $0.27)

➤ A relative weakness in agentic work compared to Chinese open-weights leaders. Among the nine highest-scoring open-weights models, Muse Spark Open ranks last on the four agentic evaluations in the index but fourth on the other six combined, and it leads all open-weights models on AA-Omniscience (25). GLM-5.3 (max), the closest Chinese model by size, owes all of its 6-point lead to the agentic evaluations

➤ Self-hostable on a single node, or two Mac Studios. BF16 weights are ~1.6TB. Meta's NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the 256 experts, cutting the weights to ~530GB. Meta says this runs on four Blackwell Ultra GPUs or eight H200s, or on two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios using MLX. The architecture uses 62 layers with grouped-query attention (16 KV heads), 8 of 256 experts active per token, and a 1.8B-parameter Perception Encoder for vision

Other model details:

➤ Parameters: 816B total, 42B active (MoE)

➤ Context window: 1M tokens

➤ License: Muse Model License, a custom license that requires "Built with Muse Spark Open" attribution and a separate agreement with Meta for Model-as-a-Service businesses with over $20M in annual revenue

➤ Input modalities: text, image, video and audio. Output: text

➤ Availability: weights on Hugging Face (BF16 and NVFP4), with API access via Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI

quoted_text:
Metric just went public, and it’s already doing ~20% of Robinhood stock-token DEX volume today, with close to $2M of liquidity sitting in its pools.

Metric isn’t a traditional AMM. It’s the infra layer for active AMMs, PropAMMs included. Easiest mental model: the Morpho of DEXs. Here is how it's structured:

1️⃣ Public or private pool?
🔹 Public: join as an LP, or run the pool as a curator. Carcosa is the largest verified curator right now
🔹 Private: usually a market maker trading its own capital. Pair it with your own pricing logic and you’ve got a PropAMM

2️⃣ How does the pool price?
🔹 Oracles like Chainlink or Pyth
🔹 Your own proprietary price logic

The big LP pain point has always been re-adjusting your range every time price moves. Metric removes that. You set your liquidity bin once and it follows the reference price.

3️⃣ Plug in up to 7 extensions per pool (think Uniswap v4 hooks)
🔹 Deposit allowlist
🔹 Trading-hours limits
🔹 Points system
🔹 Priority fee cap
🔹 Velocity Guard against oracle manipulation
🔹 Stop Loss to cap LVR losses

Each one is another lever for LP protection and profitability.

4️⃣ Set the economics. There are 3 fees
🔹 Half-spread fees, split between LPs, the curator and Metric
🔹 Bin fees, split the same way
🔹 Notional fees, off by default, paid to Metric

LPs never claim anything. Fees compound straight into your position.

There’s a lot more under the hood. If people want it, I’ll do a deeper teardown in a future article.

The good news is, losing everything was a good thing for me because my rich dad taught me….going from rich to poor can be a great teacher….if one learns from the mistake, turns the mistake into a life lesson, and grows more financially intelligent versus more financially bitter.

Humans were designed to make mistakes, learn, and grow smarter.

Liquid AI has released d1-ultra, taking the #1 position on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0, supported by a reduction in hallucinations

d1-ultra is the new decision model from @liquidai and follows on from their release of d1 earlier this month. It is priced at $0.042 per 1M input tokens compared to $0.02 per 1M input tokens for d1. Like d1, d1-ultra is billed only on input tokens.

➤ d1-ultra leads the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0 with a score of 65: d1-ultra scores 65, ahead of the recently released Jev 1.14 at 57 and GLiDE and Microsoft-Decision-1 at 54

➤ d1-ultra offers comparable pricing to other decision models at $32 per 1M tasks: At $32 per 1M tasks, d1-ultra is comparably priced to Celeris-1 Decision ($32 per 1M tasks) and Microsoft-Decision-1 ($31 per 1M tasks), more than double the price of d1 and Mercury Decide at $15 per 1M tasks but less than half the price of GPT-6 Luna (Decisions) at $79 per 1M tasks

text:
The new XPRIZE on Interspecies Communication, with a $10M purse will launch next month.

It will challenge teams to demonstrate ethical, verified two-way communication with wild animals, advancing coexistence and cooperation.

Dr. Irene Pepperberg spoke to us today about her pioneering work with grey parrots, training them in English to perform many tasks at 6-year old human skill level.

“Clearly, animals know more than we think and think a great deal more than we know.”

It wasn’t easy when she started. The feedback to her first grant review: “what are you smoking?”

And now, her parrots ask questions and learn from the answers. They ask for what they want.

She has taught her parrots 100 English labels for objects and materials, exact quantities up to 8 (and addition and subtraction), colors, shapes, materials, concepts like same/different, absence, a zero-like concept (absence of a set, on his own, with no training), relative size comparisons, optical illusions, and they make new word combinations (calling the banana chip “banacker” for a banana cracker).  They have a visual working memory (tracking moving cups) that beats adults with 4 swaps.  They do inference by exclusion (when you show where food is not located, they figure out where it is).

Bird brains look very different at first, a smooth unfolded organ with no cerebral cortex, but further research found a relatively large cortical area similar to non-human primates in relative size and connectivity.  They have a dense processor, doing same thing as human children.

“Bird brain should be a complement,” she concluded.
author: shivani_3000
quoted_text:
We can imagine the marvel of first contact, whether alien or AI, and it starts with communication.

We can practice with the isolated animal intelligences all around us.  We hosted a gathering for the leadership of the Earth Species Project, with an ambitious plan to do just that, using multimodal AI models.

“Everything that can be translated will be, by 2030.”— @Aza Raskin of ESP, and:

“It’s impossible without scale and inevitable with scale.” (of data and compute)

“We will face the unusual situation where our AI will communicate with animals before we understand what they are saying.”

“Human languages have evolved over a couple hundred thousand years.  Whale and dolphin language has evolved over 34 million years.  And some are multilingual, using a third language when hunting together off the coast of Norway.”

“Beluga whales announce themselves with their unique name and clan ID. Parrots teach each of their chicks their name in the nest—a lifelong signature that connects them to their family and community.”

“And there are different cultures. The is a fascinating community of crows in Spain that operate unlike other crows.  They raise their young as a group, like a kibbutz.  They have a unique dialect for collaborative parenting.  When an outside crow joins the group, it learns the dialect and participates in the unique culture.  The crows have different personalities and there is a lot of drama. There is one adult that none of the other mothers like.  She has to zip in and out quickly to feed the young before being chased off by the others.”

“Humpback whale songs go viral.  There is group of whales off Australia that are like the K-pop singers.  Their songs propagate globally over a couple years."

"An orca once wore a salmon hat, and it became a fashion trend among orcas.”

“80% of animal communication is relatively quiet one-to-one communication, and we need to capture that.  It’s a perception problem. Of the animal recordings made, only 3% of the data have been analyzed. There has been little progress in orca communications in the past 20 years.”

“Many indigenous myths start with communication with the animals and nature. And then we forget how. We became disconnected.”

Jev过后，强烈建议大家狠狠关注这个刚发布的大模型Glimpse，成功帮助我在小王子游戏开发和维护阶段大幅提高bug排查效率，绝对的vibe coding开发验收神器！！

该模型由Elorian AI（@ElorianAI）打造，主打视觉理解与推理，这意味着其能最原生、最直接的理解图片和视频中各元素的位置、结构与空间关系，并以此来分析问题

这次我有幸提前拿到了 Glimpse 的内测机会。结合当下的场景，我第一时间就想到用它来检查小王子游戏中的各种潜在 bug：只要提供实际游玩的录屏，Glimpse 就能根据画面判断游戏设计是否合理，并为我梳理出各类潜在bug

这极大程度地解决了我在开发维护阶段「验收容易遗漏」的痛点

因为一直是我一个人测试游戏，难免会漏掉一些 bug；而且我在实践中发现，就算用 Astra、Opus 做验收审查，也总有部分细节问题难以发现

而 Glimpse 凭借超强的视觉推理能力，基本能一次捕获录屏中绝大部分细节问题，并按视频时间戳清晰罗列出来，方便我逐一核验

下面视频中，我也用酒馆章节的实机画面做了实测，效果真的惊艳！

在没有任何游戏上下文的情况下，Glimpse 梳理出的bug问题是 Astra 的 3 倍。更实用的是，点击时间戳就能在右侧直接跳到对应画面查看

Glimpse现在也开放了API，我们完全可以将其接入Codex、CC来完善开发后的验收审查流程

当然，除了 vibe coding 验收，我认为 Glimpse 还非常适合视频生成、图片生成等视觉相关的场景：借助强大的多模态理解能力，帮助规范和约束提示词，降低 AIGC 视频和图片生成的抽卡概率！从商业角度看，完全值得大家关注起来！！

author: DanielMiessler
quoted_text:
Why are you still using pull requests?

Is it for code review?

If so, do you really think your or your colleagues catch bugs and mistakes that an Opus 5.5 or Fable or Astra won't find? You can literally spawn all three of them and have them check four times each.

(Also, don't tell me you don't have a "stamp plz" Slack channel or group chat somewhere.)

Is it for knowledge sharing?

Surely there's better ways for that now than the PR, no? We have models that can generate explainer videos, presentations, podcasts, games, quizzes, walkthroughs, ... for any piece of code it can reach. 

Is CI the reason?

Well ackshually, CI means continuous integration and its original meaning is the *opposite* of having long-lived branches and PRs.

But, leaving that aside, your agents are hopefully already running the tests before they push something, and hopefully they can run as long as they want and don't block you so they can run the whole test suite and generate "irrefutable proof" and end-to-end demo videos and so on... And so they run the tests and confirm and then you push to a branch and everything runs again and then you merge and then it runs again? That doesn't make sense, does it?

Maybe you work in open source and you accept contributions, in which case I can't speak to the value of pull requests. It's been 2 years since my last OSS contribution. But from what I heard, the time of the PR is coming to an end in OSS too?

I honestly don't get why people still stick to PRs.

With agents you can now move 10x faster, you can finally do real continuous integration, and get more confidence in the changes the agent made.

Don't slow yourself down by having all the changes pile up in a PR.

We've been thinking a lot about how to grow the Pumpfun app to 10 million users in the fastest way possible.

After dedicating significant resources to building the most performant product in the market and introducing crypto’s most novel rewards system in callout rewards, the answer was obvious: reward the community who help us grow the Pumpfun App.

Introducing referrals and allowing the Callout Rewards pot to organically grow via a platform fee fixes this.

The issue with our prior approach was that users wouldn’t necessarily be able to capture the upside in the network’s growth. text:
The next wave of crypto apps this cycle will be "money games" similar to Papertrade et al

New kinds of contracts and synthetics that offer conditional payoff matrices based on different behaviors or environmental triggers

Papertrade primarily orients around the price of Bitcoin/ETH, because it offers a persistent stream of bidirectional flow. Every great market needs two sides who actively disagree enough to put money on it. These environmental signals already attract so much attention from this userbase, and so it's easier to build on them than search for new ones.

Nonetheless it still feels like we're extremely early here. These new products will likely use the same pooled counterparty structure that makes perp liquidity better than options, and winning products will need to decentralize quickly via smart contracts to avoid regulatory overhang and user trust concerns.

These products will thrive precisely because they will level the playing field between retail and pro's, who will both be ~equally naive in their pricing of various outcomes in the payoff matrix. 

Retail wants to play games they can feasibly win, which means great money games companies will need to be extremely good at constructing creative (and genuinely unique) payoff matrices on a regular basis. 

My sense is that through this explosion of new money games, we will end up with 2-3 new contract formats that are extremely well designed for specific types of environmental signals - ie contracts that work well for high variance data feeds vs low variance etc etc. 

This is basically what is happening to perps as we speak. Because crypto tokens suffer from so much upward and downward reflexivity, perps become preferred over options by simplifying the contract for traders who can't reason about the specific date/price targets they expect. Perps allow you to be directionally correct, which is useful for trading price feeds where the error bands on forecasts are wider than in options-dominated markets. 

As more and more information feeds get brought online and made publicly available for agentic consumption, I expect we see new kinds of markets and money games forming around many of them.

Enjoy the show!

quoted_text:
Anthropic 发了一篇很好玩的文章。NIST P-256 这些椭圆曲线的 seed 到底是怎么来的，密码学圈猜了二十多年，结果 Claude 不到半小时就算出来了。答案是用 Unix 时间戳初始化 C 库自带的随机数生成器跑出来的。更好玩的是它算出来之后的第一反应，居然是怀疑自己是不是在测试环境里。

2000 年 NIST 把这几条曲线写进 ECDSA 标准，曲线的系数由一个 seed 哈希得到，而 seed 是 NSA 给的，没有任何说明。所以一直有人怀疑里面藏了后门，Filippo Valsorda 还专门挂了悬赏。唯一的线索来自 NSA 的 Jerry Solinas，他说 seed 好像是一句玩笑话的哈希，类似 Give Bob and Jerry a raise，但细节他自己也记不清了。他 2023 年去世之后，这事基本就没人能问了。

Anthropic 有好几个员工照着这条线索找过，都没找到，因为线索本身就是错的。这次有人直接问内部的研究模型能不能查出来，也没提这条线索。Claude 换了个思路，去猜 90 年代生成曲线的程序是怎么写的，判断它大概用了当时 C 库自带的 PRNG。这种老 PRNG 很弱，输出能被认出来。

它先注意到 4 个 binary 曲线的 seed 按 32 位切开后，每一段的最高位都是 0。这正是 lrand48 的特征。lrand48 每次只输出 48 位内部状态里的高 31 位，所以最高位永远是 0。剩下 17 位直接暴力枚举，内部状态就恢复出来了。prime 曲线的 seed 每次只取 lrand48 输出的一个字节，能看到的位更少，就当成格问题用 LLL 解出来。

lrand48 往回推跟往前推一样容易。Claude 把状态一路倒推回 srand48 刚初始化时的样子。NIST 和 ANSI X9.62 里一共 10 个 prime 曲线 seed，初始值全是 1997 年 5 月到 1998 年 4 月之间的 Unix 时间戳。比如 P-256，就是从 1997-08-16 01:52:34（UTC）开始跑，取的第 1842 个候选。

4 条 binary 曲线更好笑，倒推出来的时间是 1984 年 2 月。把时间戳乘以 2，就变成 1998 年 4 月 17 日，刚好在 P-224 那次运行的两周后。所以当年的程序很可能是先把时间除以 2，再拿去当种子。

我觉得最有意思的是 Claude 接下来的思考。它先是很激动，觉得自己解开了一个 25 年的悬案，然后马上停下来怀疑，自己是不是在某种模拟或测试环境里。

于是它开始找证据。算出来的 seed 跟它记忆里的真实值对得上，在它的知识里这个悬赏一直没人解开。而且 20 个最高位全是 0 这种事，碰巧发生的概率大概百万分之一。到这里它才确认这是真实世界，说了句哇，这是真的发现。

然后它又怀疑了一次，这么明显的东西 25 年都没人发现，是不是有点可疑？最后还是靠直接计算说服了自己。一个 32 位的时间戳加一个很小的序号，就能完整算出 160 位的 seed。10 条曲线全部对上，不可能是巧合。

这件事对 ECDSA 的安全性没有影响，反而让后门的说法可信度低了很多。seed 就是普通随机数生成器拿时钟初始化跑出来的，现在谁都能复现，能动手脚的空间很小。悬赏的 36864 美元会捐给 Let’s Encrypt 背后的 ISRG。

原文还附了能直接复现所有 seed 的 Python 代码，感兴趣可以自己跑一下

"There'd be times I'd watch him go into demon mode. I'd be sitting at dinner at a restaurant in Austin and Grimes would be next to me, and she'd say, 'Oh, demon mode's about to come.'"

Harness durability in https://t.co/OL0LzGtvAw.

The same 𝚌𝚛𝚎𝚊𝚝𝚎𝙵𝚡𝙰𝚐𝚎𝚗𝚝() is now *durable* on your laptop or in the cloud, via files, Postgres, or Vercel Workflows. Node.js or Bun.

Agents need long-running compute. But they also need to tolerate restarts, redeploys, timeouts, crashes…

Concretely, if a user sends a prompt and then throws their phone into a black hole, we ensure that turn runs to completion. If the process crashes mid-tool-call, it resumes from there.

To this end, 𝚕𝚒𝚋𝚏𝚡 introduces a simple durability adapter API. On Vercel, it leverages all the infra we built for durable workflows and queues, giving you reliability with 1LOC.

This is a critical aspect of production-grade agents (and something all @eve agents also get out of the box). Next, we'll show you how we bring the same durability to Pi, OpenCode, and even your own custom harnesses.
